glitter, said -the river, I glitter in the sun, From dawn of dewy morning Until the day be done. From man's sowing to his reaping, From his toiling to his sleeping, I whisper to the weary', By the way. I strew my jewels lightly, As I pierce themeadows brightly, I glitter, glitter, glitter, Day by day. I carol, said the song bird,

I carol as I rise From the gates of clanging labour To the stillness of the skies. , As I woo the human spirit My rapture to inherit, • I drop my consolation On earth's throng. While human tears are falling, My burden not recalling. I shame the Laing death-knell By my song. We gird the earth with laughter, The children cried in mirth. We pray your cease from sorrow, 0 careful ones of earth! Where the anguish sore is pressing Shall our love come with caressing, And steal away the sharpness From the'thorn ! The whisper of the river, And voice of birds for ever, Forbid your lamentations, Morn by morn! CLARA TRWATTES.

superstructure on. A man may learn infidelity frcm books and from men, but never from nature. What the moral army needs just now is more rank and file and fewer brigadier-generals. Hair, as an article of commerce, varies greatly in price. Gray, golden. and auburn are the most valuable colours. The value of hair increases very rapidly in proportion to its length. Thus, while eight-inch hair sells at about a shilling an ounce, hair thirty-six inches long realises as much as thirty shillings an ounce, and all lengths beyond this command fancy prices. The light colours are furnished chiefly by Germany and Austria, and the south of France stipplies the darker shades in greatest abun- dance. A PRIVATE WORD OF ADVICE.—Why are some good people never able to get on with other good people? Evi- dently one or both parties have an obscure corner or two to clean. Along with sterling virtues, and many _ good qualities, they may be too self-willed, opinionatea, or have some unpleasant odd cranks and twists, or may- be they are what the Scotch call "pernickety," too par- ticular, having one or more small disagreeable ways, and bothersome little formal rules of life, which are as un- alterable as the laws of the Medes and Persians—things which are no great harm in themselves, but which are a great bore to those who have to put up with them, and especially to those who have to serve them. I believe if they had to stand the same thing from others they would find, it about as irksome as wearing a strait jacket. "Oh, well," you say, "of course it isn't nice among our acquaintances; but aren't servants hired to do our work?" Certainly, but they are not hired to put up with your irritating peculiarities as well. Try to put yourself in their place, and how would it feel to meekly bear it all? Remember, "as ye would that others should do unto you, do ye even so to them." That is the rule, and in its application the Bible draws no line where to stop; it includes all. By walking in an atmo- sphere of Christian politeness, instead of keeping our- selves and others in hot water, we shall find that with few exceptions we can get on smoothly with others: 2 for. "with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again."—The Quiver. UNIBRELLAs.—I hardly know any article among a man's (or woman's) belongings thatmore readily helps you to get: to his (or her) character, and I think if ever I choose a wife it should be by that crucial test; its ex- pression, if I may use the word, is the reflex of its owner's personality. We can't help feeling that the pos- sessor of a discoloured green gingham, with a pale yellow border, the ribs bulging, the points all at loggerheads with each other, tied round the waist with a piece of string, something after the "Paul Pry "type, must be of a different character from the bearer of a neat, trim, bright silk one, so accurately wossnd round the stick it might almost pass for a cane, and buttoned with such a precision that you can hardly tell it has a waist. The stick of an umbrella, and notably the handle—oh, ,Tes, the handle—the "figure-head," if I may so call it, has likewise its story to tell, and tells it very intelligibly. Not that the people who carry umbrellas design these handles, but they select them, and very often after their own image. There is the plain, sensible, straightforward, hooked handle, useful to lean upon handy to hold, convenient to bang up; nothing whimsical or capricious about it. The man who chooses that knows the serious side of life, he has a calling or a business to attend to, and doesn't want to be bothered with any needier preoccupations; he buys an umbrella simply to keep his hat and coat, and perhaps also himself, dry; he doesn't go in for taste and fashion, and lie is not particular, so that the stick and handle of his umbrella are in one piece and the hoot a strong and tenacious one. The varieties in umbrella handles nowadays are endless—endless as the human types who purchase them—i/ y en a pour toes lee Wits. The subject is one that has become too vast for discus- sion; nevertheless, to treat it broadly, we may recognise the sour, crabbed, prim, and highly-proper female pro- prietress of that umbrella, the severity of whose handle testifies to its congeniality with the hand that holds it, just as we know at first sight the jolly, genial, open- hearted old fellow who grasps that large, smooth, ivory knob, without a crease or a crevice in its clear, round, honest, bald surface 7 no arriere pewit, no double-dealing there.—De Omnibus Rebus. MIMICRY IN TROPICAL AFRICA.—A NATURALIST DE- CEITED.—The pitch ;of intricate perfection to which mimicry has attained in an undisturbed and unglaciated country like Central Africa is so marvellous and incredi- ble, that one almost hesitates to utter what his eyes have seen. Before going to Africa I was of course familiar with the accounts of mimetic insects to be found in the works of Bates, Belt, Wallace, and other naturalists, but no description prepares one in the least for the surprise which awaits him when first he en- counters these species in nature. My introduction to them occurred on the borders of Lake Shirwa—one of the smaller and less known of the great African lakes— and I shall record the incident exactly as I find it in my notes. I had stopped one day among some tall, dry grass to mark a reading of the aneroid, when one of my • 'men suddenly shouted " Chirombo !" " Chirombos* means an inedible beast of any kind, and I turned round to aee where the animal was. The native pointed straight at myself. I could see nothing, but he ap- proached, and pointing close to a wisp of hay which had fallen uptsn my coat, repeated " Chirombo !" Believing that it must be some insect among the hay, I topir it in my fingers, looked over it and told him point there was no " Chirombo " there. He smiled, and pointing win to the hay, exclaimed "Moio !"—" It's alive?" The hay itself was the Chirotnbo. I do not exsggerate when I say that that wisp of hay was no more- like an insect than my aneroid barometer. I had mentally re- solved never to be taken in by any of these mimetic frauds; I was incredulous enough any suspect that the descriptions of Wallace and the others were somewhat highly coloured; but I confess to have been completely stultified- and beaten by the very first mimetic 'form I met. . . .—Good Words. SWOEE PACTS.—Henry Coates, of 11, Cheatham-place, Adelaide-street, in the borough of Kingston-upon-Hull, , railway employe, appeared before Mr. E. Singleton, a Commissioner to Administer Oaths in the Supreme Court ' 6f Judicature, and made oath as follows :—" He affirmed that he had been totally unable to work for a long time, and had been confined to his bed for a considerable period ;- that he had tried various doctors and many reme- dies, but that he grew worse instead of better; that at that time his joints were so swollen that he could not wear boots, and two crutches were hardly sufficient to support him. After having heard of St. Jacobs Oil, he purchased a bottle. In twelve hours he found relief, and persevering in its use, he is now cured of rheumatism, works daily, and can not only walk with case without a stick, but can run; he enthusiastically recommends this great remedy to anyone suffering from any form of rheumatism, as it has notionly dons wonders for him jaut n'any of his Mends."—Hull News.

SITAIMAT IBEANt SIGNS. By Alma-Warm Uncle Batchelor was prevailed upon to relate another story before the hour of separation arrived. Many of the guests had a long way to travel home, and the evening was wearing on apace, so no time was to be lost. He began by saying that the thought of baiting his horse at a certain inn suggested a story cif a sign. , When a youngster I was much interested in the study of signs..l do not allude to those abstract and intangible things which politicians call "the signs of the times," but to the veritable signs which everybody may run and read, and,which generally supply the nomenclature of public-houses. But I did not care much about heraldic signs, such as the "Fitz-fooslem's Arms," or for emblematical signs such as "The Legs of Man," or "The Rose and Thistle ;" but my 'delight was in signs zoological, from •` The Red Lipn "down to "The Grey Cat.' / think nearly every quadruped in the animal king- dom is represented on some sign or other, but there are also some depicted which Natural History seems to ignore, such as dragons and griffins, and I remember that my curiosity was much exercised in regard to those fabulous or mythological creatures. I was glad to know, however, that the tame and domestic animals were in the majority in our neighbourhood. I can remember a period in the history of our village—that village is now a considerable town—when it boasted of an inn yclept "The Running Pig." True, it was not a very palatial establishment, notwithstanding its aristocratic ensignia. I have a very vivid recollection of "The Running Pig," but I will decant upon the artistic merits of its sign- board, or rather the slab of slate on which the porcine mammal was supposed to be portrayed. Ido not think I was at that time a very competent judge of live pork in a picture, but I did regard the anatomy of that par- ticular pig with wonder. "Mine host" of that long- supplanted hostelry, which adorned a squalid purline of I which this perverse generation knows nothing, was. in I addition to his vocation as a caterer to thirsty silbjects, a purveyor of salt in exchange. for rags and bones. The van in which his merchandise was conveyed was a mar- ket box on wheels, and it was drawn by a large dog, which once deprived me of a portion of my corduroy— I that portio'n on which I had been accustomed to sit. Yes, I remember that " dorg." But I also remember the sign of "The Running Pig" I had the following quotation inscribed upon it in rather uncouth characters : All ye that's dry do not pass by, • But mv good ale come in and y ; • My porter's good, my price is low, So drink a pint before you go. • Now I will not pursue that pig any further. All memory of it would long since have faded from my. mind were it not that, as you know A thing of beauty is a joy for ever. But there was anotheggrotesque sign which most 'of you will know, called "The Load of Mischief." I never Passed that inn at Henfield when an urchin without stopping to gaze at that pictorial puzzle; for a very comical puzzle it was to me. The inn still flourishes under the burden of the name, but the symbolical picture is "faded and gone?' In my schooldays it seemed comparatively fresh, but I had a very hazy and vague idea of the meaning of the sign. I will tell you what that infallible oracle the "oldest inhabitant" once told me about it. When "The Load of Mischief." was built and opened for the accommodation of man and beast, the proprietor Intended to call it "The Rising Sun," and a local limner was engaged to depict the glorious orb of day peeping over the eastern horizon on a signboard almost as large at 3 the door. One fine day, while the sign was reared I against the front of the inn waiting to be suspended from the swing-bracket which was being fixed for it, a i wayfaring man of unpretentious appearance attracted by the knot of admiring villagers which „stood around it, walked.up. "Ah ! here is the work of a.country debater, who, no oubt. imagines himself a Correggio; he muttered, as looked at the picture with the eye of a critic. He nquired of a bystander who had painted it; but the painter, who vras,ln the crowd, overheard the question,' and he proudly announced himself as "the artist," evidently considering his work a elief-d'auttre. • "There is a great deal too much ultramarine in your sky, and you have no perspective," said the strange connoisseur. The painter, with no little surprise at his audacity, replied. " Wha, mon, thad's a graclely blue sky, an' thad gilded sun is prospective." "Yes," said the critic, "your sky is blue—too blue by half!: "Aw're allus done rni sky-signs thad way, an' there's never nooabody fun ony faut afore. Connot yo' see as thad sun is comm' up in a cleon blue sky ?" "Yes, and no painter in his senses would represent a sunrise in a sky of solid blue, and ultramarine too." " Cotifeawnd yore impidence ! Wod done yo' know abeawt artist work? Aw'll latch yo' a brush an' some paint an' yo' shall hey a doo ad mendin' id, aa yo're so clever." So saying he went into the inn and brought out a quantity of painting materials, never dreaming that the stranger could understand their use; but when he asked for a easel to be brought out, the painter began t 6 stare. An easel, however, was fetched, and the sign placed, upon it. Some of the spectators of this little scene thought it exceedingly presumptuous on the part of the strange critic to disparage the skill of their local genius, whom they had always considered a perfect master of his art. " Neaw, Mr. Faultfinder, gad to work." said the dauber, laying a pallette and a mawl-stick before him, together with sundry brushes and colours; "gad to work, bud aw'll watch as tha spoils nowt." I The stranger took up a large brush, and in the twinkling of an eye put out the rising sun! • "Stop! yo're ruinin' thad sign, yo' thick heyd !" frantically exclaimed the poor painter. " Yo've done a peawnd's worth o' damage o'ready." "Be patient," calmly said the critic. "All that I spoilt I'll restore or indemnify." Then, using merely the handle of a pencil or fitch, he sketched,in a masterly manner, the outlines of a man carrying a woman astride his neck, and a monkey sat upon the shoulder of the woman, tugging at her cap, a magpie being perched , upon the head of the monkey. The face of the man I was a striking caricature of the astonished painter, and the spectators, who were at first disposed to resent the interference of the strange critic, now began to applaud vociferously, the "worthy host" himself being the first to shout "Bravo !"and even thepainter's wrath changed to awful admiration, as the magic touches i brought out the details of the picture. 'Ai! aw see neaw," cried the poor sign-dauber. " Yo're nos foo' ad thad craft. Aw see, yro've put' a toathery cleawds th' sky, bud th' rising sun's done for." Just as the stranger artist was giving the picture the finishing touches with pencils and colours, which he produced from his wallet, a gentleman rode up to the , group of admirers, and on seeing the Painting, inquired for the name of the painter, offering fifty guineas. for the sign as it stood. • ' "Oh ! it's my sign," said the interested publican. " This painting isn't to be sowd," said the dauber, who had not painted it. "No," said the landlord. "because it's already sold and partly paid for in advance, but if the gentleman desires to treat for the purchase, I am open to deal with him." " Oppen to deol wi' him, are yo'? Bud id belongs to me yet. Wod does id matter to yo' if a brother gives me a bit of a lift? Yo' other'd a rising sun, an' this isn't one. Id's Ina property, an' id's me earn sell id !" cried the village genius, in expostulatory tones. "You rogue," replied the landlord, "it's painted on my boards, and it's•my sign, an' yo' heyn't painted id. What do you call it, Mestur Artist ?" "I think," replied the real painter of the picture, "you had best call it 'The Load of Mischief" for perhaps the most mischievous things in the world are a woman, a monkey, and a magpie, and they seem to have made mischief here already." "I think," said the gentleman, "we had better go inside and arrange the matter." ' "But suppose, said the genuineartist, "I don't choose to sell."

A woman never reaches middle life; she is :always young until she gets old enough to boast of her age. "What is the best uniform to fight in ?" asked George IV. of a pliant Lifeguardsman. after the battle of Water- loo. "Shirt-sleeves, your Majesty," responded the man. STHE ZEBRA'S COAT ITS PROTECTIO:st—When We look, for instance, at the coat of a zebra with its thunder and lightning pattern of black and white stripes, we should think such a conspicuous object designed to court rather than to elude attention. But the effect in nature is jut the opposite. The black and white somehow take away the sense of a. solid body altogether; the two colours seem to blend into the most inconspicuous gray, and at close quarters the effect is as of bars of light seen through the branches of shrubs. I have found myself in the forest gazing at what I supposed to be a solitary zebra, its presence betrayed by some motion due to my I approach, and suddenly realised that I was surrounded by an entire herd which were all invisible until they I moved.—Good Words.

"Ah ! but you s u .Indlit the way of a poor innkeeper ma. g a bargain. I'll pay yon well for .your job.' "Bud yo' wodn't goa ageeati one o' yor own trade, as 'hes a big little family o childer, wod,lo'?" "Well, come inside," cried the gentleman, "and I'll double my bid for the sign. Bring it inside." Now, as the story goes, the gentleman knew by certain characteristics; obvious to the eyes of a compe- tent connoiseur such as himself, the picture was a ran- domwork of a celebrated but erratic English painter. Some say it was Cox, and others say it was Morland, btt at,any rate the original "Load of Mischief" was bought, and every interested party was compensated and satis- fied. It was, however, stipulated that a copy of it should be taken by a competent artist, to be hung as the sign of the inn. It was said that the original was at the lord of the manor's London residence. This story concluded the post-prandial entertainment at the celebration of Tom o' Giles's twenty-first birthday at 1 ewit Nook. • " When shall we all meet again?"

13T HUGH BBITE. Watching the multitude of weavers in our midst come and go, but never enquiring into the.mysteries of)heir craft, the general impression of the uvinitiated seems to be that if a man wishes to learn to weave all he has to dole to spend a few hours (at nr.r.st) over a loom, to be shown its various parts, thread a shuttle, and then take off his coat and beCome a full-fledged four-loom weaver. I might have had this impression if I hadn't had the conceit knocked out of me by a futile attempt to weave on. this basis. Two weeks of my boyhood were devoted to the savage amusement of being a " tenter " to Mr. Thrums; a veteran four-loom weaver. One week was devoted to a trial (I think trial is the right word to uie here, whether applied to Mr. Thrums or myself), and the other to con- tinuous sentences of punishment. Thrums, I remember wore glasses and had big hands; at least I used to think his hands were big, but I had only the weight of them to judge by, and, of course, I might be Mistaken. He taught me how to "prick a cop,' with the result that about a dozen cops, each left the shape of a worsted ball after a dog had chewed it. Even at this time I , look upon that cop pricking as quite a feat. You watch a weaver do this, and you will think it is the simplest thing thing in the world, but try it. It is only a few weeks since I tried it for the sake of "Auld Lang, Syne," but my right hand had lost its cunning, for I turned that cop inside out before I, recognised that Old Thrums tuition had fallen in "stony places." If you were ever in a fair-sized weaving shed in full work, you would be struck by the absence of that deep. silence common to deserts. I haven't been to the Niagara Falls myself, but if there is any more noise at that place than in a weaving shed, the auricular organsi of Niagara tourists are in danger otheing paralysed. I used to watch Old Thrums' mouth move, but no sound reached me from it, and he was compelled to take one of ray ears between his finger and thumb to create a telephonic connection. When I first we* into the shed, I noticed very particularly a way most of the weavers had of rocking backward and forward with the motion of the loom slay, and catching the slay with one hand every alternate movement it made. This strtick me as being a very amusing pastime, anti I asked Old Thrums why they did it. He shaded his mouth with one hand, and bawled in my ear," Cose thi want," which has left rather an ambiguous impression on my mind to this day. However, I tried that rocking business, but instead of catching the moving slay, my hand dived in amongst the ends. I may be excused for digressing here tojnform those who haven't missed the slay that there is a roller between you and the slay—a most diabolical, prickly roller. As the deceitful slay came back quicker than you could wink one eye, my hand was caught napping against that roller, and the effect obtained, fro it the thumb nail to /the wrist inclusive, was an of a cobbler's rasp painted a bright crimson. Old Thrums boxed npy ears fpr introducing a new pattern heading in his cloth, although it was intro- duced at the expense of my blood. With the help of a little Indian ink, tattooing might be done quickly and effectively by the above process. Old Thrums' greatest objection however, seemed to be against my studying the theoretical part of the busi- ness. Poe instance, I conjectured in my mind that it one shuttle did so much work two shuttles were bound to do double. With a view to attaining this object, I put two shuttles in a loom at once, one at each end, and started it. I don't know whether it is customary for shuttles so placed to-rise up in the middle like two game cocks or not, but at this trial they did, making a space for their exit by breaking a few score of ends, which .01d Thrums called a "mash." There ought to have been medals struck in honour of Old Thrums piecing up that mash. Perhaps I ought to say "mashes," for, rightly speaking, there had been two when Old Thrums had done with me. lam not surprised at the cockney who was going through one of our weaving sheds for the first time,. and saw a." mash" of -this sort, when he remarked, "Good heavens! is it all spoiled ? ' meaning all the material about the loom. At a time like this, theoretical weavers may appreciate ' he skill required to keep a few looms from getting trong side up. It is also the time when the " masher ' feels as if he would like' to hide in a weft skip if his. fighting weight is under eleven stone, i.e., if there is a man about of the nature of Old Thrums. There is a very interesting thing known to' weavers as a "float," which consists of a *sore place in the cloth. The first really decent float that I remember was about two inches wide. I watched it weave down with a keen interest, and wondering whether it Would get wider or narrower, or whether it would weave itself right; but, as usual, in the most interesting pertions of the work Old Thrums interrupted my speculations by stopping the loom with one hand, and making me cough with the other. He was even unfeeling enough to make a remark about my being a " gaumless foo " and added , that I should "never mak' a weiver " if I lived to be "as owd as Methooslum." A female weaver who worked next to Oid Thrums remarked, after she had examined the float, but while looking at me, that "it owt to be punched eawt o' t' shop," which I thought did not exhibit much (.1 that tenderness supposed to emanate from the female heart. When anything of this sort occurred, Old Thrums commenced opening and shutting his mouth, and rolling his eyes in a dreadful manner towards the main portion of the shed, as if he was making faces for a wager, and immediately a host of fierce eyes darted revengefuliouks upon me from all quarters. This is a system of telegraphing little known at the Post Office, but well understood in the weaving shed, where the vibration of the human voice carries about two inches. The reason I quitted this interesting occupation was very peculiar, in fact, mysterious. Old Thrums had just returned from a visit to a man whom he called " tle cutlooker," when he suddenly told me ,to put my coat on and go home, and that he would send for me when he wanted me; but as I have been in different parts of the world since then, he may have sent for me when I wasn't in; anyway, I haven't seen him since. I don't want to calumniate Old Thrums, as he may be dead, but he is certainly responsible for the technical baldness of this paper. At some future time I propose to enter into disquisition of that most ancient of weavers, the spider ;• the nuMbers of the weft he uses; the amount a China clay he puts in, and the way he threads his shuttle.

Sr. HELENS V. MonscAmnE.---This match was played at St. .Helens on Saturday. Owitig, to the disappointment occasioned by the non-appearance of a team a few, weeks ago, the St. Helens Club had the "gate" free, and there was a very large attendance.sThe around 'was not fit for football, being.very hard: The; visitors came with a good team and were fortunatejn scoring a drop goal in the first lialf to the home team 'S flVe minors, the Saints having the best of the game. In the second half, More- cambe' scored a lucky try, St. Helens having repeated hard lines, being robbed of a try by the spectators ea- eroaching over the touch line. The match ended in favour of Morecambe by onfi goal, one try, and two minors to six minors, • • lASSOCIATWI(RULES. DENTON v. EARLESTOWN.—This match was played at Denton on Saturday. Earles- town, by grand pass.sing; • scored, and Denton equalised shortly afterwards., . At half-time the score was one goal each. No further score was added during the second half, the game thus ending in a drew. ' Catsrnft COI:LEOE,V. A special meeting of the committed •of the Wigan and District Football Association was held at Wigan on Wednesday night, to consider protests against the Larks- town and Haydock clubs in reference to the con,petition for the challenge cup. There was a good h attendance, Mr. J. Green (Westhoughton) presiding. Representa- tives were present from the following clubs :—Wigan, Westhoughton, Earlestown, Haydock, Adlingtem,Springs Branch, Haydock St. James's, Ashton-in-Makerfield, A;litchti Association, Park-lane, and Wigan St. Paul's. In the 3rd round of the cuphcontest Earlestown (last year's winners and present holders) threw out Adlington by five goals to none, and Haydock beat Westhoughton by four goals to _three. Roth Adlington and West- houghton protested against their opponents, how- ever. !on the ground that as they took " part in the Haydoek Park sports last August they had come underl the rules relating to professionals. The protests in each' case were taken under Rule 5. which reads— "Any club competing for any prize offered by any private individual or individuals unless the nett proceeds go to some football club or clubs charity or charities, shall cease to be ipembers of this Association.;" and also undei Rule 16, the latter portion of which reads as fol- lows—" Players competing for any money prize in foot- ball bOntests shall be considered professionals." The committee discussed the question at considerable length, and ultimately decided—though not unanimously—that both Rarlestown (cupholders) and Haydock should be thrown out of the present season's competition. This decision will affect several cubs mthe Association, and the ultimate outcome is a matter of ,conjecture. The decision has occasioned considerable dcitemenp in foot- ball circles, as every player who took part in the football dontestsat the Haydock Park ports is thereby made into a professional.

N9TES BY THE 'WAY. WEST LANCANHIRB CUP.—WIDNES V. ASPTILL.—Great interest is centred in the meeting of these clubs at Widnes *to-day in the first tie of the West Lancashire Cup, and the committee of the local club are making pre- parations for a monstre attendance of spectators. It is generally anticipated that the winner will have a most rosy chance of winning the cup' outright. As is well •knoWn Ascaill are the present holders of the trophy, but the iocal' club are nevertheless favourites for to-day's contest Last time the clubs met, abciut a; month ago, the "Chemicals "literally ran away with the "colliers," and piled up a most heavy score, but since that date Aspull have wonderfully improved their form, and did a good performance a fortnight ago by defeating Leeds Parish Church. That to-days match will be hard fought is certain, and the following team will worthily repre- sent Widnes :—S. Bingham, back; E. Farrell, J. Parkin- son, and F. Pluimpton, three quarters *,• R. Barker and T. Wilkinson, half backs; W. Kiddie, G. Woods, W. I3ar- ber, J. Hardman, J. Bingham, y. Hughes, J. Gandy, T. Pennington, arid J. H. Smith (captain), forwards. The unsettled wintry weather of the past few weeks has considerably interfered with the Rugby matches in St. Helens,. and there has scarcely been a contest worth mentioning. Last Saturday the St. Helens Club had a free match to recompense their supporters for a disap- pointment they experienced 4 few weeks ago. . Their op- ponents were Morecambe, and the latter were lucky to secure the verdict in the scores at the close. The St. Helens Association and XewtOn-le-Willows played their return match on tile ground of the first named at Cowley Hill-lane' and the home team again won by five goals to one. The last meeting, between the _elu4s resulted in a victory for St. Helens by four goals to two. , • The Haydoek team met Blackpool on the latter's ground, and a grandly contested game, in which the play was more even than the score indicates, re.sulted m a win for Blackpool by three goals to none. Black- pool goalkeeper was largely accountable for this result‘. The Eaflestown Club sent a weak eleven to meet Den- ton at Manchester, and they did a clever thing in making a drawof one goal each. *Latterly the Earlestewn Club has been playing in splendid forte:and if it is'kept up--:- supposing.the protest against them by, Westhoughton is not sustained—their prospects of again winning the Wigan and District Cup, which they at present hold, are very rosy.

The busybody labours without thanks, talks without credit, lives without love, dies without tears, witnout pity—save that some say, "It was a pity he .died no sooner." .7 • • The little one, being a guest of her grandma, had been liberally feasted, when a second dish of .pudding came I on. Looking at the steaming dish, she exclaimed, with a I sigh, "Say, gran'ma, I wish I was twins."

The total Ineinte for the past year has been £497 is 3d, and the expenditure £399 9s 6d. As will be seen by the annexed balance sheet, the amount available for divi- dend is £lOl 14s 'lid; out of which itisproposed to pay a dividend of £2 per cent, carrying forward a balance et £l5 14s ma. It has been considered necessary to expend a further sum in more fully providing against the con- tingency of fire, by means of indiarubber hose pipes fixed in the stage galleries. In.connection with this sub- ject, the shareholders will be glad to learn that the borough surveyor recently expressed himself as tho- roughly satisfied with the structure of the building, and with the arrangements already in force ,for providing , against panic. Three of the directors, Mr. John White, Dr. Mackie, and Mr. William Long retire by rotation. They are eligible for re-election. It will be necessary also Ito appoint an auditor.—The ZnAnkstaii, in moving the adoption of the report, said they would notice ,that the receipts were rather more than those of last year convierably over those ofithe year before. They would notice that in the item " dramatic performances, con- certs, &c." the increase was considerable, whereas every other item showed a decrease. He thought that proved that their action in reference to the re-construction of the stage, and the erection of a proscenium, &c., was a wise one, for without that it was very likely they should not have had sufficient revenue to pay a dividend. 'The hall seemed to have been 'pretty well let, and they could not expect to increase their receitits very materially above what they had last year.—Mr.l Prams remarked that there had been a great loss on the Sunday services.—Alderman CHANDLEY, in second- ing the motion that the report and statement of ac- I counts be adopted, said he could not but express sur- prise that, when they had had such a profitable year as regarded performances, concerts, &c., the dividend was rep greatly disproportionate. He thought the expenses , had been great, and he referred to an item for neWals of scenery, properties for stage, &c." (211 18s Bd.) and insurance kao 12s 6d, —. The CHAIRMAN said the item for insurance was re-N markably low for that class of building, and had been fixed subject to the alteratidns that had been 'made.— Alderman PAVIEB thought the item fot rates and taxes (248 9s sa) might be reduced if a representation was made to the proper authorities.—The SECRETARY said the gross assessment was 2140.—The CHAIRMAN thought that matter might be left to the directors ; they had had that matter up before. He also remarked that that Undertaking had not been gone into with the object of making money, although they decided to conduct it on commercial principles.—The report was then adopted.— It was then agreed on the motion of Alderman Myles, tliat a dividend of £2 per cent should be paid.—With regird to the three retiring directoPk, the CHAIRMAN said he had received a note which stated that "Dr. Mackie's health prevents him taking any part in, any business at present." He was afraid from what he heard,that Dr. Mackie was not in a position to he very useful as a ditecter, and he begged to propose that Mr. John White, Mr: W. Long, and Mr. W. Owen be appointed directors. ' —Alderman Drams seconded this proposal ; which, was agreed to.—Alderman CHANDLEY moved that Alderman Holmes be re-elected audinor, and that the sum of one guinea be paid to him for his services.—Mr. Picroir seconded this proposal, which was agreed to.—On the motion of Mr. PICTON, a vote of thanks to the directors wai passed; arid it was agreed that they should be paid an honorarium of one guinea each —A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

Bud th' poncake bubbled, frothed, un fizzed;: Five minutes flew, un yet id hissed. "Cum Ned!" sed Moses, stur thi fist, • "tdi stummick's eawt o' wark !" Bud Ned dud nowt bud gape un stare, Ut th' bubblin' stuff as steomed i'th' air; Then shook his heyd un sed ,t; It's quare! Bud if wernd set, aw'll burn id.' Ten minutes passed. Then such a -crack 0' laffin' rooase, as th' door swung back, I.Tn in coom Bob's wife, lookin' black, As Moses rooared eawt "Turn id !" Hoo looked at t,h' chaps, ut th' stuff, then t' fire, Then went no further to inquire, I Bud laft, as if hur heart's desire Wur to dee thaer wi' grinnin'. Th' chaps stared. CHAPTER VII. CROSSED IN LOVE. Tom Chi/ton was evidently one of those individuals who are perpetually putting in an appearance at moments when they are by no means wanted. Erratic' restless mortals are apt to do this. • 'Tom Chilton was erratic and restless. Ile had gone to America because he was tired of England; he had returned at the end of two years because he was tired of America; by the same rule, in his daily life he was never still. Under the slightest pretext generally busi- ness he imagined he had to attend to, he would ga off miles when a penny letter would have answered every purpose. That he never lost by this promptness of action, he at least felt very certain, and the fact that his means increased as time progressed would seem to substantiate his statement. Hie quarters, of coursepro tern., are scarcely cheery ones. Men of Tom Chilton's calibre do not go in for luxury, and though it pleases the vanity of the man to be spick-and-span in his attire when in company„ his home surroundings sould tend to shew that he is sorely in want of a good wife. Two grimy ground-floor rooms in a narrow street off the Strand, high tea laid out on the table but scarcely in as picturesque a form as that amphibious meal is sometimes represented I Nothing matches among the crockery, "In these days it is not the fashion for china to match," someone observes, but then there is a wide difference between artistio oddness and the barbarous clashing of colour which the table in Ovid-street presented. True, in revenge, it was laden with viands; more food stood upon it than it would seem 'possible for Tom Chilton to consume in a week, it was evident , that he expected a guest —yes, there were' covers for two. Scarcely a guest either for whom he has the very I greatest respect, for he has taken off his smart clothes and wears a short well-worn smoking coat which had once been red, but now looks as though it had been washed in sea water. In this garment he sits by the open window, a Well: coloured clay pipe in his month. "A quarter to six," he mutters, glancing at an adjacent clock ; "it is time she was here if she ever means to come at all." Shot Can it be possible that if is a woman Toni Chilton is going to receive? It' so, it is very certain that he believes her to be a hungry one. Yes, there she comes bustling down the street, crimsoned-faced and hot-looking, though she has, got out of the omnibus at the corner. She is not young, has no pretensions to being young or prepossessing, or to anything else that would appear an apparent reason for Tom Chilton to have put himself out of the way to invite her to tea. Yet be starts up when he sees her, opens the door for her, takes the bag she carries and sets it on a side table • establishes her in as comfortable an armchair as the room affords, and finally places a foot-stool under feet. All. however, with no avail, if he imagines she will be gracious. She wipes her face over with a half folded handker- chief, with which she finally flops herself, wishing you to believe that the said handkerchief is a fan, and says with some severity, "What a fool you are, Tom; but then, Ler' bless us, you always were a fool." "What have I done now, Aunt Purvis " asks Tom with a sort of mock air of humility. Yes, the gnest Tom Chilton had just received was none other than Mrs. Purvis, Lady Fedora Stanhope's housekeeper ; though by no twisting could the con- necting link between her and Tom be tortured into aunt-ship; yet for so many years now had he called her aunt, he was almost lieginning to think she was one. "Look at that table and say you're not a fool," she answered ; " you'll die in the workhus', Tom, you will, for you waste more than you earn." ",Do I 7" he said, laughing,while his eyes twinkled,' for Tom knew full well that his own requirements were so moderate that he at times dreaded lest he should be accused of some of the parsimonious habits of the old lady he called Aunt Purvis. "It's all in your honour," he went on, . wheeling his chair round- to the table, "so come along, and be cheery. Oat West, where I come from, we alway s give our guest the most and the best-.we can afford.' His genial tone seemed to ;restore her over-balanced equanimity, and she tried to look pleased as she said, "Well, I am a cross-grained old woman, I know; at Least, go Miss Irene is always telling me, but I can't help it, lam that worritted. " Tom did not seem anxious to enter on the subject of Dirs. Purvis's worries,so interrupted at once by saying, "How beautiful Miss Irene is, .qtiite as pretty as she promised to be when a child." • "Why, whenever did you see Miss Irene ? " "At the Wandsworth-station two or three evenings ago, with her brother and Phyllis Knight." . This annonncement.seemed to have very much the same effect as setting a match to a. fuse. All Mrs. Purvis's concentrated, anger blazed np.' "Them Knights," she almost shrieked; "Miss Irene is always with tnem Knights, and Lady:Fedora ought to be ashamed of herself for allowing it; but there, I've said all I can say on the subject ; but if she • don't live to rue the day as she allowed it, my name 'ain't Sarah Purvis, that's all." " Good gracious in what does the danger consist?", "Oil and water, my dear Tom, you can't mix 'em, • can yoM2 No—well no more can you mix these two distinct and different families; it ain't nature. Fancy they Knights being grafted on to the Stanhopes I Simon's a good sort, but he ain't a gent, and don't want to be; he'd do well enough if that silly fool of a wife of his would let him alone; but she's one of they sort who's always for getting up in life, and she never knows when she's atop of the highest hill as her poor little legs will ever climb." Tom Chilton, to whom the jealousy Mrs. Purvis en- tertained for Mrs. Knight was nothing new, began to laugh as he passed a plate of salmon to his so-called kinswoman. "And the young woman, Phyllis," he asked, "is she as stuck up as her mother?" Mts. Purvis paused before she took the plate he offered, and looked at him very straight. "You was once spooney on that gal, Tom; what are your feeline now 1" "I 'think that she, like Miss Irene, has much im proved during the two years I have been away, and I came back fully resolved to ask her to be my wife—. " But what, Tom 2" "She is changed." , "Changed—that is just it—she is changed." Mrs. Purvis was by this time voraciously eating the salmon she had been chiding Tom for providing, and it was between the mouthfuls that she gave him her sentiments on the subject of Phyllis. "A minx—a stuck up minx like her mother—that's what she is. You had best leave her alone, boy. She'll never be a lady though she thinks she will, but she'll never be an honest working man's wife neither. She's spoiled. Simon Knight filled his basket with rotten eggs; but there, if young men will be fools and not see their way straight when it's afore 'em, it's no one's fault but their own." Tom Chilton smiled as Mrs. Purvis thus gave way to her feelings. Ile knew of old the story of how Simon Kbight had jiJted Sarah Purvis—Who, not- withstanding her brevet, rank of mistress, had never married—for pretty Hamel Brown, the miller's daughter, at Warleigh vi.lage. It was almost as much Sarah Purvis 's own fault as Simon's, for in those days when they were young, and Sarah thought herself a dark-eyed beauty, she gave herself great airs, and was not sure that Simon Knight, who bad come down to Warleich to put up some farm buildings for Mr. Stanhope, was good enough for her. She was then the children's nurse, and made much of by Lady Fedora; it was only since they had been too old to require her services that she had been raised to the dignity of housekeeper. Twenty years ago she, thought it very grand to flout the young builder who strove to win her, and nut to acknowledge that sbe loved him, though she did so with her whole heart. . Simon -Knight, however, never had any idea of being played with, and be transferred his attentions and affections to pretty Hannah Brown, whose beauty far exceeded that of Sarah Purvis, but who was by no means so clever and managing a woman. The day that Simon Knight married was as if vinegar had been poured into Sara% Purvis' life, though it was only in later years that she had ac- knowledged her liking foe Simon; there was little doubt, though, that thea vinegar had been steadily working ever since that wedding morning,and atforty- five she was an oldish woman, with a sharp temper and a bit of tongue. If Simon Knight hnd elected to marry Sarah Purvis instead of Hannah at the mill, what a difference it might have made in the lives of the rising generation of the Stanhopes I Ay ; truly the acts of their dependents are frequently the hinges on which great families hang; even the' conversation between Tom Chilton and the crusty housekeeper would have the effect of opening doors which some member of the Stanhope family would perhaps have gladly kept closed. For a minute or two after Mrs. Purvie' outburst, Tom Chilton heaped

'MR things on her plate, and pressed her to eat, with a vulgarity that was quite overpowering, but which apparently delighted Mrs. Purvis, for she actually smiled on Toni, who took advantage of her genial mood to ask suddenly, "Have I your consent,Aunt Parvis,to marry Phyllis Knight if I can win her ?" Mrs. Purvis threw down her knife and fork in abso• lute astonishment. Why do you ask me this ? " she cried, "unless it's money your wanting, and—" "Stop, stop, stop,' he interrupted, "understand that I don't want a farthing, only your blessing and advice."

Mrs. Purvis took up her knife and fork again, and recommenced eating very slowly; however, she was only half convinced. "I love Phyllis Knight," Tom Chilton went on. "I have loved her for three or four years, and I did think :le loved me. I want you to tell, me what has changed her." _ _
Mrs. Purvis' brows, which were rather shaggy, con. tracted. _ _

"I have told you, uppishness," she answered tartly. He shook his head. , " Uppishness would Rot kill her love for me or make her what she is now." "And pray what is she now?" "Miserable—unhappy--very silent for her,and when she does speak she is almost as sharp-tongued as—" "As nasty cross old Aunt Purvis ; oh, I know," said the housekeeper, interrupting him, "there is only one thing as ever makes a pretty girl sharp tongued, and that is when she is crossed in love." "But why should Phyllis be crossed in love, when I love her even more devotedly now than F did before I went to America?"
I

" You ! You don't imagine she is a pining for yon do you now, Tom ? " "You don't wish to insinuate that she is in love with another man?" Mrs. Purvis nodded her head nearly off. "That's just about it," she said, "and it will be hes

ruin." • "Tell me, tell me his naipe," almost gasped • awakening Tom. " Why, Mr. Geoffrey, of course. You don't suppose as Phyllis is always with they great folk for nothing." "And does Mr. Geoffrey love Phyllis ?" " Spooney I suppose, as they calls it, but he'll get over it, never fear. If you want Phyllis, Tom, you'll just have to bide your time." "Take Phyllis when Mr. Geoffrey has tired of her I No, Aunt Purvis, never. I may be a rough man and no gentleman, but I'll have naught to do with this grand Mr. Stanhope's leavings." "Not so fast, Tom, not so fast; don't let your blood boil up, that won't further you ; just listen to me. Though Mr. Ferdinand is my boy—l love him as if he was my own child—yet I brought up Geoffrey; and I know him through and through. He is the very honoura,blest young Man as ever was born. He wouldn't leave no woman in the lurch, least of all Phyllis. The gal is in love with him, he's spooney on her. It ain't dawned on him yet what a fool he is making of hisself. When it does he'll run away; for as to marrying Phyllis he'll never think of such • a thing. It would break Lacly Fedora's heart, and the master would blow his brains out." "And you wish me to come into the breach and' carry off- the girl. I thank you, Aunt ?aryls, I am not so devoted to the Siimboyes as you are." "It ain't for he sake of the Stanhopes, ,but your own; if you wdnt Phyllis you will have to catch her at the rebound. Don't be down-hearted, my dear boy; you're sure to win. She's only passing through the silly stage; Most gals has it as they has measles." "I should like to kill Geoffrey Stanhope," muttered Tom. "Should you now? Well, I hope you haven't brought no bowie kniyes to England." ....what right has a man like this Stanhope to inter. fere with a girl of Phyllis'is rank—to come between me and my love," ' Tom went on, "to wear for her a while like a'gay feather hi his cap, which he throws away, when he is tired of it, and replaces by one of another colour?" ' "'Taint that at all. I tell you it ain't. Geoffrey don't know as he loves Phyllis Knight; don't know it no more than nothing," "Then someone had better tell him. I should say - perhaps you, Aunt Purvis, who have always professed affection,for me,would kindly undertake this." "Me ? Mr. Geoffrey never speaks to me . except to say in his civil voice Good morning, Purvis I' " • "Well, get your pet Mr. Ferdinand to do it." "TX two brothers ain't very chummy, but I might - hint the subject to Ferdinand ; he'd roar it out at Geoffrey some day when ho was in a passion." "And BO my winning or losing Phyllis Knight hangs on Ferdinand roaring at Geoffrey when he's in a passion. I have a mind to go back to America by the next packet." "Nonsense, Tom, don't you do it. It will be all right I tell you. You might have took up with a girl I should have liked better than Phyllis Knight, but since she's Your fancy, and you don't want no money, I'll help you." But Mrs. Purvis's promise by no magma raised Tones spirits,as it would have done if he had never heard this tale about Geoffrey Stanhope. Looking very dejected, and having already given up pressing the comestibles , on his so-called relation, he sdid with much serious- ness, , "'Remember there must be no pressure brought to bear in the form of Simon Knight. Phyllis must of 4 her' own free will lay her hand in mine and say, Tom, the happiest thing that can happen to me In life will be to be .yonr wife,' or I will none of her." -a Humph," grunted Mrs. Purvis, "some folks are exacting—most men when they want a pretty girl don't make no conditions; howsomever I'll do my best.' And if Tom Chilton was considerably more thought- ful and down-spirited after that meeting in Ovid-street than he had been before it, the effect on Mrs. Purvis was quite an opposite one. To part the Knights from the Stenhopee was the main object of her existence. "And if I can't do it now they two is both in lows with Pnyllis,well,Sarah Pinvis ain't no good at plots," she repeated over and over to herself as she finally made her way towards Eaton-square. On Thursday last, the village of Vallorta, near-Zogno, and north ot Bergamo, was -sur- prised by twe aNalanches, the first of which descended ,o the ikirts of the village, on the north -side, 'hut without doing any damage. The second, 'nowever, buried nearly half of the village?, 'smashing in about ten houses as completely as it might 'hove done houses of card. The catastrophe 00- curled in the very early morning, but it was not until ._eAter -sunset that the news teethed Bergamo, about 12 miles distant. immediately a relief party started 'for the scene of the disaster, consisting of some Military surgeons, and detachments of carabineers and engineers. On their arrival. they joieed their efforts to those already .engaged in digging a way to the buried dwellings; and during the evening and ensuing_ night 23 dead 'bodies were found and brought out from the ruins of 'their' homes. Ten persons were found still alive, nntl though much injured, it is hoped to preserve their lives. . 'LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE AND THE INDIAN
ARMY CON I RACTS.

Mr. 'HOTLX asked the Under-Secretary of State for , 'lndia it the terms which the Secretary of State consigens misleading in the advertisements by the Superintendent of Army Clothing, Madras, for tenders for the year '188990, are those of the paragraph numbered 3 lathe sPecitittlalons, viz.." articles of European mandfacture ..are not 'required." If so, would those terms exclude goods •made in Lancashire and Yorkshire. and would they freely admit goods made in the United States of America; what was the total cost of advertisements last year, the goods amounting to £17,000 in value, of which only £24 in value were contracted for; and will the Secretary of State for India feel, obliged, in the interests of the public service, to cancel any and all oentracts entered into in contravention of the pledge giventp this House on the 10th March, 1887. Sir'Jontr Goan said the lion-. gentleman correctly in- .dicated the points in the advertisement which the Sec- retary of State thought misleading, and his hypothesis appears to be practically correct. As regarded the goods of the United States, the advertisement would riot be 'likely to have any practical effect. The Secretary of State did not know how much that advertisement cost. He had some doubt as to whether the Secretary. of State had power to cancel the contracts, and, if heini.d, he did not consider it would be to the interest of tbe-ptiblic service to do so. Mr. Howarm asked whether it was intended that goods mannfactured in the United Kingdom sholld be ex- eluded ?—Sir JOHN GORST had answered that question several times before. It was not intended —ln answer to Mr. Hoyle, Sir Soutst GORST said it was correct that he last year said the rule of the Secretary of State was that there should be fair competition. • MISCELLANEOUS.

The House went into Committee on the Civil Service Supplementary Estimates, which amounted to £139,000, Mr. JACKSON stating that last year the sum was £515,000. On a vote of £13,000 for national education buildings in Ireland, Lord RAIMOLPH CATIRCAttt Complained that the Ulster Canal was dragged into a vote for the building of schools. He regarded that as a good example of the 'ridiculous jumble in which estimates were presented to Parliament.—The vote was agreed to.

The next, one Of £12,000 for the erection of a museum of science add art in Dublin, Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL declared to be quite as discreditable as the last, the total estimate of the whole work having been increased from 2100,000 to £l4s,ooo.—Criticism was offered by Mr. Bratilaugh and other members, but.siltimately the vote was agrend to. On a vote intended to give sanction to certain in; creases in the salaries of officials in the Bankruptcy De- partment, Mr. WurrLEy said the Official Receiver at 'Liverpool was paid only £l,oock a year, whereas at Man- chester the Official Receiver got £1,200 a year; yet bankruptcy'businem at Liverpool had been considerably in,excess of. that in Manchester.—There was nothing, said Sir 'MICHAEL Illcxs-BEAcH, included in the vote with reerence to the matter, but application had been made to the Board of Trade, and it would be considered.— The mote was agreed to, as were other votes. On the mote of £6,550 for expenses of officers of county courts, revising barriiters, &c., in Ireland. 'Mr. SH*W-LITTEVRE said he had no desire to repeat the statements he had made in his speech on Thursday with regard to the prosecutions under the Coercion Act, but he wished to point out that no answer had been made to He had made a somewhat serious charge with re- ference to the administration of the law in Woodford and Loughren, and had stated, as the result of his own experience, that the Coercion Act wag being used as a means of oppression in the interests of the landlords. lie bad stated six or seven cases where, in his opinion, gross injustice had been done by the resident magis- trates, and, although these cases had not been sprung upon the Chief Secretary, the right hon. gentleman had not attempted to answer them. In the ROUSSO of a long discussion, Mr. J. E. ELLTS, Mr. Dittos, and others reiterated the charges against Mr. C. Roche, Capt. Sengrave, and other resident magistrates. —Mr. A, J. BALFOUR and the SOLICITOR-UENERAL for IRELAND, in reply, pointed to the results of appeals from their decisions as justification for their decisions, and ultimately the mote was agreed to on a division by 195 to 124.
AU the remaining votes except five were agreed to, and a 12 o'clock, in accordance with the new rule, the Committee adjourned, amid ,pheers.

div.p: THE SWEATING SYSTEM.

The Earl of lIIINIUVEN called attention to the report Of the Board of Trade on the sweating system at the East End of London by the labour correspondent of the Board. He said he intended to confine himself to the sweating system as carried on in a particular district, although he was aware that sweating was carried on in ail the great manufacturing centres of the country. Although only touching the fringe of the subject, the whole principle underlying the evils of the system would be involved. The principle of contract between masters and Workmen, wholesome in itself, had been aggravated by competition, and the immigration of unskilled and pauper immigrants. The present state of things, as, shown by the repbrt, was a disgrace to our civilisation. He stigmatised the system as slavery, with all its dis- advantages, without any of its advantages. The hours of labour varied from 14 to 16 and 18 hours a day, and oVertime was not counted. Women employed by the sweaters were bound to work as hard as the men, because in the clothing trade all the parts of the garments must be ready simultaneously. Experience showed that 'women were not protected by the Factory Act, because, unless women didxhe work required,they would be thrown out of employ, and, not being acquamted with any other class of work, they must either de the task or 1 He strongly advocated the efficsept carry- out of the provisions of the Factory and Wont- shops Act q and increasing the fines on those wholin- fringed the • regulations,- so as to render them a real,- punishment to evil - doers. If the law were not enforced, than it. ought to he repealed The Government, he hoped, would make a full .and searching inquiry into all the circumstances of the sweating system. He recommended an inquiry by a Select Committee with power to examine witnesses on oath, and to give an indemnity, to witnesses giving evi- dence. The noble lord' concluded by moving the aktioirftment of a Select Committee to inquire into thq sweating systenkin the East End of London. Lord Smuniuner seconded the motiOn.

Lord tkinnuanz and the Archbishop of CANTERBURY ,supported the appointment of a Select Committee. The Earl of °snow said the contract tailoring trade in the East End of London was almost entirely in the hands of the Jewi, and nineteen-twentieths of the people employed by the sweaters were Polish or German Jews. The Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. Answering Mr. Powell Williams, Mr. MATTHIMS said that he bad consulted the Lord Chancellor and the Lord

Chief Ittsbc.e as to the sentenoe of flogging indicted at Liverpool 'for a crime unattended by violence. Those authorities concurred in the opinion that flogging should be reserved for offences attended by violence, as "%cilia the tendency of recent legislation, and steps would accordingly be taken by the Government to repeal 'the .Lct under which the sentences in question were passed. The Finer Lord!) of the lIIRASURY, in reply to Mr. Bigger., said the hon. member would be gratified to learn that there would be no charge whatever to the ptiblic in connection -with the banquet, given 'lSt the Foreign Office, in November last, to the delegatesto the International Sugar Bounties Conference'. Baron Henry He Worms did not intend to involve any public charge whatever in connection with his visit to Paris, Brussels, Berlin, and the Hague, in relation to the suppression of bounties. (Loud cheers.) He undertook the journey Wholly for the public-service, and the public were greatly indebted to him for the work he bad done. '(Renewd

• cheers.) 'Rep.ying to Mr. Hoyle, Baron Hansa Ds WORMS said the greater number of the Colonies had not yet replied to the circular sent round to them, with a view to in- •ducing them to bring Colonial Law into harmony with the Merchandise Marks Act, 1887. but what answers had been received were of a satisfactory nature, and a reminder was being sent to those Colonies which had . not yet answered.—ln reply to questions by Mr. Dixon Hartland, the PRRSIDERT of the BOARD of TRADE said that under the Merchandise Marks there would be no objection to the importation of goods with only numbers and letters on the boxes or labels; but the hon. member would not expect him to express any opinion as to the legality or otherwise of anything done to the goods after they had passed the Customs authorities, such as adding the words "yards" or "dozens" after they were warehoused for the purposes of sale. The words, "foreign make," though net quite clear, would suffice to pass the goods, unless they were the make of some particular manufacturer or dealer in ' this country. (Hear, hear.") COMMITTEES ON THE ESTIMATES.

Mr. Sous Ennis asked the First Lord of the Treasury whether the Government proposed to accede to the sug- gestion of the late Select Committee en Army and Navy Estimates that it should be re-appointedoand whether the Government proposed the appointment of a Select Committee on the Civil Service Estimates. Mr. SMITH Said it was the intention of the Government to go considerably further than the re-appointment of the Committee, as ihey were most anxious that an oppor- tunity should be afforded hon. members of informing themselves of the details of the Estimates arfer as possible. It was the intention of the Government to propose the appointment of three select committees on estimates, one to which the Army Estimates would be referred, another for the Navy, and a third for the consideration of the votes for the revenue department of the 'l!ost Office. THE RULES OF PROCEDURE.—THE CLOSURE. Mr. W. FL SMITH moved the second of the new rules, which is to the effect that questions for the closure of debate shall be decided in the affirmative if not less than one hundred members vote in the majoritrin 'support of the motion. He trusted the House would accept the proposed mpdification, for it was made In the interest of the House. It had been found impossible,to.close de- bate with a small House, owing to the absence of the requisite two hundred members to support the motion. MR. H. CHAPLIN objected to the proposal to reduce the majority, and said that he shrank at the present moment from going an-- further with the principal of the Closure.

Mr. Dittos congraallated the Liberal party on having been the first to introduce the closure, and maintained that it was certainly a Radical proposal. He reminded the House that for fourteen weary nights he sat on those benches when the Fourth Party were obstructing one rule--(cheers and laughter)—proposed by The member for Midlothian, and he did not thank there was ever a more scandalous example of obstruction. (Hear, hear.) The'Fourth Party was then supported by the Conserva- tives, and now they saw the Conservative party adjust- ing a rope round their own neeka. (Opposition laughter.) Lord R. CHURCHILL, in repudiating the charges of ob- struction brought against himself and members of the Fourth Party, said he was sure the front Opposition bench would confirm the statement that to whatever length the Obstruction went it always enjoyed the fullest sympathy of the whole Irish party. (Ministerial laughter) The noble lord proceeded to say that the Government would hate done better to have rubbed along witlytheold closure rule a little longer, especially in view of the revolutionary change just effected with regard to the sittings of the House. Mr. CRAIG SRLLAR supported the motion, while Sir R. FOWLER expressed regret that the leader of the House should have proposed to amend the closure and make its application easier.--Sir L. PLAYFAIR advised the abolition of the intervention of the Speaker or Chair Man in deciding whether the closure should be put or not, ' and to let the responsibility rest solely with the Govern- ment and the House itself.---The POSTMASTER-GENERAL said he thought the interests of the minority were best protected by retaining the action of the Speaker and Chairman. • . • •Mr. °norms Moßmor opposed the rule.'

Ma. W. If. Sum said'ihe Government had been forced to have recourse to it, and he hoped the House would adop Counwirr, while utterly distrusting the ceeenre by majority. saw no objection to the change. The presence of a quoram from a large majority was not the main security against injustice. The security at present was contained in a veto of the chair.—After a few remarks from Sir Walter Barthelot, the House divided.—Mr. Chaplin and Mr. Osborne Morgan being named as tellers from the Noes. The figures were : For the Proposal Against 101 DISORDERLY CONDUCT. "r" Mr. W. H. Spore then moved rule 3, giv ng to the Speaker or Chairman power either to. order members guilty of disorderly conduct to withdraw immediately from the House during the remainder of the day's sitting, or to call upon the House to adjudicate in the matter. The rule also provided that members so ordered shall withdraw from the precincts of ,the House altogethen The right bon. gentleman pointed out that the rule was directed against a disorderly member whoever he might be, and not against any one section of the souse. (Mr. T. M. HRALY : Hear, hear.) Such a power as was now proposed to,be placed in the hands of the Speaker and Chairman was, he believed, vested in the president of every great assembly. Mr. WHITBREAD said he feared the provision which enables the Speaker to call upon the House to decide as to whether an hon. member's conduct was or was not disorderly, would be likely to lead to a waste of time and further disorder. (Hear, hear) Mr. Thum 110.8 strongly of the opinion that the power of punishing members should rest will the House itself, and not with any one man. (Irish cheers.) Sir. LYON PLAYFAIR moved the omissixt of the part of the rule ordering 'member:pi to withdraw from the pre- cincts of the House.—Sir -R. PAoirr seconded the amendment, which, after being discussed by Mr. Court? ney and Lord It. Churchill, was opposed by. Mr. W. H. Smith and Sir M. Hicks-Beach and supported by Sir Geo. TreVelyan, Mr. Bradlaugh, and Mr. Staveley Hill.—Mr. Itiocise argued that the House was not more 'disorderly than was the case when he entered it 12 years ago. (Laughter.)—The amendment was negatived by 136 to 85.

Mr. Warn=An proposed an amendment to the effect that the withdrawal of suspended member from the precincts of the House should be made conditionally "if Mr. Speaker or the Chairman so directed."--On a divi- sMn, this was rejected by 117 to 89. Sir Hr. TYLER next moved an amendment exempting suspended members from sitting on committees on private bills, but Mr. Hstraaos pointed out that this yould cause great hardship on those who were contest* jig bills, if suspension of a member put an end to the inquiry.—Mr. W. H. SMITH ad.nitted the hardship, and declined to accept the amendment. The rule was then put as a whole. For the, rule . -134 Against 76-60 The fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth proposed new rules, dealing with irrelevance or tediousnesS m debate arranging the order of Government business; going into Committee of the whole House; and with the proposi- tion of amendments on the report stage of any bill, were also agreed to. The ninth rule, on the subject of taking divisions, was discussed for some time, and the debate' was adjourned on the motion of Mr. Bradlaugh. The House adjourned at 12 o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes after twelve o'clock. THE NEW RULES OF PROCEDURE. The debate on the Procedure Rules was resumed. After the second reading of the Metropolitan Board of 'Works (Theatres) Bill had been postponed, Rule 9 came up for consideration. It was to the effect that the Speaker might at his discretion take the vote of the House by calling.upon members to rise in their places when his decision was challenged, and if he thought fit he could either declare the result at once or name tellers for a division. It was the opinion of many hon. mem- bers in the discussion that followed that the names of the minority should be recorded. Mr. Smith could not conceive it possible that the Speaker would exercise his authority so as to prevent a record of the minority and the majority on the second reading of a bill. The object of the • Government was to pre- vent frivolous, vexatious, . and repeated divi- sions, which wasted time. With the view "'of giving the security the House seemed to desire, he would be prepared to move that this rule should not apply to stages of a bill.—An amendment moved by Mr. SnAw- LEFEY RE to omit the words "the Speaker may at his dis- cretion" and substitute " if in his opinion the division is frivolous and vexatiously claimed" was agreed to without a division; and the House ultimately divided ore the rule as amended, the voting being—for the rule 236, against 93; majority 143.—Rule 10 was then dis: cussed and agreed to. It is a rule for the discontinu- ance of the stages of Committee and Report on the Ad- dress to her Majesty conveying the thanks of the HOMO for the Queen's Speech at the opening of the session.— Mr. GLAnsroNE spoke in favout of the rule.--Mr. Suns moved Rule 11, giving priority after Whitsuntide to bills most advanced, and said the object was to facilitate pri- vate legislation.—Mr. BRYCE proposed an amendment urg- ing that all public bills introduced at the beginning of the session should be set down in the order-book for second reading on a- list styled "The SecOnd Reading List for

div.head: PROFANE PARROT.
div.p: A PROFANE PARROT.

Herbert Harold Mackanv of Plumstestd, was sum- moned, at Woolwich Pollee Court. on Saturday. for un- lawfuly detaining n paroquet, the property of William Harris, of 7, Paget-road Plumstead.—The complaint said that he lost the paroquet--a dark green one—on Mon- day, June 13, and heard nothing more.of it till Dec. 31, when, being informed that the accused had a parnqUet in bis possession which had been caught the same week that be had lost his, he went to his house and asked to see it. Be was not allowed to see it till the following day, after a description of it and of what it could say, and t 1 '•fendant poo-poohed his claim. The bird was a yiniii;; one, and had tiet its full plumage, and at the timelt was lost was beginning to moult. A ring was just beginning to show round its neck. It could say " Toby," "Polly wants her breakfast," and such like. —ln cross-examination by the defendant's solicitor, wit- ness admitted that when asked by Mackavoy parrot had any aistinctive mark he did not mention that it had a ring round its neck; but he would swear that he did not say that it had not n ring.—Several witnesses were called, who deposed flirq they saw the compl4• ant's parrot about the' garden, between the complain- ant's and defendant's heitsis, which were only 100 yards start, from the day on which it was lost till the,follow- mg Friday.—William Mackavoy swore that his brother caught the parrot on June 3rd. He saw it the following day, and heard it speak several sentences. The follow- ing week witness again saw it, and it could then talk very Ihiently, and repeated the following distinctly:— Oh, deli:. aoetar. Polly is sick— Bun for the doctor— qulck. quick: the doctor, he's gene away; • . Why the devil didn't he stay? (Loud laughter.) Witness was present when the com- plainant's wile elairo4 the parrot on New Year's Day, and she then admitted that she was only teaching it to talk, and that it could say but a few sentences.—After hearing other witnesses, Mr. Marsham said he was of opinion that It was Harris's bird, and Mackavoy must gyre it up on payment of Ips., the value of the cage.— Mr. Bryceson (defendant's tiolicitor) : Another ss. ought to be allowecj for the bird's keep.—Mr. Marsham : He has had the pleasure of its company, and that is a set- off against the keep. He appears to have taught it a lot of things that would have been better left alone.— The defenaant gave the 10s. paid by the complainant to. the poor-box.

div.head: DEPTFORD ELECTION.'
div.p: DEPTFORD ELECTION.'

At eight o'clock on' Wednesday morning the poll was opened in Deptford at twelve stations. Dir. Evelyn, late Conservative member, resigned in con- sequence of his altered views on the Irish question, and Mr. Darling, Q.C., sought to obtain the seat as Conservative and Unionist candidate; while Mt. Wilfrid Blunt was the selected Gladstonian Liberal representative. Mr. and Mrs Darling left the Con- servative head-quarters shortly before eight o'clock to visit the working-class voters. Lady Ann Blunt, who is lighting the battle for her imprisoned hus- band, was also_early astir, and was received favour- ably by the populace on both sides. A large num- ber of carriages, lent by the partisans of the candi- dates, were brought into requisition for the convey- ance of voters to the polling stations. In Deptford proper, where the artisan and industrial classes Predominate, the Liberals were, thqught to have a considerable majority but New Cross and Brockley; which are largely residential , quarters, were expected to go for the opp osite party. There are about 10,470 registered electors. ' During the day Air. Shaw-Lefevre‘yisited the poll- ing stations. The Marquis of Hartington's carilage was lent to the Conservatives, while Lady Harcourt lent hers to the Liberals. It was rumoured luring , the evening that several members of Parliament taking part in the election had been assaulted, but it appeared that although they were the vic- tims of some horseplay, the members were net ac- tually attacked.
