Tits DOUBLE MURDER BY A MOTHER. The inquest concerning the death of two children, named Aston, which occurred at Upton Park, Essex, under circumstances which, by her own statement and other evidence, indicated they were murdered by the mother, was resumed on Monday. The jury con- sidered a verdict of wilful murder shotild be recorded against the mother, Emma Elizabeth Aston, but they were of opinion that she was not, i, I ~:r sound mind when she committed the crime. THE RAILWAY BONDS FRAUD.-- The five men, Weston, Hill, Baker, Johnson, and Fairfax, were again brought up at Marylebone Police C,ourCon Saturday, eharged with conspiring to obtain £30,000 by false pretences. It was stated on Friday that another Aarge would be preferred against two of the prisonerson Saturday, but the prosecutor declined doing so. The Hamilton Railway Company, Canada, write thanking the Scotland Yard authorities for their efforts. The prisoners were committed for trial.

Mr. Charles Richard Bannestre Legh, justice of the Peace, and Deputy Lieutenant of Cheshire, died at Ad- lington Hall at 8 30. on Sunday morning, aged 67. Deceased was a direct descendant frem John de Legh, who acquired Adlington in 1316. When eight.years of age deceased succeeded his father, who was drowned at Antwerp in 1829. During the minority the estates were administered by Lord Chancellor Erskine, and in 1846 deceased married Annabelle, daughter of the Rev. Henri Wright, Vicar of Mottram St. Andrew, since deceased, by whom he had one son (died 1884) and two daughters.

A Das, sv WAVE.—The occurrence is reported of a huge wave at Baracoa, Cuba, which according to pub- fished account, struck the boach, broke, and flowed in- land, carrying away many native huts and several good houses before it. After sweeping in fully 400 ft., the water flowed back to the ocean. Nearly 300 huts and houses'were destroyed, but no lives were lost, for the people saw it coming and fled to the hills. The beach was swept clear of every habitation that stood upon it. The wave was not a tidal wave, but the result of a three days' north wind.

DESTRUCTIVE MILL FIRE TN LIVERPOOL.—Th 43 exten- sive flour mills of Messrs. James Blackledge and Sons, in Derby-road, Bootle, Liverpool, were destroyed by fire on Saturday. The fire was discovered about three o'clock in the morning, and an alarm at once given. The Bootle and Liverpool Fire Brigades were communicated with, and several engines were soon at the mill, but the flames had got a firm hold of the building, and all efforts to subdue them were unavailing, the premises being gutted, and the fire being prevented only with the ut- most difficulty from spreading to valuable warehouse • property in the vicinity. The damage is estimated at from f...,i0,000- to R.5p,00(5. FIGHTING Dr A WELSH CHAPICL.—The Welsh news- papers on Monday reported further extraordinary scenes ab Hermon Independent Chapel, COnWil, where large congregations assembled on Sunday in antici- pation that the services would agiin be conducted biv the ejected minister, the Rev. J. M. Owens. The reports state that the rev, gentleman's opponents took possession of the chapel at nine o'clock in the morning, and held a service of their own at ten o'clock. However, a congre- gation of some two or three lurndred of the minister's sup- porters assembled outside the chapel. An .attempt to enter Of% edifice, for the purpose of ejecting the " Opposi- tionists," created a general snuffle, and a disgraceful scene ensued. The service which' had been commenced was given up, and fierce tights took place in the chapel.

THE TITHE WAR IN WALES.—SERIOUS CONFLICTS.— Distraints for tithes;claimed by the Rev. Skinner Jones. Rector of Ifeneglwys, Anglesey, were effected on Satur- day by Mr. Peter Son, the London agent for the Clergy Defence Association. The emergency men were pro- tected by a number of police. Notwithstanding the blinding snowstorm, a large and excited crowd, carrying sticks, assembled, but were kept at bay until the levies were completed. At the last of the nineteen farms visited, both police and emergency men were snowballed and stoned. One of the police had his cheek cut open with a stone. The chief constable of Anglesey was also struck, and others were slightly injured. No arrest was made, but names were taken with a view to prosecution. Owing to these disturbances, it is understood that the services of the military, as in Flintshire, will be employed when the sales take place. The farmers want a reduc- tion of 12 per cent., and the rector offers 10 per cent.

Posrar. TELEGRAPH Moxxy ORDERS.—As some misap- prehension appears to exist as to the use of telegraph money orders which, through the instrumentality of Mx. Henniker Heaton, M.P., are about to be introduced in Great Britain and Ireland, but only as an experiment, Mr. Heaton writes expressing the hope that the public will have ample opportunity of testing the value of the concession. Be states that through- out Australia and on the continent of Europe the system has been in operation, for many years. Any person may send by telegraph to any person with whom he may have business or to a relative a sum not exceeding £lO, the order being payable at the local post- office indicated in the telegram. The only additional cost is the price of the telegram. The fear expressed by Mr. Itaikes that there would be additional temptation to peculation on the part of the officials, has proved to be unfounded in other countries. In Australia, for instance, the losses hi twenty years did not amount to £lOO. Mr. Heaton hopes, therefore, that the experiment will be fairly tried in England.

THE ALLEGED MORDER OF A DAnurcrEE.—At the Nottingham Assizes on Saturday, a fitter named Wm. Booth was tried for the wilful murder of his daughter Louisa, aged six years, at Rudford, on February 7th. The mother of the child died last September, and the ' prisoner had been in depressed spirits ever since. He married wain, but soon separated from his second wife. He has been out of work since Christmas, but obtained employment on February 6th. The following day he stopped at home in the afternoon, cut his daughter's throat with a razor, locked the door, and gave himself into custody. Evidence showed that the prisoner's brain functions were in a disturbed and perverted condition, through alcoholicirrita,tion. when the crime was eom- mitted' but the same evening he fully realised his posi- tion. Soon after incarceration he suffered from halluci- nations and delirium tremens. It was possible that at the time the murder took place the prisoner was uncon- scious of his action.—The jury found the prisoner guilty, with a strong recommendation to mercy, and he was sentenced to death.

CONDITIONAL IMMORTALITY.—The Rev. Ed. White, the minister for nearly 40 years of St. Paul's Chapel, Kentish Town, and the chairman of the Congregational Union of England and Wales for 1886, marks in his incumbency. of the pastoral office a singular 'shifting ot opinion especially with regard to what is called eschatology—in a large section of the Christian world. Mr. White will, says the London correspondent of a Manchester paperb be recognised in Lancashire as the founder of the Conditronal Immortality Society. On Sunday night, Mr. White took. leave of his church and congregation, from whose oversight he retires after a connection of 'so many years.. He took tv /thankful retrospect of his past times of trouble and obloquy, when his people were so helpful to him, \and to the more .recent past of rejoicing when the tide had so gloriously turned that the doctrines he had promulgated had leavened Christian society in Europe, America, and the Colonies, and farther indulged in a hopeful outlook that in the future his views would triumphantly commend themselves to the conscience and conscious- ness of Christendom.
CUtiENT POLITICS.

Writing to Mr. Robert Smith, chairman of the Finance Committee of the Cheetham Reform Club, the Earl of Derby, after adverting to the "unfortunate disruption in the Liberal party," adds that he hopes "our differences may be removed or compromised after the next General Election."

Mr. T. Gair Ashton, addressing a Liberal meeting at Compstall, near Mari)le, on Saturday, referred to the con- test in the Doncaster Division, which, he said, showed the need of a good measure of registration. He hoped that a thoroughly good bill would be passed before long, so that working rilen would not have to labour under the disabilities they now had to contend with. As to the Irish difficulty, lie believed the true remedy was not separation, but a real closer union begotten biy love.

div.head: IRISH LEADERS IN LANCASHIRE.
div.p: IRISH LEADERS IN LANCASHIRE.

Mr. Michael Davitt addressed a crowded Liberal meet- ing at Leigh on Saturday. He said that opponents who were sincerely honest in their opposition had three ob- jections to Home Rule in Ireland under existing circum- stances. The first was the disloyal tendency of the majority of the people, the second the prevalence of out- rage and intimidation, and the third the fear of separa- tion and the persecution of the Irish Protestant minority. He discussed each of these three points, and insisted that loyalty to the English Government, as represented in Ireland by "that hideous institution," Dublin Castle, was impossible. As to outrage and intimidation he admitted and regretted it, but denied, with all the emphasis of his nature, that those occurrences were a common trait ' in the character of the Irish people. The source of these deplorable crimes was to be found in the existence in Ireland of one of the wotst land systema and the most odious form of government that afflicted any civilised people. He Contended that the conditions under which Mr. Gladstone would grant Home Rule precluded any idea of separation, even if the Irish people desired it; and as to the persecution of the Protestant minority, he quoted statistics .relating to the public appointments of Protestants in towns and districts where Catholics largely predominated, to show that such apprehensions were utterly groundless.

Mr. John-Dillon, M.P.', addressed a large gathering of the Liberals of Oldham on Saturday afternoon in the Colosseum in that town. His remarks, as might be ex- pected, had reference solely to the Irish question—a question, he said, which was n6t going to be charmed out of existence by the speeches of Tory statesmen, but which would remain the foremost question of the day until, it was Settled. In answer to the taunt sometimes levelkd at Irish members that they had used words of hatred towards ngland, Mr. Dillon urged that bard words had been used on both sides, and that they should now be forgotten. He.also pointed out that since the introduction of Mr. Gladstone's Irish measures a feeling of friendship had sprung up between the two peoples such as never existed beton% A resolution protesting against the tyrannical administration of the Crimes Act and sympathising with the Irish people in their hour of trial and suffering was heartily adopted.

MR. GLADSTOpIE AND THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS. Mr. Gladstone, in the March number of the an- temporary Review, contributes an article entitled, "Notes and Queries on the Irish Demand." In these pages the writer refers to his argument in a previous essay on the same subject, and, by way of addition, now asks, "What is meant by Unionism." "In one sense," he says, "Unionism is a great fact.. It is the Parliamen- tary name assumed, and undoubtedly mimed with en- tire sincerity, by a combination which, 18 months ago, included nearly 400 members of the House of Commons, which as yet may include 380, and which will still bear much depletion before the figure of the descending ma- jority comes near to the point of junction on a level with that of the ascending minority. The composition of the party is still more commanding than are its imposing numbers. It is not a party majority; it includes nearly 70 men who have been professed and habitual opponents of the Tory party, with which they now de- votedly co-operate; and in this important contingent are included many cases of keen and extreme, some of eminent, and one at least of splendid and never-to-be- forgotten Liberalism. The alliance has been tasted to the uttermost by the strain of circumstance, and it has borne the strain. The large proportion of the House of Commons has at its back nipe-tenths of the House of Lords; ninettentlis at least of what is termed the wealth of the -country, and of the vast forces Of social influence; an overwhelming share in its own estimation) of British intellect, and undoubtedly an enormous proportion -of those who have received' an academical education in England. Conservatism has for half a century faced in the field, with unequal yet not grossly unequal forces, the unbroken power of Liberalism; how much easier must its task be now, when it- has only to encounter 'the Gladstonian wing of the Liberal pare?' Such a Goliath surely can have no misgivings as to smashing so mutilated and so poor a David." - LORD SALISBURY ON THE ELECTIONS. Loki Salisbury presided on Saturday night at the first house dinner of the season of the Constitutional Club. London, and was supported by Mr. A. J. Balfour, M.P., the Lord Chancellor, Lord Halsbury, the Duke of Buc- cleuch, K.T., the Marquess of Abergavenny, E.G., the Earl of Limerick, the Earl of Kintore, the Earl of Peveraliam, Lord Bateman, and about 150 members of the club. Lord SALISBURY, who was received with, cheering, congratulated the members on the • success of the organisation of the club, for which, he said, he could not claim credit. On referring to the present position of the Conservative party, he urged organisation as the only means of holding aloft the banner of right and touch Refexrjrut. also let Mr—Balfoues remark that it

It was written ini answer to a person who, with Lord Salisbury, wasi affected by Mr. Bradlaugh's false and injurious charges,i and in answer to certain questions, one of which was whether criminal proceedings could be instituted against; him. Lord Salisbury had already admitted that Mr. Gun-i ton's letter was sent by his own authority to the person tol whom it was addressed, anti his Lordship could makes no other admissions as to any other kind of publication, as such admissions wouldebe contrary to the truth. Sri Richard continues--“ In conclusion I desire to state to you distinctly that Lord Salisbury is ready to facilitate( any proceedings in which You and his lordship shall bel bound to raise and have this issue decided, namely, Mr., Bradlaugh affirms and Lord Salisbury denies (a) that. Lord Salisbury gave a cheque to promote the meeting of the unemployed held in Trafalgar-square in February ,„I 1886; and (b) that Mr. Bradlaugh saw a cheque of Lord, Salisbury's which was given for that purpose. This, I understand, to be the sula'ance of your charge, as statadl in your letter of the 2nd December, and published int The Times of the 3rd December, 1887. /t occurs to me, that the proper and an expeditious mode of raising thisi issue will be by an order made by consent in any action 4 you may commence;to the effect that the above issue, be tried without any pleadings." Mr. Bradlaugh adds: "I am not sure that; I quite follow the effect of your various admissions; ; and disclaimers on behalf of Lord Salisbury as to; the letter signed IL T. Gunton,' dated December 501.1 To avoid misapprehension, I beg to ask you for a-d... tinct and unambiguous reply to the following question ial Are you instructed by Lord Salisbury to admit b he did cause the letter signed 'it. If you answer this question iu the affirma-1 tive,l will at once instruct my solicitor to issue a writ for 4 libel at my suit against the Marquis of Salisbury, and*• send such writ to you for undertaking to appear. div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Lord Clanricarde's agent attended at Ballinaaloe, yeti.; i terday, to receive rents from the neighbouring tenants, but not one came. Constable Michael Walshe, stationed at Jonesborough.; near Newry, has resigned torn the force, as a protest against the method in which The Crimes Act is enforced. , Officers, escorted by police, attempted, on Monday, to seize ,cattle belonging to the tenantry of Mr. Bodkin, near Tuam, they having adopted the Plan of Campaign. The tenants drovn off nearly all the beasts before the police arrived. The Bel fast Horning News. en Monday, published par. ticulars of another extraordinary outrage. It appears that while the Rev. Brother Edward, of Ardoyne Monastery, , was on his way home on Saturday night, he was attacked; by a crowd of roughs, who pelted him with mud, and called him most disgusting and offensive names. The prosecution of Mr. James Flynn, M.P., for do-i livering a speech at Kilmahulla. Cork, on January Bth,, advising tenants not to pay, rent, was continued, at: Newmarket, in that county, on Saturday, and the magis- trates, Messrs. Irwin and Sea-.I'rave, considering the charge, proved, sentenced him to 21 days' imprisonment, with- out hard labour.

At six o'clock on Monday morning the Mayoeof Cork ' was released from gaol, on the completion of the sentence, of 14 days' imprisonment, imposed on him under the; Crimes Act, for assaulting a police-sergeant His lord.; ship v7as called at half-past four, but refused to leave • before the above-mentioned hour. At eight o'clock he, visited the gaol in his capacity of visiting justice, and; on coming ont was,met by the members of the Corpora-P., tion and a large crowd. In the Irish Queen's Bench Division on Saturday, thei Lord Chief Justice delivered judgment, onthe application+ made by Mr. Sherlock. to have the verdict found by al coroner's jury, at Philipstown, King's County, linashed.j By that, verdict a wornan named Ellen Gaffney, was-, found guilty of the murder of her child, and the appli- cation to have the 'verdict quashed was made on the ground that the coroner had been guilty of gross, misconduct in allowing\the President and Vice-president of the National Lea+me to sit on the bench with hirn,ind'i assist in the conducting of the case. Mrs. Gaffney also alleged that an inquest was not necessary, and that none would have been held-butsfor the fact that her husband', had done work for a man who, VMS boycotted. The Court unanimously quashed the verdict, and gava costs' against the coroner. THE ABSENCE OF CRIME.

_ The Preement's Jourywl says: The judges, in openingi the Assizes, had little more to do than to congratulate the Grand Juries. In Meath, there were only six cases— none requiring observation. For West Meath, Jude), Harrison had a calendar of four—none requiring ; special remark. For county Clare, Judge Holmes found a calendar of two cases—none serious. In King's County, Chief Justice Morris found only three. Unfor- tunately for those who would like to say all this was due , to coercion, and that the judges' addresses were only a.: repetition of what they 'said in the same place twelve 4 months ago. Meath had then only four cases, Westmeath one, and King's County five. Judge Holmes hinted that', the lightness of the calendar in county Clare might be 4 due to the summary disposal of cases under the 00ercionl Act. It would be interNting to know what crime was,' disposed of under the Coercion Act which would other- ! wise have come before the judge.

A Parliamentary paper was issued on Monday showing the number of tenants and sub-tenants evicted in Ire- , land during the year ended 30th September. 1887; and' the number readmitted as tenants or as caretakers. The, total number evicted was 4,033: readmitted as tenants 1 or sub-tenants, 52; as caretakers, 2,330. For the various I provinces the numbers are :—Ulster: Evicted, 38;•re-; admitted as tenants or sub-tenants. 1; caretakers. 377.1 Leinster -Evicted, 596; reaainitted as tenants or,sub- tenants, 17 caretakers, 213. Connaught: Evicted,.; 1,006; readmitted as caretakers 632 Munster Evicted, I 1,3; readmittrd as tenants or sub-tenants, 34; care- takers, 1,108. A return of evictions from agricultural ' holdings in Ireland during the seine quarter tor causes : other than those included in the foregoing table, which' were for non-payment of rent, none-title, or breath of covenant., shows that 162 persons were evicted, of whom 27 were readmitted as caretakers.

Mr. J. R. Cox, M.P., was on-Tuesday 'released from, Limerick Gaol, at lialf.past nine a.m., after eom- • pleting one month's imprisonment under the Crimes Act, for a speech at Kildysart. The Mayor and other sympathisers met him, and took him in a covered car- riage to an hotel. Very few people assembled, and the services of 50 constables (urlder Mr. Irwen, stipendiary.; magistrate) drawn up near the gaol were not required.. On reaching his lintel. Mr. Cox was met by A number , of corporate officials and others, and was presented witht addresses •by them train iocal branches of the National League and Gaelic ,Athletic Association.—ln replying,. Mr. Cox denied the Chief Secretary's statement that the National League was on the vane in Clare. During the proceedings, Fattier Little, parish priest of. Six Mile Bridge, entered the room, but being informed, that a meeting was thlting place, retired, saviug.he could.' take no part in it,*owing, to the recent order Of Bishop; O'Dwyer. Mr. Cox afterwards left Limerick for Dublin, en route for Len it,.

Tnis BOUNDARY COMMISSION.—A London correS" pondent says :—The Commissioners will not suggest any extension of the present limits of the borougll of Manchester or of the city of Chester, but in the cases of the boroughs of Stockport and Stalybridge they will recommend that the parts of these boron& which a% at present in Lancashire shall be trams: ferred to Cheshire, and that part of , the borough 0 Warrington which is in Cheshire'shall be handed over to Lancashire. The case of Mossley is excer tional, for it is partly in three counties—Cheshire' Yorkshire, and Lancashire. The Commissioners, believe, propose to alter the county boundaries so se to bring it Wholly into Lancashire. The greatest trouble has been caused by the overlapping Unione• such as Stockport, Warrington, and Ashton-under' Lyne, in which the population are tolerably equalll divided between Lancashire and Cheshire. The Commissioners have, I hear, determined to let the county boundaries gtve way to the Unions to a ypnl considerable extent, but in doing so they endeavour: to give in one case an equivalent for what they take in another. . _ A GIRL SHOT BY HER SWEETHEART.-0/1 Thursday, at Galashiels, a weaver, named Andrew Wood, was re - mated to the sheriff on the charge of attempted murder. The accused was to have been married on the 10th inst. to a millwerker, named Barbara "Brown, and she was on Wednesday. night 'cleaning the house they were to occupy in Gala Park-road, when Wood, without anY warning, came in and fired a shot at her from a six chambered revolver he had purchased only on Wednek day. The bullet struck the back eif the Am% and the ' worrian ran to her father' g house, followed by the ac- cused, who was apprehended there. The bullet was es- , tracted by Drs. Murray and Menzies, but Brown lost a great deal of blood, and lies in a very critical state. After the crime Wood seemed to be in a dazed condition, and said that he would meet Barbara in heaven. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 3, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 3, 1888.

TILE House of Lords was usefully employed, on Tuesday evening, in discussing the evils of the sweating system in the Tailoring Traele of the Fast end of London. Lord DUNRAVEN movekl for the appointment of a Select Committee of Inquiry; ,and, making full use of the report on the subject Issued by Mt. BURNETT, of the Labour Depart- tient, he drew a harrOwing picture of the evils from 'which the poor suffer. " Sub-division of labour and the practice of contracting and sub-contracting are made tailoring impossible/under the old con- tons. A journeyman does not now make a coat right through;, he makes some part of it; and women and children are his competitors. Combina- tion for higher wages is almost impossible under luch circumstances; there is a large portioii of the tabour which cannot be called skilled; and thus it is that the poorest and most miserable of Polish ews and Germans, who have come tc• London hopin,g ‘e find the streets, paved with gold, are driven to herd and vaork together at starvation wages, rather than perish in the streets. The small con- tractors, utterly disregarding the Factories and Workshops Act, Utilise all sorts of dens for their 154rAnse. As Mr. BURNETT remarks :--" Base- Inents;garrets, back yards, washhouses, and all eerte of unlooked-for and unsuspected places, are the abodes of the sweater." But 'how does it hap- Pea, it may be asked, that the law can be set at defiance ?•The'answer is that the inspectors are leW whilst the sweaters are many. It would take an army of inspectors-to keep pace with the ever:- Lcuanging workshops of the sweaters. What may a bedroom to-day is a sweating-room to-mor- Tew- Hunted out of one corner, the sweater fin- ' kediately finds another -which no one other than himself would have eyes to see. And what cor- ears they are In the course of his speech, Lord bLYNRAVEN said :

ii A. very important point was the frightfully in- 1 lanitary condition of the dens in which this / 1 +inordinate amount of labour was extorted for so Vial' a remuneration. There was not the slightest I ,"jirellipt at decency in them. The rooms were des-. • Th.eced as over-crowded, ill-ventilated, and hot, the let 4 'working without their upper go:rthents, with gaagi coke tires in the place, and at night flaring sib,.!ghts; and the reports state that it was impos- -1.41:;= to conceive how human beings could exist li,',ler such conditions. He believed that the con- of the lives of these people were More inPlorable than those of any body of working-men w allY portion of the civilized or of the uncivilized ,„erld—infinittly worse, to his mind, than a state ~ absolute slavery. It was not strange that under .dfla circumstances as the report stated women were .1.;41en on the streets, and that the strongest' men _ere killed out in the course of eight or ten 'ears. • . eala We wonder that, groaning under such terrible the workers of the East ' end of I:oridon are ready to listen to any kind of doctrine that pro- nlises some mode of relief ? They have a right to ue dissatisfied; their discontent is divine ; and it is to be hoped that they will cry aloud and spare not until they are helped out of the sloifgh in which they find themselves. A question, of this kind is llot one of party, though Lord DIINRAVEN, after the confused way in which • he advocates Fair Trade, damaged his case by tryitig to make party 'capital out of it. Liberals who preach reform .'whenever there is an evil to be redressed, who • Oppose class privileges, and demand that all classes "—rich or poor—shall have a fair field and no favour, are surely not more to blame than others for the miseries arising out Of over population and - 'violated statutes. Lord OxsLow, who spoke on behalf of the Government, took some comfort in the ,thought. that most of the sufferers were foreign irataigrants ; but a knowledge of this fact does hot by any means get rill of the difficulty. This !Mich is certain, that work performed under such Conditions has a tendency to bring about similar ecrlditions in all work. If Englishmen are com- Wied to compete with foreigners in these dens of • BerY, a portion Of the misery will undoubtedly be theirs. Besides, those who are sweated in this linrrible fashion are not all foreigners; and the w'erst of it is that the evils of the system are in- sing. It is difficult to any what dan he done 511 ch a way that no injury shall arise from pted remedial measures. To settle that will, we ' b jresume, be the object of the inquiry which has agreed to on the part of the Government. one course is clear; it is obvious that the '4l)vialona of the • Factory and Worshops . Acts 6hoUld be enforced. These Acts have been eqieci- tilY framed to meet cases Of this kind; and in existence they should be carried out: ,„ leves would have it all their own way if. there ;ece no policemen; and When the 'law-breakers 'z'e gaining the upper hand th? remedy is to Over- Pfter them by increasing the number of those wh°_.are paid to maintain the law. The resources of Civilisation are siiiely not exhaustecl.even as to - ' tlatters of this kind; and the Government might for be better employed in. providing a force rr the eviction of callous sweaters in London ather than half-starved peasants in Ireland. 'When', 't waa a. case of breaking the heads of those who !„°Light to assemble peaceably in Trafalgar cquare, the authorities knew where to find • the teen for the job; and, if they were equally in • rraest in in o• sistin that the Factory Acts shall be Obeyed, the difficulty would soon be grappled Yith• Why, for instance, should th<workshop 1118Pectors not have the assistance of polieemen WanhediShe,l,:josol . Board inspectors in the heavy task imposed upon them ? ' if the East end were mapped out, and a raid made. simultaneously • n taon each district, there can be no question that tile Principal sweaters would be captured. • And _ 4.L'ilet) captured they should be made to feel that ""4 law must be obeyed. We May not be able by

any rough and ready method to grapple with the evil of• low. wages as the outcome of over popula- tion, but we can at least determine that our work- men and woikwomen shall, whilst at their daily taskithe housed as- men and women, and• not, a 4 • brute beasts.

THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER: addressed him- self thoughtfully to the subject of cremation at a luncheon, an Monday, which followed the conse- .cration of a plot of land which is being added to the Church of England portion of the Blackpool Cemetery. It does not seem that, the advocates of cremation are making much progress in Ns country, though it is something to have had the fact placed beyond question that cremation is not contrary to English law. The ,difficulty with a large number of people is, however, that they think the burning of' the ' dead' is opposed to the teachings of 6hristianity ; but •as to this we have, the assurance of Dr. Moorhouse that, •in his opinion, the question of Christianity does not 'en- ter into the matter. Indeed, he goes so far as to say that of the two modes of buriall--interment in the earth or cremation—he thinks cremation is the more Christian. St. Paul is responsible' fora great deal of the misconception that arises as .to the resurrection of the body; it is not that be preaches any such doctrine—rather the reverse— but what he does say is associated with the idea' of interment, and people viko do not think for themselves have ciane to regard burial in the earth as the rig,ht course to take in view of resur- rection. But the Bishop forcibly observes that "they halrno basis to eneourag,e the degrading superstition that every particle of matter that was buried in the grave would be raised again, nor he believe that St. Paul intended that such a con- struction should be placed upon his words?' The ftpostle has much to say about celestial bodies and bodies terrestrial, and as to being sown in`corrup- tion and raised in incorruption ; but it is a "de- grading superstition " indeed to hold that he meant literally that a dead body must be laid in the earth in order that it might be raised as a body of another kind. Science has, for ever disposed of the notion that anything of the kind can be pos- sible in the natural order of things. ' St. Paul made use Of the sower as a figure of..speech ; he laid hold of something material' to convey a spiri- tual meaning; but, as •is often the way with tuithinldng people,. they. have laid bold of the shell andlost sight of the kernel. The right view to take as to cremation is, as it seems to us, that taken by the Bishop of Manchester. It' is not a question 'in any sense of Christian doc- trine, but of public health and public convenience. There is the question, too, of sentiment; and touching this, it should be said that cremation does not commend 'itself on tliis account. But sentiment, especially as to thinks of a ceremonial kind, is more or less a matter of habit; and it is perhaps not too much to suppose that a change in custom would produce a change of feeling. The feeling in England is against cremation; , but the feeling is quite the reverse where cremation is commbn. It is not to be gainsaid that, on the 'ground of public health, there is much to be urged in favour of cremation. The instances are innu- merable of deterioration of health on the part of inhabitants living near an old churchyard. We are more careful now-a-days to take precautions against injury from over-crowded burial gromidg ; but no small risk is still incurred. What' can be worse, from a sanitary point of view, than the practice of futilely trying to preserve the dead by placing them in lead coffma and laying them in brick vaults? All that is really preserved is the power for mischief, by arresting, for' a time, the transformation of organic matter into inorganic matter. It would be better to bury the dead in wicker coffins, and facilitate the transformation rather than interfere with it. How beautifully Shakespeare refers to this when he makes Laertes say at the interment of his sister Oph4lia —lay her i' the earth, And from her fair and unpolluted flesh , Let violets spring! We are not going to try to make it out that our national bard was a crematipnist ; but we have satisfaction in calling attention to the fa,ct that the Bishop of .Manchester' takes an enlightened and unprejudiced view of the matter.

Tai Warrington Amateur Photographic Society are to be congratulated upon the excellent exhibi- tion of lantern slides which they presented to their numerous friends in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday evening. There was a large attendance, and it is not too much to say that the majority of those present were alike surprised and delighted with the remarkable series of views with which they were favoured by aid of the • magic lantern. Seeing that the Society is little more than twelve months old, sLch an exhibition must be in every' way encouraging to the members and to those Who have thoughts of engaging in work of this kind. Having made an experiment amongst friends; which has Proved so successful, the Society would elto well 't.) repeat the exhibition in the Public Hali. 1k wickuld, we cannot but think, be a means of adding to their funds, and, what they will doulotless think is of more importance, it would, while gratifying the intellectual tastes ,of a larger nurnher of their townsmen, incite others to become themselves amateur photographers. And what better recreation could a lady or gentleman have; for, as Mr. DOWNS pertinently remarked in his opening address, there is 'no reason whatever why ladies shOuld not be is sticeessful as gentle- men in amateur photography. Indeed, in figure pictures they would be likely to carry off the palm; for when it Comes to a question of grouping and the arrangement of accessories, gentlemen are "not in it" as compared with ladies., Warrington ' ,cannot be regarded as a picturesque town, though here and there old Time seerne to have spared an interesting bit; but • there are .many charming scenes within a desert miles of Market Gate. Lymm, Grip- Appleton Dingle, iiill Cliffe, and the various seats of the gentry in the neighbourhood furnish plenty of material to work upon; and that the material is of the right kind was shown by the cordial reception whichwas given, on Tuesday evening,' to views of these places. It would be a good thing if the mem- bers of the Society, some time ere long,- would direct their attention to a Special series Of views of Warringtati and the neighbourhood, to be framed in a uniform style, and given or sold to the 'town for permanent exhibition in the Museum, or the Art Gallery. They would certainly be as great an adornment as some of the indifferent specimens of art which find a place there—not to mention the washed-out \Turners, which are so little like what. they were when they left Tianier's hands as to be, as they hang, a mockery of his genius. Our local antiqUarians have laboured hard and long to givo,us a-glimpse, here and there, of what War- rington was in .the past .and we do not see how our local .photographer; could do better than give us pictures of Warrington and the neighboilthbod
.fr?'l J.-:

as they are, seen to-day. Besides, as the. stoam diggers are at work, changing the face of the landscape daily and hoirly, our 1 amateurs need, as to some ,districts, ,to take time .by . the fore- lock, or the golden mothent will be gone. • A thing,of,beauV must be secured before, it can he treasured. as a. joy for ever; ~and it should also be ieniembered that time, tide, and the steam navvy wait for no man.

TOTTCH:AND GO." • A correspondent of the "Field" sends a spicy story of a terrible combat between three bulls and an alligator. He writes from the United States, the land of big things (stories included), , and, after reading the picturesque account of the do- ings of that alligator, viT are tempted to exclaim with: Polonius--=" Very like a whale."

It transpires that Baron de Worms" entertained the members of.the Sugar Bounties,Confcrence at -his own expense. He has done good b stealth, and hhished to bid, it fame. . There is no denying new that the Sugar Bounties Conference' was the sweetest thing of the kind yet. known.

The King of &rata has a "good life" as a man, but a "bad life" as a king. He wants to insure for 280,000, but it is stated that none of the continental or English offices will take the risk. Kings have a sudden way of popping off, or being popped off; in the east. The Czar is not the only monarch who feels the force, of the phrase "'Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown."

There was another struggle, on Sunday, at Con. wil, in Wales, for the possession of 'an Indepen- dent chapel. It is reported that "the service, which had been commenced, was given ' up, and fierce fightt took place in the dispel." Surely it is carrying" indepemlence " too far when people seek; as Butler has it, to —prove their doctrine orthodox By apostolic blows and knocks.

When people will fight, it is as well to let there have their fill of it. There has been a vacancy, at St.Helens, in Windle Ward, and the Liberals tried 'so to arrange matters as to avoid a contest. But no, the Tories would fight. The fight cams off on Tuesday, and the result was that Mr. Henry Mar- tin, Liberal, received 1,083 votes, and Mr. Zrolan Kitchen, Conservaiive, 702 votes. Kitchen was turned up-side down, so to speak. He .was found, not only at the bottom of the poll, but very much bruised. But he would fight.

Another miner has paid the penalty of his life for neglecting inquest, propthe roof where he was work- ing; At the, held at Whiston the other day, on the death of a young man named William Yates, it transpired that he had neglected to set a ar bat the end way'', as suggested by his brother, and the result was a fall of roof and the loss of a life. The fatality ought to act as a warning to other colliers. The law of gravity is inVariable in its action, and is least of all to be disregarded in a coal • pit. • . .

Patrick Sculley seems to have had a high, old time of it on Sunday night. He was quite on theloose, which is another way of saying that he got tight. About mid-night he floundered into the AXersey at Howley Quay Wharf, and, being too drunk to get out himself, had to be helped out by a policeman who, for once, was at hand just when he was wanted. How Patrick managed to escape drown- ing is a mystery—unlgss it be assumed that. the Mersey brew, like the 'Egyptian darkness, was so thick that it could be cut with a knife. In that case, having flopped in, he "stuck where he let."

Mr. R. A. Naylor has, it seems, become a Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature; but this is by no means equivalent, as might be sup- posed, to' the statement that he has become a literary "fellow." The Royal Society of Literature is very obliging; no test is required—not even passing the let standard, or writing a letter to a newspaper. The essential qualification is for a "fellow" to be willing to pay a three guinea en- trance fee, and a subscription of two 'guineas an- nually. It looks well to have after one's name.; and "'fellow s and his money are soon parted.

Mr. Joseph Jackson, of St. Helens, formerly a member of the Prescot Board of Gliardians and of the St. Helens Town Council, died on Monday from an attack of bronchitis and inflammation, of the bowels. It is remarked that he took told while attending the funeral of the late Mr. W. Birchall, a fortnight ago. A record of the number of per- sons who have fallen ill and died after attending funerals would be as startling as it would be melan- choly. The depression of nund incident to inter- ments renders the body peculiarly susceptible to evil effects of a AM at the graveside. A last tribute of respect is dearly paid when it results in illness—to say nothing of death.

It is satisfactory to observe that there are Con- servatives even, who object to the £25,000 which has been expended on Sir H. Wolff's midsion to Constantinople.. The "St. James's Gazette" does not hesitate to characterise the expenditure as sk gross abuse of public money. There is a strong opinion in some quarters that such work as has been done would have been better pbrforrned by our Ambassadors at Cons.tantinople and Cairo. But something had to be done for Lord Itandolph Churchill's supporter; and it will be interesting to see what sort of a defence of this job his lord- ship will make in his now character as an econo— mist of the first water.

The London newspapers have set a good 'ex- amole in refusing to accept the full reports "pro- pared" by outsiders, of the speeches at the Con- stitutional Club dinner—an example which is all the more striking seeing that it covers a speech made by the Prime Minister. The idea which is entertained in certain narrow minds is that repor- ters ought to steal round to the back door, and be content to receive such scraps of food and news as these dunderheads think fit to bestow. Fortu- nately for the public, the average pressman is not built that way; and the result is that the dunder- heads are occasionally brought to their senses.

Some of the members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, and of the Rural Sanitary Authority, have curious notions of their duty. They have been laughing to scorn the sensible suggestion of Mr. Brunner that they should appoint a commit- tee to consider the provisions of the new Local Government Bill as soon as it appeared, and for- wat:d him the result of their deliberations. He offers to be of service to them, and they throw his letter aside. Board of Guardians ase they called And a good name truly, for when some of the mem- bers lay their heads together there is wood enough about for two or three boards.

It is not often—in fact, altogether too seldom— that publicans or beersellers are summoned for permitting drunkenness on their premises; but a case was. heard at Runcorn on Monday, in which the landlord of the Friendlip Tavern was charged with this offence. Mr. Percy. Davies, of Warring- ton, appeared for the defence, and a stout defe.nce he made in the absence of witnesses to support his statements. Two constables swore to a man who, waa drunk braving a glass of beer in front of him; and as, on the other side, there was the unsup- ported statement that the beer belonged to some one else, the magistrates could not do other than record a conviction, the landlord .being fined 20s. • and costs.

At the close of the case, Mr. Percy Davies said if I he had known that there was a teetotaller on the bench he should have objected to his hearing the case. But what an absurd objection to take I S7perintenclont Hollingsworth, as prodecutor, might just as well, on the other hand, have ob- jected to the other magistrate, if he knew he wits in the habit of taking a gl?ss of beer. We shall hear next in a case of adulteration of ob- jection to magistrates who are known to have a dislike to impure food. In fact, if procedure of this sort is to be the order of the day, we may expect to hear of offenders objecting to being tried at all. .

REMOVAL OF MESSRS. LEVER REMMERS SOAP WORICS.—" The Liverpool Daily Pest" says : —We understand that Messrs. Lever Brothers, of War- rington, manufacturers of the well...known- " Sun- light Soap," have arranged to transfertheir works from that town to Lower Bebington; where they have purchased fifty acres of land lying between Birkenhead and Chester-road and the railway, and close to the site of the old' cement works, at the head of Bromborough Pool. It is state& that this step has been necessitated in oonseqpence of the Manchester Ship Canal intsilering with Messrs. Lever's present works at Warrington. Plans for the new factory, prepared by Mr. Owen, architect, Warrington, have been approved by the Roads and Health Committee of the Lower Bebington Local Board, and it is expected that the building contract will be settled next week, and operations com- menced forthwith. Already a quantity of plant has been brought to Bebington Station.. It is pro- bable that by the end of . July next the factory will be in full working or ler, and as there will be at least c)00 hands employed,. the importance of the matter to the neighbourhood will be considerable ' It is stated that a portion of the land willte used for thv erection of workmen's cottages. A short branclrrailway will connect the new works with

Bebington Stsition, and the Pool wilr be utilised for the conveyance of goods between the works and the Mersey by means of a steam barge.. The ceremony of cutting the first sod in connection with the works has been fixed to take place. this (Saturday) afternoon, and subsequently there will be a dinnen. to celebrate the occasion.

div.head: CONCERT AT WIDNES.
div.p: CONCERT AT WIDNES.

In aid of the Widnes Baptist Chapel a grand eon- curt was given in the Drill Hall, on Monday even,- lug, and it is gratifying to be able to record that the spacious building was filled with an apprecia- Live audience. The general arrangements had been admirably carried out by Mr. Priestnall, the task oi engaging the vocalists and instrumen- talists was wi th. porn mendable judgment left to. Mr. Jude, principal of the Liverpool College of Music, .It isalmost unnecessary to say thrst the trust was not misplaced,. and the concert was one of the most pleasant and enlOyable that a Widm.s.ancli- ance has had an opportunity of listening, to,. The artistes were Mdlle Marianne Fenna, of the Royal Albert Hall oratorio. concerts, Pm., Madame Anderson,. of Man- chester.. Leeds, and Liverpool, Mr. Ben Robarts,." primo tenore," Mr. F. H. Seddon, principal basso. Liverpool Cathedral, and Miss M. Juanita Jortes, geld medallist and prize winner. There was one great disappointment. Mdlle Feline was suffering from a most seriouseekl, and her medirral adviser had forbidden her to leaue her apart- ments, but in spite of this ediet she put jam an appear- ance, and chasmed those present with her vocalisatio n of "The nightingale." She was compelka.d to return and bow her acknowlecirnent. The items put down to, her name were "0 Luci di guest animal' (Donizetta), and the operatic scena "Tam Titania"• (Mignon). bat the audience had to forego the pleasure of hearing these elections. Madame Anderson kindly aided in making up for this clefiCioncy by rendering, an extra wee, The reputation •Madame Anderson has attained is too widespread to need more thart a pa.ssing mention, and it will suffice to say that she sang with conspicuous lability "In the chimney corner," "Jeanette and Jeanot.7 and "The three wishes." She was twice recalled, and on the last. occasion she responded with an exquisite rendering of the ever welcome ballad " Home, sweet home." Mr. Ben Roberts contributed "l'he pilgrim of love" and "The skipper," and for each effort he was deservedly honoured with an encore. He sang with much taste and expression. Mr. F. H. Seddon has a pecularly expres- sive bass voice, which he uses with skill and judgment, and he treated the audience to capital renderings of "Thy sentinel am I" and." Plymouth Sound," and he was re- called. Mr. Jude made three appearances and en each • occasion he was enthusiastically encored. 171 e gdse two performances on the harmonium with his accustomed

facility of execution, and sang with much pathos and power "The old arm chair." A feature of the evenhw's entertainment was the brilliantly executed solos on the pianoforte by Miss M. Juanita Jones, who was enthusi- astically recalled for her playing of "Fantasia Balmoral." A most agreeable entertainment concluded with "God save the Queen" by the company. It should be men- tioned that the Soap Works Brass Band performed selections before the commencement of the programme. The duties of chairman were ably undertaken by Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., and his services were suitably acknowledged on the proposition of the Rev. R. Yeat- man, seconded by Mr. W. Clarke.
A RUNCORN FISH DEALER'S FILL.-CLAIM
FOR DAMAGES.

lii the Nisi Prins Court at LiVerpoOl Assizes on Wednesday, before Justice Cave `and a special jury, the case .of Sinnott the London and North-Wes- tern Railway Company came on for hearing.. This was an action brought by Peter Sinnott, a fish dealer, of Runcorn, to recover damages for personal injuries sustained by him through the negligence of the defendants' servants. The defence was a denial of ; negligence and an allegation of contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff.—Mr; Gully, Q.C. M.P., and Mr. Mulholland appeared for the plaintiff, and the coin-. eau was represented by Mr. Bigham, Q.c., and Mr. Page.—ln stating the facts of the case, Mr. Gully said the plaintiff met with a serious accidentiat Runcorn sta- tion on the morning of July 21. In the course of his business, the plaintiff was in the habit of travelling by early morning trains from Runcorn to Liverpool. On the morning of•the above date he arrived at the station it twenty minutes to three o'clock in order to catch the 2-50 a.m. express., and entered on the up platform. In order to get across the lino to read' ; the Liverpool train it was necessary to cross a covered wooden bridge. This bridge was approached by sixteen steps, and there was a landing and eight more steps. and on the other side there was the same number of steps to descend. Over each landing there was usually a lamp, but' on this 'morning neither lamp was lighted. The plaintiff went up the bridge which was in total dark- ness, and as he walked across he saw a flash of light from the signal box,- which rather dazzled his sight. He felt his way along in order to de.scetid the opposite steps, but appeared to have approached. them sooner than he expected; and before he could save himself he fell down the stens Being a man of 21 stoneraged 47 years, and of muscular frame, he fell with great force, injuring him- self severely. He was still ill, staying at Holsby, and a serious affection of the heart had superVened since the accident'. He would recover to a certain extent, but never completely. Mr. Gully submitted that it was the duty of a company who invited people to travel by their trains and to cross a bridge to shave the approaches in a 'safe condition. On the question of damages, he might inform the jury that before the accident the plaintiff was making £I.W a. year. He only now made one half by his busmesa, which was carried on by his wife and son. It was a fact that in 1881,when a master mariner bypro- fession, the plaintiff was injured at Normanton, and the • Midland Railway Company paid him £2,500 as compensatiiit. The accident caused the plaintiff's 'brain to. be. affected, and 'he was advised' to give up his profession. He then became a fish salesman, but he nad recovered from the first accident Sufficiently to make him healthvetgain and able to follow his business. The plaihtiff still remained at Helsby, and his eifitlence had been taken, an he could not come to the ceint.—Evid- .ence was then' called, and the plaintiff's wife, in cross- examination, stated that when her husband was injured in 1881 the elector said her husband would not recover completely... Redid recover in abMt three years. Wit- ness gave evidence as to the morning being dark, and Mr. Gully said the almanac wouid be the best witness on the point. The sun rose that morning at nine mi- nutes past feurorclixdc.—Drs. Robinson and Mi'Dougall, of Rtincorn;.gave evidence as to the plaintiff' S condition; and' that he had recovered from the temporary effects of the fitst accident, except that he'veas subject ta fits of excitability. The first-mentiotted in cross-examina- tion said he examined the plaintiff the . day after the accident,. and found .no bruises. Mr. Mitchell Banks; of Liverpool, also said that the splaintiff was suf- fering fromslibeit NO an affection of the heart,.which weretheeffects of the accident, assuming that up to that time the plaintiffihad been, as he was informed, a4malthy man—For-the defence, Mr. Bigham said that on the morning of the accident the weather was beautiful and ; bright,, and it wee' not dark, though it was. not, of course; broad daylight. There were no lamps lighted ion thelailding .ofs the bridge, but there was sufficient light. for persons Its cross in safety provided they used reasonable care:. The plaintiff was crossing the bridge when the Loncloretrain was passing thrsugh thestation, and imagining it was his train must have hurriedialong, and in his hurry slipped down the steps. Counsel asked the jury vehetherthey were going to pay damages to a man who, not using reasonable care, tripped upend fell down some steps.---William Leach, porter at the station; Sergeant Woolley„James Cowley, fishmonger, Widnes; Owen; a signalman; R. Smith, stationmaster; and Police- Constable Kettle, \ Runcoim, gave evidence . that the ' weather was, fine and light at the: time of the aceident.—Dr. B. Mangan'' Runcorn, said he wee crassing the bridge on the morn- ihg of • the- accident, and found the plaintiff lying at the bottom, of the steps. That was perfectly clear; and witness.conki see him quite plainly'. In cross- examination, the Niftiness said that in September, 1885, , he examined the plaintiff for an insurance seciety, and reported thathe • was perfectly healthy—Mr. Chauncey Puzey, surgeon, Liverpool, said he saw the plaintiff on behalf ef the defendant, company. The first tane he 'was told by the plaintiff that when crossing the bridge he heard a train underneath, and he hurried and fell down the steps. Afternsteds the plaintiff corrected this and said he was not hureying. He found the plaintiff's pulse . was weak, rapid, and irregular; such asordeltt have been expected from a condition of indigestion. On the second occasion; in August,lse found it better. This irregularity might have been caused by a fall, but a feeble movement of the heart was a.synaptom of enlargement of the heart with fatiiness. In October he again saw the 'plaintiff, and his rendition was improved. He did not notice any- thing which indicated heart disease. Seeing him againi in February his cendition appeared better. The plain- tiff's present . condition was consistent with natural causes.—Mr. Davitilion, Liverpool, also gave evidence' that the plaintiff 'suffered from enlargement of the heart,, which must havo been coming on for some time before the accident. He agreed with Dr. Puzey that the fall would not conduce to any permanent effects.—The jury found for the defendants, and his Lordship gave 'judg- ment.

' BAD FISH FOR SALE AT WIDNES.-0-At. Whines Petty Sessions; on Thursday, before Mr. A: R. Gla,dstorie and Mr. 3: Brock, David.. WelSby, of Wigan, was charged with offering for sale, on the 11th ult., 142 herrings and eight .pieces of codfish, which were putrid. Mr. Allen, clerk to the Local 3oard, prosecuted. • The assistant., nuisance inspector saw the defendant hawking the fish about the town, and had them examined, ~vith the -re- sult that they were condemned as unsound. The magiS- tmtes afterwards ordered them to be destroyed.—The de- fendant, who was liable to a penalty of £2O for each piece ot fish, was fined 20s and 'costs, or 14 days' impri- sonment. .. DESTROYING PROPERTY AT RuNcoux.—On .Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, m _Willia Wilson and JameA nett, boys; Were charged with damaging' property 00 Mill-brow, belonging to Miss Ann Pennington, of Liver- pool.—Mr. W. Fisher, agent to Miss Pennington, who owns considerable property in thd (Own; prosecuted, and said Miss Pennington had suffered much loss through damage done to her property at Mill-brow. Boys seemed to consider they had a . righ to do what they thought proper, and sometime ago a shipPon was de- molished. The tenants of the property had frequently complained of depredations on the property, and on the 21st February, the defendants and several other boys had smashed open the door of a'shed.—After hearing the evidence the Bench fined each defendant 6d• and costs lOs 6d. '

ADULTEILLTED COFFEE AT .RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions; on Monday, before Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. a Davies, poorge Myers. shopkeeper, of Weston, was summoned for unlawfully selling, on the 3rd but, two ounces of coffee which was not of the nature, substance, and quality demanded. The defendant paid he pur- chased the coffee from a wholesale dealer, and it waswar- ranted as pure.—P.C. Jackson deposed to •,eretering the defendant's shop and obtained two ounces of coffee on payment of 21d. The coffee was taken from a eannister, which was standing on the -counter.—Seperintendent Hollingworth produced the certificate of the county ana- lyst; which stated that the coffee was adulterated with 40 per cent of chicory. A line of /Os and costs, 28s 6d, was imposed. A BzeA• NCI IMPOSTER AT WIDNES. —At Widnes Court, on Monday, a young man named John Marley, of no fixed residence, was committed to gaol for three months, with • hard labour, for soliciting alms by means of a letter which purported to be written by George Page, basketmaker, 24, Chapel- street, Widnes, and which stated that the prisoner was a worthy man, the only support of his bedridden mother, arid that unfortunately was deaf and dumb. Prisoner had succeeded in obtaining several sums of 'money of different people, but at last he was seen by P.C. Thomp- son (392), who apprehended him and conveyed him to the Police Statiop, where it was discovered that he was neither deaf nor dumb.—Prisoner pleaded in extenuation Of the offence that he was starving, and he snust do something to obtain food.—The Bench, in passing sen- tence, observed that he must be .thankful that he was not sent to the querter sessions, where he would have been more severely dealt with. YOUNG Tanners AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petter Sessions on Thursday, James Walter Dixon, aged 13, of Dock- street, and Thomas Billington, aged nine, of Bridge- street, were charged with having, on the 24th ult., stolen , a pair of trousers,. value 3s 6d, hermetic shop of Mr. Gee. THE WIDNES, WOUNDING CASE.—At the Liverpool ANSiZeS, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Grantham, John Murphy, 35, labourer, was indicted for having at Widnes, on the 4th of February; inflicted grievous , bodily harm opon Patrick Malone. The circumstances showed that the two men are employed at the chemical vil,rks at Widnes, and that on tia e date named they were public-house, in the evening, together with a third man. They had a spar in a friendly way; .Prisoner left first. Not long afterwards Malone also left, and a little distance away heard someone in the darkness calling to him. On going towards the voice he saw.a,man with his , arm raised, and the next moment he was struck with a sulphur brick, which inflicted a very serious injury over his right eye, and knocked him down Insensible. The voice he recognised as being that of the prisoner. The accused was found guilty of unlawfully wounding, and was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour.

Of these two were inquest casts, and of the•re- maining 23 deaths four were due to bronchitis, four to consumption of the bowels, three to convulsions, two to heart disease, two to cancer of the liver, and one each to inflammation of the lungs, paralysis, inflammation of the lining membrane of the heart, 'blood poisoning, softening of the.brain, natural decay, diphtherisk,,, and croup. The above 25 deaths show.an average rate of a little over 19 per 1,000 of the estimated population • ,:.end exclusive of the inquest cases of a portion ouer 16 per 1,000.

__- The Law Clerk drew attention to the remarks of Mr. Brundrit at the meeting of the shareholders of the Water- works Company, on Monday, and which will be found in another part of this journal. He said the statements were misleading, and were not correct. It ought not to go uncontradicted that the Board was responsible for the waterworks spending over £6OO. The Board Rent £l6O. When the first bill was introduced by the Liverpool Cor- poration. the Board got an agreement that should the district of Runcorn ever require a water supply beyond - what the Runcorn Waterworks give them, they could tap the Vyrnwy mains on fair terms, either, disectiy; if the Board had purchased the waterworks, and, if not, through the mains of the Waterworks Company by ar- rangement. The Corporation gave an undertaking that they would put this agreement in the next Act, and they did so. It was only then that the Waterworks Company made an effort fqr their own protection. They wanted to throw out the clause the Board had obtained, and to get a clause inserted making it illegal to supply water to Runcorn. So long as the Runcorn Waterworks could supply the town of Runcorn well and good; but if there should be a failure from their source, then the , 'Board of Commissioners were in a position to ask the Liverpool Corporation togive them a. supply.-Mr. Light- burn said whatever arrangement the Board had made with the Liverpool Corporatimhthey could not use water front • their pipes without the consent of the Waterworks.,- The Law Clerk Suppose the town bought the Water- works then we could take water direct from the mains of the Liverpool Corporation.,—The Law Clerk, imanswer to Mr. Lightburn, said they could take a million gallona a day from the Liverpool mains.' The Corporation could stop the supply by giving five yttirs notice.—Mr. Speak-- man also supported the Commissioners' position, and. 'stated that the clause would be bf the utmost benefit to., the community.—Mr. Meadowcrol; pointed out that whilst the Commissioners had Safeguarded the interests. of the town as regarded water as far back as 1880 the Waterworks Company took no action until 1886. He denied there was any desire to infringe upon the rights of the Waterworks Company. There was no other public business.

GIVE ITS THE TRUTH.

"The Christian Union* of Friday, January 20th, says :—Some tuna since we quoted from the " Glou- cester Herald" an article announcing and describ- ing the complete victory of Warner's Seim Cure over that terrible malady known as Bright's Dis- ease. The same article was copied into many of the leading papers of England, and in most cases notes were appended stating that its source was above suspicion. Considering the fact that this disease has bafffed the best efforts of the medical profession for over fifty years, we were surprised that our ex- changes did not consider the matter important enough to call for editorial comment. It seems strange that the Press, supposed to have the inter- est of the people, and especially the sick ones, at heart, sh 3uld silently receive the news that a terri- ble disease has apparently received its death-blow, and been conquered. We thought their silence necessarily cast very grave doubts upon the truth- fulness of bhe statements. • We, therefore, proceeded with caution—but at the risk of being the innocent means of advertising a medicine of doubtful efficacy—to call attention to the SAFE Cure, with a statement that one or two things must be true— either a wonderfulcure for a dread disease has been dis- covered, or else a set of respectable men had combined with a well-knosen and reliable paper to 'swindle the credulous in a very bad way. Our readers will agree with us that it is no small matter to sufferers which of these be the fact. But how is it to be decided? Will the medical profession discuss the matter, analyse the cure and:test its efficacy ? :Or will the doctors pass it by with the remark that it might be u.s4ful in certain pecu- • liar cases? ' We do not know whether the medical men are doing 'their duty to the public by analysing and testing this new and pretentious cure, but we do know that the pub- lic are testing it for themselves. As we mentioned a short time since, Mr. J. H. Kihninster, of Kingsholme, Gloucester, had been reclaimed to health by the use of the SAFE Cure, even after his medical advisers could do him no good, and his death was expected at any time. Mr. Kilminster is 'Bandmaster of the Ist Gloucester Engineers, and his case has become widely known, and by his friends his complete recovery is considered little short of a miracle. Mr. John Hope, of 24, Cottingham- street, Sheffield, has received the most marvellous bene- fits from the use of the SAFE Cure, although two phy- sicians could only succeed in "patching him up a little." Others of our people have taken the Sere Cure with benefit, and others are now taking it. This is all very well in its way, and no doubt time will see Warner's SAFE Cure more fully established. In the meantime Bright's Disease is killing the people, and the dying patients are afraid to try the remedy unless ordered by that awe-inspiring functionary! the medical man. Look- ing upon the doctors as ordinary men of- business who hate successful opponents just as other business men do, it is not surprising that they do not receive with open arms the nostrums of all who force So-called specifics upon the public; but we, as an advanced nation, expect more from our medical men. We like to think of them as a band of warriors drawn up to frustrate the ravages of disease, and to weaken the common enemy at every available point, and by every conceivable means. What a sorry spectacle an army would present if each officer and soldier were to look with jealousy upon the attempts of all others to crush the opposing forces ! Let a man who may be deemed the perfection of insignificance invent an appliance or method to aid in the destruction of his fellow-man in war, and his attempt will be grate- fully acknowledged by the War Office, as an encourage- ment, whether it be promising of good or not; and if his invention should prove, upon examination, to be of real value, his name will be mule for ever, while those who use his weapons will be untiring in the sound of his , praise. But the inventor of a new kind of ammunition to be used in the war against disease has no tribunal by which the efficacy of his discovery may be triad and judged. In most cases, whether it be good or bad, it is met by those who ought to be capable of judging and testing with a few doubting and slighting remarks. There are, however, some who will give an honest opinion even against their own interest, as witness the large number of the more intelligent physicians who are gradually being won over to acknowledge the merits of Warner's SAFE Cure.
