WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday merning. There were present the Rev. G. IF. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. J. Houghton, Kilshall, Jolley, Voisey, Isher- wood, Moore, Darhyshire9 W. Houghton, Ratcliffe, Clarke, Wright, Blackhurst, Owen; J. C. Sutton (clerk), andS.Satton (deputy clerk).
SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees committee reported that fees had been allowed in 68 old and 17 new cases.—On the motion of
Mr. BLACIEHUUST, the minutes were adopted.
THE BOUNDARIES QUESTION.

With regard to the Government Commission to inquire into the boundaries question, the CLERK stated he had had a letter from the Hon. T. 11. W. Pelham, asking as to which would be the best place for the Commissioners to meet in Warrington, and he had written to say that the Council Chamber would, with the permission of the Mayor, be at their service, or, supposing they wanted some O other place, the Assembly-room at the Lion Hotel could no doubt be had. There would no doubt be due publication of the meeting, which he expected would be held in the month of March.—Mr. JOLLEY said he had seen it stated byes London correspondent that the portion of the Warrington Union which is in Cheshire wag to be brought into Lancashire.—The CLERK said he did not think it was possible to come to any other conclusion than that they (the Guardians) had advised them to come to—that waS to include the Cheshire townships of the ' Union in Lancashire.—The subject than dropped. , • VACCINATION AT EARLESTOWN. . The CLEas said he had a letter from Mr:Cooper, vac- cination offieer of the Newton district.—Mr. W. HOUGH- TON said he should like to make an explanation with re- gard to this subject. At the previous meeting, when, he made his remark about vaccination, he had only had I the return in his hand a few seconds, and he had taken , the wrong column and given the wrong percentage. He I had seen the return since, and had discovered the mis- take. But independent of that there was in the returns a very high percentage of what were described as re- movals in the Newton district. There were about 6 per cent, of the births that had been removed to places that could not be reached, or could not be found, and what Was much worse than that, there were no fewer than 13 cases marked as ref u,sals to submit to the Vaccination Act. That, ho thought, was a very dark feature in the ' case. In the township of Warrington there were only, 4 per cent. of removals, and he wanted to know how it was that there were so many as six per Cent. of removals in Newton. In the town- ship of Warrington there were tie refusals, but , in Sankey there' were two refusals and onel removal. He thought that people ought to be compelled to submit to the law in this matter.—The communica- tiotf from Mr. Cooper was then read, and in this it was stated that the true reason for the number of removals would be found In the state of trade. Two of the prin- cipal works in Earlestown had greatly reduced the num- ber of hands employed, and, of course, the men had gone elsewhere in search of work. If the Board examined the returns they would find that there'were 904 per cent. finally accounted for, that was to say, vaccinated, dead, aitd nine.unsusceptible to vaccination; a little over two per cent. postponed; under two per cent. not accounted for; and Si per cent. removed.—The CLERK said he should suggest, from his experience of vaccination and of the difficulties to be encountered, that that was a very fair return.—Mr. If. HOUGHTON said it was an explana- tion as to the removals, but it said nothing as to the refusals —The CLERK said the season of the year had often to do with that.—Mr. W. Honewrox said the doctor glowed tliey were fit to be vaccinated, yet they were not vaccinated.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he thought he knew something about that matter, and he believed that if they would not put pressure on they would find it.? great deal better, and would get more children vaccina- ted than they otherwise would. As fag people leaving the district, he was sorry to say it was he case, and if they weat through Vulcan they Would find half the win- dows of the cottages boarded up.—Mr. VOISEY thought it should go from that Beata that there was an obligation on people to submit to:vaccination, and that that Board would never sanction any step towards disregarding that obligation on the part of parents.—The CHAIRMAN said that had already been stated on a placard that had been issued by the Board.—Mr. YOISEY said it was cleat' to him that at Earlestown there was a disposition on the part of some people to oppose vaccination and there had been some little hesitation expressaion that Board. —The CHAIRMAN said there were different opinions on that question held by the members of the Board, but their opinions could only carry weight so far as indivi- duals were concerned. The action of the Board had always been the takingiof the proper legal course with respect to any cases of that kind. As long as the law said a certain thing must be done, it was the duty of the Board to carry out the law. Officers had been called up from time to time and reprimanded, alid if any case of neglect in carrying out the Vaccination Acts could be proved against any officer, no doubt the same course would be pursued.—Mr. JOLLEY thought it was the duty of the Board to see that the law was carried out.—Mr. CLARKE said if the, law was bad, they had no right to enforce a bad law the same as they would do a good law. (Oh!) He could refer them to Boards of Guardians that were determined not to en- force the law. There were more than a dozen Boards of Guardians to-day that did not enforce that law, and they must have as gentlemen fit to be Guardians a reason for not enforcing the law. There were members on that Board who seemed anxious to have the law enforced in Earlestown particularly. (No, no.)—The Cusremee said that if any gentleman there was dissatisfied with the returns from Earlestown it was because there was neglect in that district more than in 'any other district, and not because it was-Earlestown. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. CLARKE said he maintained that the vaccination law was a bad law—bad in its effects and its 'results. He had referred some time ago to cases in which in his opinion the lives of children had been des- troyed by vaccination, but there was no record went to the Local Government Board about a thing of that sort. There was nothing said about the bad effects, but only about the good. He could refer to magistrates and law- yers, and even Queen's Councillors, who opposed that law, and these gentlemen must have some reason for doing so. A law must be either good or bad; it could not be both, and if they enforced- that la*, they ought to have a reason for it. For his part, he knew it was a ' bad law, and, as one member of the Board, he should not give his sanction for its enforcement.—Mr. VOISEY said they could not accept Mr. Clarke as an authority upon that question. The good or bad effects of vaccination could be seen by statistics collected by Government, or .obtained from other sources, and the evidence as to its good effects were so overwhelming that they ought not to allow any discussion on the subje& Mr. Clarkecame with general statements, but let him place statistics on the table that they could examine. On a former occa- sion Mr. Clarke mentioned three cases, but before he sat down he accounted for one of them by saying that the doctor had certified the cause of death to be convulsions from teething.—Mr. HOUGHTON said the returns he re- ferred to were for 1886, which showed that there were positive refusals to have the children vaccinated. He thought that for the protection of the children and the fami- lies of poor deluded people--(laughter)-the law ought to be enforced. He had no hesitation in moving that in the 13 cases of refusal to vaccinate at Newton, and the two cases at Sankey, prosecutions be commenced unless the law was complied with.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he would be very glad if Newton could be struck out of the War- rington Union.—Mr. JOLLEY : You are a separatist, then'?—Mr. RAI'CLiFFB: Yes.—Mr. BLACKHURST : Go in for repeal of the Union. (Laughter.)—Mr. RATCLIFFE said he should be glad to do so. They talked about the "black spot" on the Mersey, but there was one black spot, and that was Warrington. (Laughter.)—The CLERK said he agreed with Mr. Ratcliffe that vaccination was now very much more satisfactory in the Newton district than it was a few years ago. lie did not think continued prosecutions would help them any, and before when the magistrates found that cases came upon them pretty quickly they reduced ate fines from £1 t 01.65, ,fis and then to Is and it was not a
, • e desirable thing. to take these'people into court and. Vava them fined is Bnly. He_thought the best way was to take a broad view of the whole question, and inasmuch . _

as those returns went to the Local Government . Board and they would indicate if they were not satisfactory he would ask Mr. Houghton not to press his resolution. With regard to the three cases referred to somebody had sent up to the Local Government Board an extract of
Mr. darke's remarks and Dr. Buchanan came down a

few days after, sent by the president of the Local Gov- ernment Board to investigate the cases. ilerequirecl to see the registers of the deaths of the cases alluded ,fik and he then went to Dr. Watkins to make due inquiry. This showed the attention that was given to these

matters by the Local Government Board and no doubt if anything had resulted from the examination of Dr. Buchanan they should have heard something more about it.—Mr. DARHYSHIRE said he did not quite agree with the Clerk when he said that forbearance in carrying out the Vaccination Act had brought about the better state of things. He thought it was just the contrary bald that the determination of that Board to carry out the Act and the bringing of such a number before the magistrates had brought about the better state of things. (Hear, hear.) They could riot expect the officer of that Board to carry out the duties imposed upon him if the Board it- self was giving way, and they must protect the officer when the Local Government Board wrote for an explana- tion why the vaccination was not in a better state. They must say that it wasbecause the Board had not im- pressed it upon the officer, and because—he was going to say—the Board was weak-kneed. (Hear, hear, andi laughter.) 'He agreed with Mr. Houghton that as long' as it was the law they ought to carry it out.—Mr. RAT- CLIFFE said that from a sanitary point of view there was not a healthier township in Lancashire than Newton. They had no back-yards and alleys there. In Warring- ton the people should be vaccinated every day. (Laugh- ter.)—The CHAIRMAN said it was a question they ...wished to approach in as kindly a spirit as possible, becaup the people who refused to have their children'vaccinatedlacfed —though it might be mistakenly—in the interests of their children. For his part he did not think this was the time of the year to take any extraordinarily vigorous action in respect to such people. That Board had by no means failed in its duties, for its officers were instructed to carry out the law. They had before them no com- plaint that their officers were not doing their duty, and, therefore, if Mr Houghton could scalps way to withdraw his resolution he (the chairman) should feel personally obliged to him, not because he thought the proposed action would be inadvisable under certain cupditions, but because he thought that at that time it would be in- opportune.—Mr. JOLLEY asked what was the difference between the returns for 1886 and MT.—Mr. HOUGHTON replied that for the first half of 1887 they were about the same as in 1886.—1 n the course of a little further dis- cussion it was stated that in six of the 13 cases at Earles- town there had been prosecutions, and it was decided that particulars as to each case should be obtained for the next meeting, Mr. Houghton withdrawing his proposal. GUARDIANS SAND CONTRACTS. Mr Iserznwoon asked if members of the Board could enter into contracts with the Board in the name either of a foreman, manager, and partner, and thus take the con- tracts out of the hands of the public generally. Be also alleged that the contract for the erection of a partition at Padgate School was in the name of the foreman of a member of the Board. He had found on looking through the accounts that a great deal of money was paid to members of the Board, but so far they had been shielded by being members Of limited firms, but in this instance he was referring to it was not a limited company.—The CI-VM Said that as far as a limited compang was con- cerned the members did not come under the Act of Par- liament, but apart from that there could be no doubt that a person being a guardian and having an iuterest in a contract was liable to be pursued for a penalty of £5O, which is parable to the person who sues. 1£ a member of the Board was so indiscreet as to enter into a c6ntritet in the name of his foreman he might be sued at the next assizes for £5O. Mr. Isherwood would hate that runedy at law if he liked to enforce it. He (the Clerk) however acLvised to the pffect that it was not desirable for the Board to go behind the names by which contracts were signed, and he mentioned that the contract in question only amounted to £l2 12s.—The CaermoN thought that if contracts were sent in in the manner described it was entirely at the risk of those who sent them in. It would, however, cause endless confusion to the Board if they acted on any other line than that suggested by the clerk. —The discussion on the matter soon after dropped. The relief cases ere then taken.
(To be eoetinued.)

TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 3 1888 AEHIP-CAAdRkS., 1!Y. AND .110 W THEY WILL AFFECT WARRINGTON Al 2! -TAR DISTRICT! NO. 7.—TITE. NEW RAILWAYS. In addition to. the arches Which ' are to carry the • , intended new Portion of the Warrington and Mtrin= ,chatn Railway eve? the various roads between Wash-lane, at Latchford, and the road, to the left from the Dog and Dart, at Grappenh all, the new embankment will also be pierced with roadways in Wilderspool Meadows for the use and convenience of Messrs. Greene], Whitley, and Co., the owners of these meadows. Communication between the fields on both sides of the present embankment is afforded, by an under bridge at a point not far from the Runcorn ,and Latcliford mina', and easily visible to the right of any one walking ,along the banks of that canal from the Black Bear Bridge in the direction of Wilderspool, or to the left of a person going in the opposite direction. This right 'of way into be pro- tided for in the new embankment by an under bridge 40 feet wide close to and opposite the present bridge. At other points of the existing railway, in Wilderspool Meadows,and nearer to Warrington than the' underbridge referred to, there are level cross- ings for intercommunication between the two sides of the railway. 'Here again the right of way is,to be respected and it is 'enacted "fdor the protection of" Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Company, that opposite each level crossing, or at any other points to be mutually agreed upon, there shall be under bridges of suitable width and height thy:nigh the embankment that is to be. It may be a matter of curiosity to some people to know what is to be- come -of the old -railway after the new one has taken its place. At the farther side of Latchford station, wheit it is encroached upon by the channel of the Shin Canal, it wiU, of course, have to be entirely demolished; but for a considerable dis- tance at bath ends there will be no necessity of this kind for its removal, and, so far as we know, with the exception of that part lying in Wilderspool Meadows, there is no direction laid down as to its ultimate treatment. But with regard to the por- tion extending from the commencement of the deviation near Wilderepooll level crossing to the canal, it: is provided that if it shall vest in the Ship Canal Company, and shall cease to be used for rail- way purposes, and shall not be required by the company for other purposes, the lirewery.Company are to have the option of purchasing it prior to any others than the London and North-Western Rail- way Company. This condition likewise applies to any land belonging to the Ship Canal, Company be- tween the existing Warrington and Altrineham railway and the deviation -railway. The Wilder- spool Brewery Company are still further protected by a clause .which provides that if the present means of access and 'frontage of the company to the portion of the existing Warrington ifid Altrinc7 ham railway, through Wilderspool Meadows, or if such portion of the railway shall not continue to be used as a railway, or branch railway, or siding, the Ship Canal Company shall, if requested so to do by' the brewery company, by notice in writing, within two years after the receipt of such notice, make such provision as shall be necessary to give the Brewery Company an equivalent right of access and frontage to the new railway; or in default of this the Brewery Company are to be fully compen- sated for any loss or injury thereby. sustained. As most people are aware, one of, the most for- midable antagonists that the Ship Canal Company had to encounter in. the Parliamentary Committee rooms was the London and North-Western Railway Company, and, though the greatest of our railway corporations may not have succeeded in all it de- sired to do when it began its strenuous opposition to the Ship Canal prlject, it certainly was success- ful in getting some rigorous provisions put into the Ship Canal Act to safeguard its own interests. Some of these provisions, which have reference to the de- viation railways, we will glance at in the present article. With regard to the new embankments, it is provided that .wherever they exceeded fifteen feet in heLlit—as they will do on the greater part of the deviations of both the Warrington and Al- trincham railway and the main lines between Bank Quay and Moore and Daresbury Stations—they are to be so constructed that tke lower half of their height will be of rock or stone, and the remaining part of wood dry material. Before the present Latchford Station is at all interfered with, a new goods- and passenger station is to be made and completed, with suitable approaches, sidings, and signals, at such a point as the principal engineer of the London and North-Western Company shall reasonably re- quire. Before the railway company can be required to abandon any part of their present lines, or works, three conditions are specifically 'mentioned as hav- ing to be complied with by the Canal Company. The first is that everything in cOnnection with the .new portions of the railway, such as stations, sid- ings, apparatus, and all other requisites and conve- niences, have to be in all respects completed to the reasonable satisfaction of the Railway Company's principal engineer. And, farther than this, the new lines will have to be in existence and in. working order six months, for during that period they will be used for goods traffic alone, the passenger trains being still run along the older route. The second condition is that at the end of six months the tie* works will have to be approved by the Board of. Trade ; aand the third provisos states that, unless at the expiration of a still farther period of three months after the new lines and works have secured the approval of the Board of Trade, they are also approved by the engineer of the Railway Company—or in case of difference, by an engineer of the Board of Trade— as being in as good and workable a condition In all respects, reasonable wear and tear excepted, as when they were approved by the Board of Trade at the end Of six months they will have to be main- tained at the expense ef the Canal Company until the old lines are finally abandoned by the London and North-Western Railw.ay Company. The new railways are to be constructed without obstructing ' or impeding or in any way interfering with the free ' and uninterrupted and safe use of the existing rail- ways and sidings: and if any obstruction or impedi- ment is caused the Canal 'Company are to forfeit to the London and North-Western Railway Company the modest sum of .£2OO as ascertained damages for every hour or part of an hour during which the ob- struction or interference continues; and this, be it remembered, is without prejudice to any remedy the London and North-Western Railway • Company may have by injunction or otherwise. It may be gathered from what is stated above that for some time, for six months at all events and it may be longer, there will be in the neighbourhood of Warrington duplicate sets of railways working, namely, on the WarringtOn and Altrincham railway and on the railways which run from Bank Quay south to Crewe and Chester. One set comprising the railways now existing will be used for passenger trains and the other set—the deviation railways that are to be—will be used exclusively for goods traffic. These six or more months may be said to be the period of .probation of the new portions of railway, and during this time it is probable that much extra expense will be incurred. All these ex- penses will, as might be expected, be borne by the Ship Canal Company, who, it is expressly down in the Ship Canal Act, shall "mike full compensation to the North-Western Company .for all damages or injury which shall, or may be sustained or suffered by them in consequence or byreason of the eicercise of the powers of this Act 'with respect to the said deviation railways, and in respect of any additional exßense to which that company will be put in maintaining their railways and, works, when deviated under the authority a this Act, or con- Sequent upon such deviations; and also in respect of any increased expense of working the traffic on their railways, including signalling ; ' and the com- pensation to be paid will be. such a sum, failing agreement, as shall be determined. by arbitration under or according to the provisions of the Lands Clauses Acts. LEGAL PROCEEDINGS.

Applicaticn was made on Saturday to Mr,,Justice North, in the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, for a direction to the liquidators to dis- tribute among the ordinary shareholders £4 a share out of the purchase money paid by the Manchester Ship Canal Company for the Navigation Company's undertakings. The effect of his lordship's previous decision in the same matter was that all the share- holders, ordinary and preference, stood on the same footing in regard to the distributiop of the surplus of the fund, and the ordinary shareholders applied to the liquidators for the payment to them of so much as they were admittedly entitled to; but the liquidators, dealing with such large figures, declined to "Act without the direction of the court.

-- -- Mr. Cozens Hardy, Q.C., M.P., made the application on behalf of Mr. Birch,•who had been appointed to repre- sent the ordinary shareholders for the purpose, as he had previously been appOinted to raise the question between the ordinary and preference shareholders. He stated that the assets, after providing for the liqui- dated and unliquidated claims, -including all law charges and costs of liquidation, were esti- mated by the liquidators to amount to £830,000. of -which his lordship's decision gave the ordinary shareholders seveqrthirteenths and the preference share- holders six-thirteenths. The argument on the part of the ordinary shareholders was that they were entitled to the whole, and an appeal was pending on that pointd It had been suggested that the preference shareholders might have a right to have their dividends equalised with those of the ordinary shareholders, and conceding that for the present purpose the extra dividend would amount;to £62,000, the ordinary shareholders having had 8 per cent., while the preference shareholders had had a fixed dividend of 5 per cent. There had also been paid a bonus of ss. per share, which would make another £7,500, so that £70.500 would be sufficient to meet any possible claim that the preference shareholders might establish beyond the share given to them by the lodgment, and deducting 'that sum there would remain £759,500 for distribution. eeven-thirteenths of that would be more than £400,000, which sum, as there were 100,000 ordinary shares, would give the holders the £4 a share which the petitioner asked for. Mr. Justice North doubted whether he could interfere in a voluntary liquidation in the way suggested. Mr. Cozens Hardy reminded his lordship that the liquidators had told the ordinary shareholders ,that they would not pay the money without the direction of the court.

Mr. J. Napier Biggins, Q.C., who appeared for the liquidators, did not apprehend that there would be any question as to the jurisdiction of the court. There were, • he stated, considerable unliquidated claims, but the liquidators were satisfied that they would not amount to more than £50,000, and as far as they coald see £BOO,OOO would remain for division if matters sto•Vd exactly as they were left by his lordship's decision; but other ques- tions might be raised by the preference shareholders, and larger law costs might be incurred than were at pre- sent anticipated. Mr. Swinton Eady, for Mr. Scliolefield, the representa- tive of the preference shareholders asked his lordship not to make any immediate order shareholders, the distribution of the fund. 'lf the ordinary shareholders would accept his lordships's judgment, and, then make an end of the litigation, there would be no reason for the liquidators to continue to hold so large a sum ; but the fund once distributed could not be got back, and the ordinary shareholders would be encouraged to carry on a protrac- ted litigation, in which they would have everything to ri gain and nothing to lose. • I Mr. Justice North gave liberty to the liquidators to make an interim payment of £3 a share to the ordinary shareholders, but ordered the costs of the application to be paid out of the ordinary shareholders' share of the fund.

JOHN MORi.EY AT OXFORD.—Mr. John Morley re- plied at the Oxford Union Society on Wednesday night, to Lord Randolph Churchill's speech of last week. He said he thought that Lord Randolph's prophecies with respect to the probable course of events in regard to self-government in Ireland would within two orthree years be seen to have been as futile, as random, and as ill-founded ah the prophecy he made in 1884 as to the effects of the enlargement of thed franchise in Ireland. The right hon! gentleman ridi- culed the noble lord's reasons for shelving Hcirne and said that if the time ever carne when this •*country should be called upon to face a world in arms she would only have her resources undivided to meet the 'world on condition that her statesmen and her people had plucked up the root of strife in Ireland and turned the . domestic enemy at our gates Into our friend and our ally. The Crimes Act had not achieved ant' of the ends for which it was passed, and while not defending all that the Irish members had done, he claimed for them that they had wrung advantages from Parliament and from the land- lords for the downtrodden people of Ireland. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY. -NIGHT.

The polling at Deptford, though it does not seat Mr. Blunt in the House of Commons, is an addition to the almost unbroken series of Liberal triumphsra fresh line in the writing on the wall at which the Con- servatives are looking on with growing apprehension. Mr. Darling has been returned by a majority of 275. That is considerably less than half ot the majority ,at the last eleetion—less by 352 votes. In the pecu- liar circumstances of the time, the highly strained condition ef politics, and. the tremendous efforts

made to retain- for the Ministry what has always been a Tory borough, this is a distinct advance of the Liberal flag. But there is another fact to be taken into account, which immensely adds to the significance of the result. Deptford was contested in 1885, at which time Liberalism, reinforced by tlie ' recent Reform 13ill,was sweeping like an irresistible wave over the country. In the main result Mr. Gladstone was returned by an overwhelming major- ity. Then came the adoption of the Home Rule scheme, the shock to weaker brethren, and the revulsion of 1886, when the Conservative majority at Deptford and elsewhere materially swelled. What Deptford showed yesterday was that in that borough, situated within the influence of the great Tory camp of London, Liberalism has not only re- gained its position of 1885, but has battered it by 92 votes. This is a pregnant fact, the bearing of which will be seen in the incontestable assertion that if a General Election were to take place to- morrow, and in every borough and county, there were to be a proportionate increase of the. Liberal vote, Mr. Gladstone would be returned to power by an overwhelming majority. . .

-This Week the Ho—use of Commons has been meet- ing at three o'clock in the afternoon, completing opkosed business by midnight, and ioyously going home immediately afterwards. This is an amizing and complete revolution in procedure that alraost takes away the breath of old stagers.. Yet it was completed in a single night's sitting of moderate length and most encouraging dullness. It really begins to look as if "after all," as Mr. Goschen once said, it is aby no means undesirable thing to have an occis. ional brief spell of Conservative Govern- ment. It was in such circumstances that the.coun- try got a truly Liberal Reform Bill at the hands of Mr. Disraeli. and it is in such circumstances that the House of Commons has at last, after grumblirjg round the* subject for twenty years. and pottering with it for ten, suddenly and swiftly obtained a thorough Reform of Parliamentary Procedure. Had Mr. Gladstone been in office just now, it is prob- able that, looking back upon his experience ot the autumn session of 1884 he would not have dared ,to bring in such a boldly simple scheme ,as is now actually in operation.* When he introduced the closure, he was glad enough, after 14 nights' ob- struction, to pass a practically unworkable scheme, involving the retention within call of the whip of 200 members. Even this concession the very men who Rave now placed the closure on a working basis, grudgingly yielded. Now they come, hat in hand, with a really drastic schem,e, and beg the House of Commons to accepeqt. "Why, certainly," say the Liberal opposition, and the thing is done. The ruyiditrwith which this great and beneficial

change in prOcedure has been miZde is typical of the general condition of affairs in the House of Com- mons at the present Moment. It is a place I have know q pretty intimately for fourteen years, and Ido ilk recall any period when the prospects of doing business were brighter. The only parallel was in'the session pf 1874, when Mr. Disraeli had

just surprisingly been returned to power. But at eliat time there was no work to be done. Parlia- ment and the nation were a.little wearied with the overstrained energy with which the colossal work accomplished by the Parliament of 1868 had been carried forward. Mr. Disraeli was just the man to give the required rest, and so the session droned easily through, the Opposition being practically derasO. Things are very different to-day. There is work to do, and a dispoeition to do it. The Local Government Bill, which Mr. Ritchie is to introduce on Monday fortnight, will suffice for an average session. Under the Wise and magnanimous policy by which tile Opposition ,is just now guided, there is a rare opportunity of passing a satisfactory measure. I should say on the.whole that the country is more likely to get a thoroughly good Local Government Bill this aession than it would, sax, five sessions hence, when the Liberals are again in power, and, having settled the Home Rule question, are able to turn their attentiorr to the demands of Great Britain. As has been shown in respect of the Closure Rule, the best corrective of crass Conserva- tism is not in a powerful Liberal Ministry in office, But'a rather tottering band of Tories. It is not probable that Sir Morel! Mackenzie will receive in direct shape any mohey fee that will re- munerate him for the expenditure of time incurred by his visit to San Remo. In these degenerate days no royal personage of German birth or extraction is accustomed to equal the munificence of the tradi-,1 tional potentate. But in other ways it will be well worth his while. He leaves an enormous practice in London, a good deal of which is daily dealt with , by histiocum tenons. But even in San RBIIIO his time , is not fully occupied with attendance upon the • Crown Prince, and in wrangles with the jealous German doctors whom the well-meant but unfortu- nate interference of " the Emperor sends to the Crown Prince's bedside. Wealthy patients are glad enough of the excuse of repairing to San Remo at this season of the year to aee their favourite doctor, and Sir Morel! Mackenzie has a morning levee only less numerous and less remunerative than that which awaits him in London. As for the poor Crown Prince, who has finally established the already well grown fortune of the English specialist, his life is slowly but surely fading out. The semi-official tele i geams which appear n the papers, throughout Europe still make the best of itt But some of Sir Morel! Mackenzie's professional brethren in London, in daily and intimate communication with him, know too well his opinion of the case. Lord Salisbury has been shanied into something like a withdrawal of the too cute letter written o,n his behalf by his solicitor shirking responsibility for a communication in ,which the Prime Minister bad instructed his private secretary to brand Mbr. Brad- laugh as a wilful perjurer. This letter found its way to ' the newspapers, and Lord Salisbury, chal- lenged to facilitate trial before a jury, took refuge in the plea that he had not authorised the publica- tion. Since then he has slightly shifted his ground. But as yet Mr. Bradlaugh hp,a no means of bringing him into court as a defendant. Bat unless the action threatened by Mr. Peters against Mr. Brad- laugh beltbindoned, we may yet see Lord Salisbmy in court. He will be summoned as a witness, and will have full opportunity of disproving Mr. Brad- laughrs reiterated and precise statement that Lord Salisbury had provided funds for a political meeting got up in Trafalgar-square. A fortnight ago I related the retest episode in the moving history of Mr. Benson, the forger of world- wide renown. Your readers 'will doubtleas remem- ber that immediately upon his release from a term of penal servitude, he Was crossing the Atlantic with Mr. Abbey, to whom he introduced himaelf • under an assumed name as the correspondent of the- " Paris ligaro." He learned from Mr: ' Abbey all ' his plans for a tour in the -United States, which in- cluded a visitto the city of Mexico. As soon as he landed.in the States Benson .posted off to the city of Mexico, introduced himself as Marcus Mayer, agent iii advance of Mr. Abbey, sold thousands Of tickets for Patti's first concert, and then levanted with the money. After a sharp hunt he was arres- ted and taken to New York, where he wis charged with forgeiry. The London police, who take a pro- found'interest in Benson's movements, have just re- ceived a communication from their colleagues in New York, which shows the forger still triumphant. His great-coup at the city of Mexico was planned

with exquisite skill and foresight. On his arrival he presented to the manager of the theatre which had been engaged for Patti a letter, purporting to be signed by Mr. Abbey, in vlbhich Benson was introduced as Marcus Mayer, and was authorised to issue tickets, take the money and make all ar- rangements.. The police.relied upon the prodnc- tion of this letter to establish the charge of forgery. But on sending to the City of Mexico for it they discoverell it was—riot in existence. Benson, knowing that in order to establish a charge of for- gery it would be necessary to put the forged docu- ment in evidence, had possessed himself Of tile letter by an ingenious device. A day or two aftft sending the forged letter to the manager, he called on him to explain that he had mislaid his letter 'of introduction to the United States Minister at Mexico, and begged the manager to give him Mr. Abbey's letter, whieh, he said, would serve that purpose. The unsuspecting manager returned the incriminating document, which Benson carried off With him when he left the City of Mexico, with pockets full of dollars drawn from the deluded public. _

At each succeeding AcademY there is always a great deal of interest felt about the latest associ- ate. The public are anxious to see whether the choice of the profession was on the whole good or not. This year the work of the youngest member will, for other reasons, be probably the most talked- of picture on the walls. Mr. Richmond has just returned from Berlin, where Prince Bismarck has given him sittings. The new associate is best known, by his portraits of women and children. He has preeminently sympathy with grace and delicacy, and feminine loveliness. What will he do with Prince Bismarck? Mr. 101 l will be more at home with Mr. Gladstone. The two portraits will be amongst "the pictures of the year.' lam glad to see that the poor old Grosvenor is not to be quite boycotted. Some at least of the old fiiends are faithful. The rival institution, which is being built day and night, has plenty of money at its back, and its success is assured.

div.p: TION.
DEPUTATION TO THE WATCH COMMITTEE.

A meeting of the committee of the Warrington Temperance Federation was held at the 'Coffee Tavern; in Horsemarket-street, on Monday eSening, when the subject of Mr. Justice Grantham's obser- vations at Liverpool on the drink traffic came under consideration. It was thought desirable that .the substance of these remarks should be made as public as possible, and that a deputation should be appoin- ted to wait upon the Watch Committee of the Town Council with a view to calling attention to his lord- ship's remarks, and the desirability of more strictly enforcing the law as it affects licensed houses. Ac- cordingly, when the Watch Committee met on Thursday afternoon, they were waited upon by a deputation consiOng of the Rev John Yonge, Coun- cillor H. Roberts, Mr. E. Twiss, and Mr. John Walker.

Councillor Ronitins, in introducing the deputa- tion, said that they, as members of the Warrington Temperance Federation, were much struck with the remarks that Mr. Justice Grantham had made with regard tb drink and crime, and the desirability of punishing publicans who served liquor to intoxica- ted persons, and they had theeefore thought it de- sirable to wait upon the Watch Committee. They were not there to find fault in any way with the action of the police or of the Watch Committee, but it was their wish to act in harmony With all parties with a view to ultimately lessening the number of offences in the borough. The Rev. Jogri YONGE said that it was far from

-- their wish that they should be thought to be there to complain of what was being done, but they de- sired to nromote the welfare of the boroulth by les- sening drunkenness as far as possible. The Tem- perance Federation, reeognising the Watch Com- mittee as the body having authority in regard to these matters, had drawn up,a memorial upon the subject, which, with their permission, he would read. Mr. Yonge then read the memorial, which was as follows :

"To His Worship the Mayor and the members of the Watch Committee. Gentlemen, we the undersigned ratepayers, representing the Warrington Temperance Federation, respectfully beg to call your attention to the number, of persons convicted for drunkenness in War- rington in 1887, as shown by the Chief Constable's re- port, and request you to compare therewith the number of licensed victuallers and beerhouse keepers convicted during the same period. In this connection, we desire you to consider the remarks made by Mr. Justice Gran- tham at the recent Liverpool Assizes. His Lordship, in passing sentence upon John Gordon for the attempted murder of his wife—a crime committed under the in- fluence of drink, said—" He did not know what' could be done to punish publicans. Their great art seemed to be to get a house at the corner of a stseet, and they had given the name to those who were so well known in Liverpool, and were responsible for the men who stood at corners, andwent in at one door, and out at the other. That they had difficulties to contend with in mitny plaza( he admitted, but he was certain they did not do as they might do, and as they ought to do. He would not do more at that time than desire that the attention ' of the magistrates might be drawn to the facts which had come out at that trial, so that they might even now tare steps in that case, because it was not too late to institute proceedings by which people wile served drunken people might be punished:. With these remarks of the learned judge before us, we feel most strongly that the conviction of only four publicans, as against 500 convicted for drunkenness is most inadequate, and we earnestly hope that you will impress upon the police the import,nee of endeavouring to trace each case of drunkenness to its source, and of prosecuting, wherever possible, the publican who serves drunken people with Intoxicating liquor. In presenting the petition, we desire to cast no reflection upon the police. Wc are only anxious, in the interests of temperance and morality, that the law should be more rigidly enforced. Signed— John Tonge, Edward Twiss, John H. Gornall, John Walker, and H. Roberts." Proceeding,. Mr. Yonge. said he had little to add beyond what was stated in the memorial. They did think that in viewS of the number of persons i who were convicted for drankenness--500 n 1887 :—in Warrington, that there was a great disparity when only four publicans and beerhou.se keepers were convicted for supplying drink to drunken per- sons That was the piint to which they more es- pecially wished to direct the attention of the Watch Committee with a view to seeing that the offending publicans were summoned and convicted. The CHAIRMAN (Alderman Harrison) and other members of the Watch Committee remarked that they were glad to receive such a deputation, as they I had one common object in view. They wished to point out that it was exceedingly difficult thing US get convictions for dipplying drink to drunken 1 persons, and that Warrington was not in an excep- tional position in the disparity which had been pointed out in this respect. Liverpool and several other• places were mentioned where there were ; but few convictions of publicans for these offences. Mr. JOHN WALKiIn said that the deputation fully 1 recognised the great difficulties by which they were s surrounded, but their Peeling was that something could be done in the direction indicated, if ; special instructions were given to the police. He' noticed that at Runcorn the police had . in one case observed a, drunken man enter . a publichouse, they had followed him„ and as it was found that the publican'was supplying him ; with more drink, it led to a conviction. It did cer- tainly seem extraordinary that they . should have r 500 people convicted for drunkenness iq one year in I Warrington, while only four .publicatis were con- - victed for supplying drink to persons who had had 1 too much. There was anothet matter heshould like

to mention. It was that there was reason to sus- pect in some cases that persons who supplied drink under off4icenses were guilty of infractions of the law by allowing liquor to be chunk on the premises. The returns for Warrington, however, showed that I no persons had been summoned for several years for offences of that dais. He thought that wag a mat- ter which might be worthy of attention, for there was no denying that these off-licenses had been the means of a large increase of drunkenness amongst females. The record of the last ten years in War- rington showed that in 1878 there were 81 females convicted for drunkenness, and in 1887 the number was 1168. This showed that the convictions bad ' more than doubled in that period, and it was.a fact which they would feel with him was a distressing one. it was satisfaqtory to note that in the same period there had been a decrease of convictions for 'drunkenness amosigst males from 592 in 183 to 332 'in 1887. It was much to be deplored than the re-, verse had taken place amongst the female" popula- tion, dud he trusted that if the off-license holders were Mind to be guilty of breaches.of the law their licenses would be refused when a renewal was sought. . The CHAiRatA.N, then intimated that the commit- tee would give, 'due attention to what the deputatiOn had said upon the subject, and that they were de- sirous of efficiently carrying out the licensing laws. • If they could see their way to improving upon what they were doing they should certainly take Steps to carry out such improvement. They were 'always careful to impress, 'upon new police officers espe- cially, the necessity of seeing that the law was

rigidly obeyed, and that offenders,against tho 114 sing law were brought to justice. Councillor ROBE UT'S then thanked the oh airman the committee for the courteous way in which deputation had been received. He was sure they would quite understand him when he said they had no desire to act inn spirit of compl but were wishful to aid the authorities in any acres they might think fit to take in carrying the law. The deputation then withdrew.

SHOCKING CRVELTY TO A CAT AT STRETTON.

At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a labourer, named John Miller, was charged with hav- ing, at Stretton, on the 7th February, ill-treated a cat.—lnspector Aplin. of the R.S.P.C.A., pmseeuted, and stated that at about half-past three On the after- noon of the day named defendant was seen coming down stairs in his house with a dats in his hand. He dashed it violently on the floor, k4.ked it acrdss the room, and afterwards took it up by its ears and struck it several times with a piece of iron or a stick, and finally tossed it into the yard and left it to the mercy of the world. The girl who saw him do this went for a policeman, who found that the .poor animal's shoulder was broken, its back bruised, its tail cut, and blood coming out of its mouth and ears.—Annie Jackson. the girl who had seen the cat ill-used, gave evidence corroborative of this state- ment.—P.C. Harrison deposed that when he went to defendant's house he found the cat lying in the coal- house on some shavings. .It was howling in a piteous manner, and when he set it on its feet it could not stand. Part of its tail Was also crushed gat. He took it to the police station, and kept it there till Inspector Aplin saw it.—lnspector Aplin said that on the nep, dayle found the cat in such. agony that he ordeAd it to be drowned, which was done. He afterwards saw defendant, who said that the reason he had beaten the cat was that it had made a "mess" in the house.—Defendant denied that he had treated the cat in the manner described. He had, he said, "got very fond of the kitten, and , would sooner hurt himsW than hurt it."—The Chair- man (Mr. E. Greenall) said it was a very cruel case indeed, and it was all nonsense to talk about his fondness for the kitten. If he had been fond of it he had shown his fondness in, an extraordinary way. He would be fined -10 s and costs, in all 375, or in default of payment a month's imprisonment.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Union Workhouse, on Thurs- day, when there were present—Mr. j:Fisher (chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. J. Lowe, J. Buckley, J. Elli- son, J. Ranson, J. Burchall, H. A. Graves J. W. Ware- ing, J. Kenwright, J. Le.Atherbarrciw, W. 'a. Ashton, E. Syder, W. Swift, J. Matthews, T. Eatock, 3. Whallpi, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). (f: '..Tttx DEATH OF Mn. JOSEPH JACKSON.—The Chairman said he extremely regretted that for the third time in successive meetings he had to announce the death of • a member of the Board. This time it was ene'of the oldest members of the Board, Mr. Joseph Jackson. Mr. Jack- son was always ready to fight the battle pf the pder, and assisted those with his purse and influence who required assistance. They all deplored his loss, aßcl he moved that a letter of condolence and sympathy be: sent to his widow and family.—Mr. Lowe seconded the motion, whieh w,as supported by Mr. Ranson and Mr. Leatherbanrow, all 'of whom spoke of the late Mr. Jackson as a true and warm- hearted Guardian.—The Motion was passed;, and the clerk was instructed to take the usual slieps for securing

the —election of a successor. RELIRF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 594 inmates of the house this week, 559 last week, and 481 in the cOrrespending week last year; 67 vagrants had been relieved, against 40 last week. • , THE FttiE Betomm.—At a meeting of the Fire Brigade Committee, on,the 20th February, the tender of Messri. , Boyden Brothers, St. Helens, fon uniforms, and of Mr. Osborn Henderson. St. Helens, for boots for the mom-; hers of the Fire Brigade, were accepted.—The inniites were passed. , , • THE WonetiousE AL7ERATIONS.—At a meeting of the Building Committee, on the 20th February, the architect submitted amended specifications for proposed alterations and additions to the Workhouse, which was ap- proved, and the clerk was instructed to advertise for tenders. PRECAUTIONS AGAINST SMALLPDX.— Localin Govern- ment Board write granting its consent to the weekly , attendance`of vaccination officers at their stations where vaccination was usually perfo•med at particular periods' of the year, in order to prevent the spread of smallpox. They also suggested that the Guardians should consider the advisability of having a house to house visitation by the vaccination officers in order to secure the vaccination of every unvaccinated person, and to promotete-vaceina- tion.—The Clerk was instructed to carry out these arrangements if necessary. Tye WINDLE VACCT.—The Local Government Beard wrote, stating that an order would shortly be issued for the election of a Guardian for Windle in the room of the. late Mr. W. Birchall. A DEAF eND DUMB PATIENT:.—The Clerk read corres- pondence from the Local Government Board in reference to the case of John Newing, of St. Helens, timekeeper at Messrs. Mcßryde's chemical works, *ho applied for part payment of the cost of maintaining his deaf and durnb' son in the Deaf and Dumb School, Manchester. He Stated that his wages were 30s Per week, and he had five young children to leep. He wished to have the son in que.:ition educated in such a manner that he would not in the future become chargeable to the xates.—The clerk was instructed to reply that the Guardians did not con- sider the applicant's position such as would warrant them granting the relief asked. P THE HUTTON VACCINATION OFFICER. A letter was read from Mr. John Pendleton, resigning his post as vac- cination officer for the Huyton district,' and Mr. Ashton gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board he would move that a successor be appointed. Tlig DEATH OF MR. W. BIRCHALL. —PI A letter was read from Mrs Birchall acknowledging receipt of the Board's letter of condolence on the death of her husband, and thanking the Guardians for their expressions of . sympathy for her and their appreciation of his services. THE CARE OP CATHOLIC OIRLS.—A letter was read from Mrs Ince-Blundell, of the Girls' Mutual Aid Society, asking permission to visit the Roman Catholic Oils leaving the Workhouse or workhouse schools, and going into service.—The Rev. Dean Finegan said the objects of the society was to look after girls after leaving schbol up to the time of their marriage, having in view the dangereto which the girlswere exposed.—The Guardians granted the application. TILE INFECTIOUS ROSPITALQUESTION.—Mr. J. T. Allen, clerk to the Witine,s Local Board, wrote on the 16th Feb- rue:7 stating that in reference to the charges for main- taining pauper cases in the Widnes Infectfous Hospital, the Local Board had decided to accept such patients only on the Guardians :undertaking to pay 3s per day for each patient, and to provide medical attendance. As those terms were almost identical with those offered to the St. Helens Corporation a few months ago, the Local Board thought there need be no difficulty in arriving at a settlement.—Mr.'iVareing reported that the depiitation of Guardians appointed at the last meeting had waited upon the Health Committee of the St. Helens Corpora- tion, who had declined to entertain the-- Guardians' defi- nition of a pauper, and .would not " budge"' from their former position oicharging 4s 8d Per day for each pa- tient. The deputation declined those terms. He was pleased they had received so favourable an offer from the Widnes Loaal Board, and. he moved that the terms named by them be accepted.—The Rev. Dean Finegan seconded.—Mr. Graves asked if the case would apply to paupers outside Widnes.—Mr. Wareing: No; only to those in Widnes.—The Rev. Dean Finegan: Will our medical officer, have to attend ,to these yeses 7—Mr. Wareing: We shall have toprovide a medical attendant, who I presume will be, as a matter of course, our own medical officer in Widnes.—The motion was then passed. • APPOINTMENTS.—On the motion of Mr. Wareing, Dr. Cooper was re-appointed medical officer foi the Widnes (Lower) district for the ensuing lasnonths a salary of £7O per annum.—On the 'm ion of Mr. Graves, Dr, Jolt was appointed Dr. Scott's deputy medical Officer for the Woolton district. THE ESTIMATE.—The clerk submitted his estimate Of probable expenditure ffor the six months ending 29th September next, which amounted to £25,460, -against £23,789 in the corresponding period last year: The estimate wa.s approved. This was the principal business.

CALIFORNIA AND BRITISH WOMEN. Sir,—The enclosed letter just received from the mother of one of the nine ladies who had gone under my aus- pices at the date of Mr. Mortimer's strange letter of Jan. 11th is most cheering to me. Others equally cheering come to me. Many Californian towns, hearing what I am doing, write to say they will form committees of Christian ladies to receive as many as I can send. I am careful that only the right kind go, examining their cre- dentials of character and ability. No one who will work can starve in a country like California.—Truly yours, M. E. PARKER. [copv.3 Paddington Cottage, Warrington, Feb. 27, 1888. Dear Mrs. Parker,—l have wanted to write to you be- fore, but waited, hoping to send my daughter's diary to you. I have felt very indignant with some of the letters which have appeared in the papers, especially Mr. White Mortimer's, as it is so contrary to wfiat I have heard from my daughter. She writes most warmly of the kindness shown her by every one, especially by your particular friends. She adds—

"The climate is truly delightful. The nights are cool, but the days are like our June. There is no doubt about the demand for educated women, for as soon as it was known that we had arrived we were inundated with ladies seeking interviews, and offering salaries from £3B to £6O per annum tb become members of their families and share their duties and love on terms of equality with them as we should in our own homes. I have been here three weeks, and find the family most kind and con- siderate. The work is done by 3-3 O; no meal after that but tea at 5-30. I have plenty of leisure." This does not look like being a "domestic servant," and expected to do the work of two or three, as Mr. Mortimer says. I may say that my daughter has £6O a year. She said on leaving that if she did no like Cali- fornia money was to be sent for her rettlk : but there is no need of that now. _ _
Virith kindest regards and sympathy, I am, yours very truly,
M. WRloffrsoN.
TIM MAYOR AND THE PUGILISTS.

_ Sir,—" Independent," who puts' on the -gloves in defence of the pugilists, and of the Mayor's action in paironrsing their entertainment, seems to have, to use a slang expression, got "the needle" to a considerable extent in consequence of 9, short letter of mine that ap- peared in a recent issue of your paper. In that letter, as far as I now recollect,' I Aced the simple question whether it was consistent with the dignity of the high position of a Mayor to act as patron of a boxing enter- tainment, even though the proceeds of such entertain- ment were to be handed over for the benefit of a chari- table institution. Apparently " Independent " thhaks that the Mayor did a very proper thing, and he is quite entitled to hold his own opinion, just as much Is I am entitled to take my own view of the matter. Your cor- respondent is quite right in supposing that I did not attend the Gaiety on the occasion in question. He asserts that boxing formed only a small portion of the entertainment. That may be so, but in the advertising of the affair the place of honour was, without question, given to the pugilistic portion, and mention was also made of the patronage of his Worship. Mr. John Knifton may be a very paragon of virtue for anything I know. Ido not in the least object to him, but I do very much object to the practise of boxing in public, which has received such a stimulus since cer- tain recent pugilistic events came off. By-the-bye, is this the same Knifton who should have met another knight of the fist named Smith and did not ? Were not two or three futile efforts made to bring off the encoun- ter, and did not the police, in some unaccountable way, get on their track? It is consistent wit). the diginity of the office of churchwarden to dodge the police and try to evade? If this Kniften is the same man I think he should either cease to be a professional pugilist, or cease to be a churchwarden.

With regard to the patronage of J. L. Sullivan by the Prince of Wales, it is not necessary for me to say much, as Ido not follow His Royal Highness as an example. It is perhaps, after all, a question as to which of the two was most honoured by•the little intercourse—the Pugilist or the Prince.—Yours Rze.,
ANTI-PUGILIST.

div.head: HAS PENKETH A MEMBER ?
div.p: HAS PENKETH A MEMBER ?

Sir,—Your report of the Board of Guardians' meeting in last Saturday's issue astonishes me—the end of it I mean. It was bad enough to be laughed. at when orally before the Board; but is it not the height of MeanifeS9 to ridicule my memory? Do the Guardians know that any office of public trust is at once and completely filled to the satisfaction of mysdif atd immediate supporters ' when my great name is simply attached thereto? Please to understand me, for I am not vain and self-conceited, and have no affectation. Ido not mean great in a busi- ness sense. A man must try ! try ! try again ! and lam attached to a business-going concern at list, and to luck lam trusting. But lam great, sir, in my own estima- tion—who isn't? Great at playing soldiers, great at Jingoism, and great at playing. "ducks and drakes." Surely my name is enough 'without my presence. In further mitigation of seeming—only seeming—neglect, I may say that I look after the township assessment, al- though the committee do not sufficientlyrespect one holding a seat oil four committees; also note the following quo- tation—" There are no poor people in Penketh, except the shopkeepers "—vide Lord Cross's speech at the Bakeries' Exhibition before the Chairman of the Com- mittee of Ways and Wass. lam not without experien&, having been on a board before and resigned on my own account. In conclusion, I will just throw out a suggestion. Could not the Guardians' fortnightly meeting be conduc- ted as we manage the county affairs here? •

" Dear old pals, jolly old pals, Rambling together in all sorts of weather, &c." Were there more Jolley fellows on the Board, and' were the meetings held at the close of the day in any proper house of business, none would attend more regularly than yours truly, Penketh, Feb. 20th.
A GUARDIAN.

P.S.—I may say that it was Dr. Arithmetic's opinion during the contest, and at the time I was elected to a seat on the Doard, that I should more properly have been elected to the House; but, however undignified it may appear, I would rather be generalissimo in my own town- ship than aspire to a position of honour that would not ‘s shoot " me—as Paddy said.

div.head: ENGLAND'S COAL SUPPLY.
div.p: ENGLAND'S COAL SUPPLY.

Sir,—lt must be admitted that at the meetinglast week of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society Mr. Robert Davies, in his few interesting remarks, touched upon a very important. subject, whitn he referred to the predicted exhaustion of dur coal supply. What would England be without her coal-beds? They are not merely the corner-stone but the entire foundation of her great industrial edifice. Deprived of them she might not sink back into that "Wild England," of which a lately de-. ceased writer gives us a forecast or even into pastoral unp9pulousness, but at best she could but retain her ocean carrying trade and be a somewhat enlarged copy of maritime Venice and Holland. Most of her great factories would ciiikappear an.d with them the population they sustain. According to Mr. Davies, the prediction is that in about 120 years time we shall be without our coal, but I think the general* estimate gives us a few' more years grace than that. The worst of it is, however, that long before the final exhaustion ,prernonitary symptoms will be felt, and I have seen it stated that the Northumbrian ceral-fields are even now much less productive than they used to be. It will be something like the beginning of the end when coals have to be taken to Newcastle. It is true that substitutes for coal are being talked about, but some of the suggestions that are made are not calculated to make us feel very hopeful. One of them is that beated air and water from the interior of the earth might be utilised, but unfor- tunately the modern Glendower who can call the spirits of heat from the " vasty deep "has not yet been heard of. it is said that at Pesth, in Hungary, a deep hole has been dug in order to bring heated water from the interior of the earth to warm the houses in that city, but I have not heard that the expmiment has turned out successful. Another scheme is that: of so focussing the rays from the sun as to generate steam, but this, even if it can be done at all, can only be done in tropical and sub-tropical countries. It will be agreed that, if we had to depend on the rays of the sun in England it would often be difficult to "get steam up." The most hopeful project of all for supplying the place of coal is thatefor producing electricity by water power, the water power to be derived from rivers, streams, and even tidal waves. In this case practice has already to some extent succeeded theory, and it is said that the fine residence of one of the most recently created peers of the realm, Lord Armstrong, is entirely lighted by electricity from a dynamo, operated upon by a small stream. But even as regards electricity it must be confessed that England, with its small and placidly flowing rivers, will be at a great disadvantage when com- pared with many other countries, with their Amazons, Mississipis, and Ganges, to say nothing of the great cataracts—inexhaustible sources of waterpower—which exist in so many parts of the world. In short, sir, the more we think of it the more we must be convinced that, whatever may be said about certain other unions more talked of, the union between the isdustrial pre-eminence of England and her coal supply is a vital one.—Yours, Warrington, Feb. 28, 1888. RECLUSE.

div.head: WARRINGTON .CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON .CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

Sir,—There is more than "A Lookeron "amused by the correspondence re the above society, the amusement be- ing increased through tIA great Lord Beaconsfield being introduced into a shopping argument. Well, sir, the precedent being set, I should like to remind "A Looker on" that Mr. Thomas Carlyle informs us that thls world is inhabited by men mostly fools, and I will endeavour to show him on which head the cap fits in this case, be it " A member's" or" A Looker on's." I will first hasten to assure our inquisitive critic that half-penny checks are considered to be not worth the cost, either in , money, time, cr trouble, which are all Money under certain circumstances, and I can assure him that any judicious housewife will always arrange to keep her expenditure out of the halfpence. Further, if tohe members desire halfponce in checks, they have only to attend a quarterly meeting and pass a resolution to that effect.

"Looker on" affects not to talk clap-trap, but does not disdain to quote some prices, prices which affect the working-man very little, and win certainly fail to do so, so long as the petty trust shops and the stores stand be- tween him and.wfiat he desires to see. Again, let me remind "Looker on "that our society pays 5 per cent per annum on all trading members' deposits, deposits that are steadily growing, the interest being added at 3d per £1 every quarter. I come now to the difference of the prices given, and would ask the reader always to remember my remarks as to standing deposits. Well, sir, I admit a difference, but I cannot admit that it rims through all things in the smile ratio, and I fearlessly make the following asser- tion :—A working-man with five children will spend for groceries about lOs per week, and I assert that you may go to the larger shops and not save more than one shil- ling as against taking 10s to the stores. What is the result? Would, or does the average working-man take the odd shilling to the bank, or is it spent on something he might really manage without? Suppose he takes it to the bank; in that case he has made 13 journeys to save 13 shillings, with interest a minus quantity, when, by spending the money at the stores he would have net- ted 21s 7d, besides interest as stated above. The differ- ence is 83 7d, besides almost forcing himself to save the other 13s. If working-men will only look at the ques- tion in this light it is evident they will raise themselves without the aid of McDougall's self-raising flour at any price.

The next point I notice is the general turnover,which, I believe, is nearer £1,200 than £l,OOO per quarter. I can assure " Looker on" that that is no small sum, and also that but for the .hated eredit he speaks of the sum would greatly increase. Let me inform "A Looker on" that if he could peep behind the scenes he would find a good many members spending a few shilling's at the stores, and a few somewhere else, for the simple reason that if they went to the stores altogether they would scion also go to the county court, and that, too, by the aid of the hated " tommy book" of former times. I can as- sure him I have myself been the means of inducing not a few to join the stores and pay off their old debts with what they could afford to spend there. I never lose an opportunity to advise anyone to obtain the despised bonus and five per cent., and to support a society that could pay 27s in the pound to-morrow. Well, Mr. Editor, with your permission, I will conclude by giving my readers two illustrations of a desire to go to this wonderfully extortionate place of mutual assist- ance, from which a " Looker on ' wishes to be sad. Pour years ago two of us seriously discussed the problem of getting out of debt, my friend being in for £2, and myself for .2.3 10s. With a small family it is something to clear that, and have your wages to join the stores with also. In twelve months my friend was clear, and I no nearer. Taking the bull by the horns, I laid my case before a mutual friend, who lent me the necessary four pounds, which I paid back in twelve months, and also paid up one of my shares with that deceptive bonus which people who are so blind cannot see. Let Looker on " cultivate the practice of advising working-men to avoid credit, and, when he has suc- ceeded, the prices between the Stores and the othershops will soon find their own level.—l remain, sir, yours truly, ONE WHO KNOWS.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

DAMAGING UNDERWOOD. At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Carter, labourer, pleaded guilty to destroying some underwood at Kingsley, the property of John Warburton on the 21. st February.— The gamekeeper to Mr. Leice;ter proved that the defen- . dant cut the underwood for pea-sticks. A great deal of damage had been done to the woods.—Defendant was fined 2s. 6d., Is. damages, and the costs, in all 12s. MEETING OF GAs SHAREHOLDERS.—At an extraordin- ary general meeting of the shareholders of the Frodsham Gas Company, Limited, Mr. H. Linaker in the chair, it was resolved unanimously that the following resolution, which was passed at the extraordinary meeting of the company held on the 4th February last—" That the Bill for dissolving the Frodsham Gas Company, Limited, and for re-incorporating the members thereof with others, and confernag powers on them for the supply of gas and water to the town of Fredsham and neighbourhood, and for other purposes, be approved, subject to such ad- ditions, alterations', and variations as Parliament may think fit to make therein," be confirmed. A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the proceedinv. FUNERAL OF MRS. PINK, OP N9ll/2X,—The funeral of Mrs. Pink, wife of Mr. Joseph Pink, of Norlev, who died Ori the 22nd ult., took place on Saturday. The Rev. C. R. Nunn' was the officiating clergyman. The arrange. silents were successfully carried out by Mr. Vert. The coffin, which was of polished oak, was supplied by Mr. Thomson the inscription on the breast-plate being : "Ellen Pink Died February 22nd, 1888. Aged 33 years." Flowers were sent by the following .—The Hon. Mrs. Lascelles, wreath; the Misses La.scelles, wreath; Mrs. George Egerton Warburton, cross; Mr. and Mrs. Vert, wreath; Mrs. Oxford, cross; the Misses Vert, wreath • Miss Falkner, wreath; Mrs. Cox, wreath; also a beautiful wreath bearing no name. The Vicar preached a sermon from St. Mark vii. 25, with special references to ..he death of Mrs. Pink. .WESLF.YAM IMPROVEMENT Ctass.—At 2 meeting of this class, held last evening week, the Rev. R. P. Berwick in the chair, the' President (Rev. J. Shipham) delivefel a lecture, the title of which was" Self —help and self edu- cation," in which he stated that in every department there were many who had raised themselves to- a higher , sphere by their own individual efforts. He believed that the law of progress was written on all the Almighty's works, and therefore we ought to go on in the improve- ment of our minds. He urged upon the members the necessity of considering what others have accomplished by perseverance, and to go and do likewise. The lec- turer then cited a number of men who have risen from the lower ranks of society, and who have won for them- selves a place of respect and honour, and this without , any extraordinary endowment. It might be asked, he said, by some people whether the Men alluded to had re- ceived higher and nobler gifts from God. To this ques- tion he might answer that he believed the majority of them were plan men. There might be •a something which is generally termed genius, but he believed this meant personal industry. Others have said genius was only common sense intensiged, or patience, or rather in- dustry and patience combined. He advised the mem- bers to understand thoroughly and master every branch , of the business or calling in which they were placed, but above all, to obtain religion. A hearty vete of thanks was then accorded to Mr. Shipham for his very able lec- ture. RELIGIOUS TRACT SOCIEIPS MEETING.—The annual meeting of the Frodsham branch of this society was held at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Mondays, under the presidency of the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, vicar of Kingsley. The Chairman said that one of the most important questions asked at the present day was, "How are we to reach the masses o'f the people?" A very good answer was given some time ago, namely, "bring the people into a personal contact with the Saviour." Therefore they could not have too much tract distributing. It did not matter much, the way in which that class of work was done, so long as the tracts were wisely chosen and given with a kindly word or two. He was surprised to hear people say they had no work to do, when this was just the sort required and . needed. Mr. S. Ormerod, the secretary to the branch, read the report of the past year's work. The total amount received in subscriptions, Sm., was £2O 10s. The average amount received for the past five years was £2O. Dr. Weaver proposed that the secretary's report be approved and adopted, and also that the officials connected with the branch be re-appointed. He remarked that the report presented was a much better one than had been given before, and he had pleasure in recommending its adoption. Mr. Richard Butcher, the deputation from the paiient society, seconded the proposition, which was carried. A vote of thanks to the chairman, and deputation, was proposed by the Rev. W. Fielding, of Aston, seconded by Mr. S. Walker, of Frodsham, and carried.

SUCCESS OF THE CHORAL SOCIETY. The Thursday evening a grand musical festival was held in the Music Hall, Chester, under the presidency of R. A. Yerburgh, Esq., 141. P. The chief attraction of the evening was a "Moral contest," for which the three I following choirs entered—The Holywell En-Harmonic, the Llyn-z-Pandy, and the Frodsham Choral Society. It fell to the lot of the latter to occupy, the stage •in turn I first, and the piece for competition was "When winds breathe soft" (Webbe.) The three choirs first sung separately, led by their respective conductors, and I afterwards they were, united and coiducted by Dr. J. C. Bridge. This gentleman was the adjudicator, and in giving his decision, said he had not the slightest hesitation in saying that the Frodsham Choral Society had fairly won the prize, which was £lO 10s. Immediately upon this intimation the audience burst forth in repeated rounds 9f applause, which were augmented in no small degree by the members of the successful choir. At 11-30 p.m. the quiet streets of Frodsham rang with the well-known "See the Conquer- ing Heroes come," sung by the choir and a large party of friends who had come to welcome them home, feeling sure that s?ccess would be theirs.
