Mr. Justice Grantham expressed his regret at the Liver- pool Assizes, on Thursday, that he could not order a whipping for burglars. • The Very Rev. William Corbet le Breton, Dean of Jer- sey, and father of Mrs. Langtry, • has died in London, after a protracted illness. Two tramcars came into collision near the foot of Wer- neth Brow, 01:ham, about five on Wednesday evening, and six passengers were injured. At Clonmel, on Wednesday, Mr. Pyne, M.P.. was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment, without hard labour, for a speech made by him on the 6th November. He was liberated on bail pending the appeal. At the Gateshead Police Court, on Wednesday, 170 miners employed by Messrs. Bowes ik.Co. at Felling and Wardley were fined 5s and costs each for having absented themselves from •work for four days without hating given notice.

div.head: EXAP
div.p: THE EXAP

THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued' front page 6.) EASTHAICHURifiIi.s "t '•`-1 A gentle air of sentiment has always blown about the canal scheme, and perhaps has not been without its effect on the popular imagination. In the early. days, when little was known about locks, there was' a notion that actual sea would ripple against our dock walls, and that, in the first of the morning perhaps, a keen nostril would be able to detect some faint odour of brine. But if we are not to hear the plash of salt waves-as "a sweet" inland murmur," a good deal of sentiment of a various kind still clings to the scheme—much of it no doubt about the ships' the canal is to bring us. We touch upon these airy' considerations because it-seems that our gain in, this respect is to be at the expense of certain neigh- bours at the other end of the canal. Eaatham cries I out against the inroads the 'Works are making on its beauty, and no doubt the canal will in some degree rob the Richmond of the Mersey of its charm. The village itself is half a mile from the line of the canal, but the Eastham-road comesinto actual touch with the works at the Ferry pier. Much of the fine woods 'between the village and the sea have been cut down, and in future the canal will bar free access to the shore. One would not like without good cause to let the ruthless steam digger loose on such a scene. It is beautiful even on these winter day, With the woods mere masses of umber and the lake-like estuary a bitter blue. But the needs of Manchester are imperious, and Eastham, must make the best of the case. Perhaps when the steam dig- ger has gone its way and the raw earth has re- ()covered its green, the place may stikl be something more than tolerable, even if the squat funnel of a steamer may sethetimes be visible through the trees, with or without a trail of smoke. Early in the "fifties" Hawthorne visited this'. country and spent some time in the Mersey district. With Eastham he was delighted. " Eastham," he writes in his "English Notes," "is the finest old English village I have seen, with a rural and pic- turesque aspect unlike anything in America, and yet possessing a familiar look, as though it were something I had dreamed abogt. . . . In the midst of it stood a venerable church of the common red freestone with a most reverend air, considerably smaller than that of Bebington, but more beauti- ful, and looking quite as old. There was ivy on its spire and elsewhere. It looked BO quiet and peaceful,.as if it had received the people into its low-arched door every Sabbath for centuries." The ivy noticed by the author of "Mosses from an Old Manse " was taken down some years ago. The Church was built about 1150, but of the original structure the tower alone remains. The font, carved Out of a solid block of red sandstone, is described as undoubted Saxon, and this of course would take it further back than 1150. In any case there seems no doubt that parts of the present building were standing when Richard's Crusaders returned from Palestine and the Saxon serf Gurth tended the pigs of Cedric in the Rotherwood forests. The nave dates from the time of the first Edward, and the aisles a century later. Several members of . the Stanley family are buried within the church. The dates on their altar tombs begin with 1612, and a i certain Sir Rowland Stanley s given out as dying "in the year of his age 96"—a man whose hair was white when the Armada set sail. In the old days life was long in this sleepy hamlet. The records on the graves in the churchyard tell of three lives which made out between them 279 years, and a yew tree still flourishes which was tknown as "the old yew of Eastham "six hundred years ago. The heart of the old tree has long since cruMbled away, but a vigorous shoot which starts out .of the trunk a few feet above the ground continues the ancient stream of life. The village clusters close about the church, and offers all sorts of broken out- line and some bewitching effects of colour. The voices of school children fill the air at times "like sunshine become audible," and when the chil- dren cease the .chorus.is taken up by the sparrows, with an occasional accompaniment from the village blacksmith. Such a place as this has to be grown; under no circumstances could it be made to order. The colour on some of the brick walls has of itself been the work of generations.fSmall wonder that in such a place the throb of the steam digger is heard with horror. -
—f`Sa

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

The material .for the effective carrying on of the work is continually being accumulated at Thelwall. As we mentioned last week, a considerable length of rail had been laid down and two or three locomotives placed upon it. During the present week more locomotives have been brought to the scene of operations, two of which bear the names of " Altrincham " and " Stret- I ford" respectively. Preparations are also being made for the erection of steam navvies, the parts of which are being placed on the ground, together with portable en- gines and numerous other apparatus. Sheds for Iva& ous purposes are being rapidly erected by the side of the i road, and n close proximity to the structure which shelters the steam saw. On the Lancashire side of the river behind Thelwall village there does not seem to be much machinery on the ground, but notwithstanding 1 this the heaps of soil from the excavations rapidly grow in size, and work there is evidently l'eing prosecuted with as much vigour as elsewhere. RUNCORN.

In this section the activity that has been displayed since the coMmencement of the operations is still continued , and the face of the country is rapidly assuming an aspect much different to that which the inhabitants have been accustomed to. Notwithstanding the frost and snow the American navvies have been hard at work at the Big Field end, and have removed an,immense quantity of sand and clay. The frost has, however, interfered with some other kinds of work, and a number of men have had to walk the streets for a few days. The first esti- mate of the amount of peat revealed on the marsh near the spoil bank is likely to be fully realised, and men have been employed in cutting it into blocks. At present it is too damp to be of much use, but the influence of a summer's sun will convert it into capital fuel. The rail- way lines have now been extended from the depot to a point about 200 yards above the works of Messrs. Wigg, Brothers and Steele; and at the commencement of the present week, an American navvy was fixed there, and has since been kept fully employed. The soil, &c., is conveyed to the spoil bank, at Norton ,by 'means of en- gines and waggons: It is expected that a second I navvy will be at work there in the course of a few days. MISSIONARY WORK.

Mr. Walker has recently appeinted a missionary to the Runcorn section in the person of Mr. John Watson, and the first service was conducted on Tuesday evening, in the Mission Church in Irwell-lane. This building had been kindly lent for the occasion. The attendance was of a very encouruing nature, and the service was of a suitable character. Mr. C. A. F. Gregson, the agent to the section, had been annormced to take the chair, but unfortunately he was unable to be present, and the duties of chairman were ably fulfilled by Mr. H. Gill, the cashier. Appropriate addresses were delivered by the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., of Holy Trinity Church; Mr. W. Shaw, the seamen's missionary; and by Mr. Watson. Gospel addresses are announced to be delivered every Sunday night at six o'clock, and navvies and their wives are particularly requested to attend. It should be stated that the services are undenominational. ACTON GRANGE.
The work here progresses. With the weather being dry, the water which has come into the cutting is not so troublesome, and it is now got rid of in a satisfactory manner.

The steam navvy has made short work of Bellhouse- lane, which is now a thing of the past. On Thursday afternoon a number of sightseers from Warrington and elsewhere stood amazed as they saw this steam navvy lift the solid road from its tenacious bed and de- posit it with a loud thud into the wagons. It was then taken away/ by the locomotive to the tip. near the wood. There is often a large numberof visitors to this section, especially oA Sundays. On the north side of the railway, near Mr. Ball's farm, men are at work with pick and spade on the solid rock, which here comes pretty near the surface. The debris is carried away by a locomotive under the two small railway arches into the fields beyond. A line of rail is shortly to be laid to extend to near Stockton Heath. CONTRACTOR'S VISIT.

Mr. Walker, the contractor, visited the line of work on Tuesday, going westwkrd by Acton Grange and Run- corn. We learn that he is so satisfied with the work and the German steam navvy that he has given an order for two more of these ponderous machines. Some idea of the magnitude of the whole of the present operations may be gathered from the list of the plant brsnk into use. There are already employed .40 locomotives, 18 team navvies, 7 excavators, 14 portable engines, 9 steam saw benches, 27 steam cranes 3 steam tugs, 14 flats and barges, 1,700 wagons, 2,g00 barrows, 5,000 tons of rails (distributed over the 10 miles covered), and 70,000 sleepers; and no less than 3,000 men are at work.

div.head: RIXTON IRLAM, &e.
div.p: RIXTON IRLAM, &e.

At Rixton and Mani the work prog,resses in all direc- tions. A considerable number of men are at work, and large embankments are being made with the soil that is being removed. Owing to the impetus given to trade, the tradesmen of Cadishead have of late been doing much better, a large proportimi of the men employed on the Irlam and Cadishead length having taken up their abode in the village. In consequence of the great de- pression in the fustian cutting industry, Cadishead has suffered very much, but the making of the canal is find- ing employment for a good deal of the surplus labour of the district.

div.head: BARTON:
div.p: BARTON:
Operations are being pushed forward with much rapi- dity- at Barton. This is very noticeable on • that portion e the Salford section near to the Barton corn mill, en

div.head: SATURIIVCr4
div.p: SATURIIVCr4

land adjoining Trafford Park. On this section, which is about four miles in length and extends from. Barton to nSalford, enurrittetqlrtnet% are engaged on the Trafford side felling timber .and rethoving surface earth. When th 4 rock is reached, blasting operations will commence, and it is proposed to afterwards use the rock for con- struction purposes. Materials for the prosecution of the ?fork are constantly arriving in this neighbourhood, and ildst Morley has obtained from the engineers of the section the contract for removing the necessary plant from eat- ricridt station fot use on the works. the soil on , this section is mostly of red sand and gravel, sand up to the present very little difficulty has been met with in exca- vating. •A raft has been constructed for carrying the Men te and from the Barton side of the river, and a large number of people, consisting for the most part of men on the look-out for a job, find their way to the works. 'Ale .centre of the canal at Barton will run where the old 'cora mill and Roman Catholic schools stand, and as a conse- quence those buildings will have to be removed.

SICK AND BURIAL FUND. Its stated that arrangements have been made by the contractor for the construction of the Ship Canal on, the Barton section to form a sick and burial fund for thermen and youths employed on the works. To provide for, this fund all men and boys engaged are to contribute from ,their wages 2.d per shift for the first three shifts made in each week. Subscribers will be entitled to IN per week, in case of sickness for the first three months, and 5s per week during the second three months. A SUGGESTION TO SHIPBUILDERS, , A circulqx in the following terms is being 'sent out to shipbuilders and shipowners: "Manchester,' February 124. 1888.'—Gentlemen,—We are requested by the Board of Directors to inform you that the railway bridges to be constructed across the Manchester Ship Canal have been designed to leave a clear headway of 75 feet above the water level. Perhaps you will be good enough to con- sider the advisability of altering your form of specifica- tion if you have been in the habit of providing your vessels with pole masts of a greater height than, say. 70 feet from light water line.—Yours faithfully, EGERTON OF TATTON, Chairman,; JOSEPH C. LEE, DEpUty-Cilair• man."
NORTHWICH DIVISION LIBERAL AMOCIATION. MEETING Or THE COUNCIL.

The annual meeting of the Council of the North- wich Division Liberal Association was held in the Central Hall, Northwich, on Saturday afternoon. The weather was highly unfavourable, but notwith- standing there was a good attendance of 'delegates from all parts of the division. Mr. John Thompson presided.

div.head: LETTER FROM MR. BRUNNER.
div.p: LETTER FROM MR. BRUNNER.

Mr. W. Handley read the following letter:- 132, Palace Chambers, Westminster, S.W., 21st Febru- ary, 1888. 14.1 y dear Handley,—Many thanks for your letter and circular. I am unfortunately unable to attend your meeting on Saturday next on account of a previous engagement. If I cduld be with you I should again endeavour to impress upon the members of the council my sense of the dignity of their office and .the great value I attach to the assistance they can give me in my work as a representative of the division. It is im- possible within the limits of a letter to say what ought to be said on this subject, and I will to-day confine myself to making one suggestion. If the council would appoint a committee with power to add to their number to report to a special meeting upon the Local Government Bill of the Government as to the amendments considered desir- able, and if the council thereupon passed a resolution setting forth the views of the council for my guidance, I should be enabled to speak with vastly increased authority in the House, and in committee.—Believe me, yours faithfully, JOHN T. BAIINNER.-Wm. Handley, Esq.

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.
• Mr. W. Handley, the secretary, ,read his annual rgport, which appeared in our issue of Saturday last. The sentiments • set forth were frequently cheered.

• nuteTtoN OF oriFicans, Mr. A. Fletcher mOved the re-election of Mr. E. H. Moss, Ravenscroft Hall, as president of the associa- tion. (Applause.) Mr. Moss took a most active in- terest in the work, and those who had any ac- quaintance with the way in which affairs were managed at Middlewich, must know the influence which Mr. Moss had in that district, and indeed throughout the division. Mr. Moss was a gentle- man who through evil report and good report ad- hered to his principles, and they could not have a worthier or a better president. (Applause.)—Mr. G. H. Deakin seconded the motion, which was heartily passed.—Mr. E. Milner moved that Mr. James Handley be elected chairman of the council. Ile remarked that Mr. Handley was a very good Liberal, and. it would be advantageous to have a chairman that resided at Runcorn, so that the sec- retary could communicate with him without diffi- culty.—The inotiou.was carried unanimously.—Mr. H. Bratt proposed that Mr. G. H. Deakin be chair- man of the executive, remarking that Mr. Deakin had occupied the . post in first-class style, and proved himself a regular attendant at the meet- ings. and a good. worker. Mr. T. Pickering seconded the motion, . which was carried unani- mously. Mr. Fletcher proposed that Mr. E. Milner be asked to accept the.' onerous office of treasurer, and that a vote of thanks be ,passed to him for his services in the past.—Mr. J. J. Dixon seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation.—Mr. G. H. Deakin proposed that Mr. Fletcher be re- elected honorary secretary. They could not pos- sibly select anyone better qualified; for Mr. Fletcher was an eminent gentleman of the penk and one with a legal mind.—Mr. Lidlsury had great pleasure in seconding the motion, which was carried tsetn. eon. —The following were elected co-optative members of the council: Messrs. W. Bunn, T. Taylor, and James Woodbine, Middlewich : D. Graham, W. Blagg. and J. Siddorn. Winsford : W. Rayner, Moul- ton : Thomas Hewitt, Marston; William Topham, Castle; D. Huges, North wich ; W. Norman and Dr. Mangan, Runcorn.

div.head: FINANCIAL STATSVSKT.
div.p: FINANCIAL STATSVSKT.

The Treasurer (Mr. E. Mimer)presented the financial statement. It appeared that tile receipts amounted to £228, and the expenditure £l7B. This left £5O in hand to meet liabilities amounting to £143, the deficit there- fore being £93 as- cogapared with £2O last year. The Treasurer pressed on the council the necessity of suppor- ting the association by subscribing to it. The principal expenditure was on registration. • This was very im- portant work, and it was reported, that Doncaster had been lost entirely through want of registration. It could not be done without expense, and they could reasonably expend £3OO, which wis not more than is per head Of the voters they had polled. Surely there ought to be no difficulty in raising that sum.—Mr. T. Gibson said a good many people did not understand that they had to pay to the council. Ile suggested that some one should be appointed at each club to collect the subscriptions.—After some discussion, it was decided on the. motion of Mr. Lidbury, seconded by Mr. Millington, that the attention of the district secretaries be called to the matter of collecting subscriptions.—The treasurer's statement was then adopted.

div.head: -FEDERATION.
div.p: THE -FEDERATION.

The following gentlemen were appointed delegates to the National Liberal Federation : Rev. F. Carter, Messrs. H. Bratt, F. J Thompson, T. Handley, G. H. Deakin, J. Millington, H. Capes. W. Molyneux, and W. Handley. Messrs. T. E. Ellis, M.P., E. H. Moss, and James Handley were elected members of the Executive of the Federation.

div.head: TS6 CLUBS.
div.p: TS6 CLUBS.

Mr. Pickering (Winsford), in pursuance of notice, called attention iotli the advisability of affiliating the local Liberal chibs with the association, and moved that the executive be instructed to devise a practical work- ing method, whereby every nlember of the association shall be a member of the local club, the clubs to be Un- der the control of the executive. He believed that such a scheme would be beneficial to the clubs and also to the association.—Mr. T. Clegg mentioned that several of the districts had no clubs.—Mr. J. Barrett (Clifton) said that was true. It was a shame to Runcorn that it should be so. The Tories had proposed to have one there but nothing came of it. Let the Liberals piopese to hi;m one, and have it. (Applause.) He would be one of the first on the list. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. H. Brett saw a great difficulty in dealing with the matter. It would be almost impossible for the association to man- age the affairs of the clubs.—Mr. T. A. Johnson con- tended that the resolution was contrary to the Home Rule principle.—Mr. T. Gibson said the Central Com- mittee would be able not only to look after the present clubs, but establish others where they were wanted.— Mr. Milner thought he,could promise that the Executive Committee would keep the matter in view, and give it their careful consideration. He reminded the members that the old idea of a political association was that it should be supported entirely by rich men, who wanted political power. Now things were different. Rich men could no longer be expected to pay money in order to secure political power, for they could not get it by so doing.—Mr. Pickering said that after that expres- sion of opinion he would not press his motion.—Mr. Fletcher suggested that it might be made an instruction to the execqtive to consider the matter. It was one of extreme importance to the Liberalism of the district. The existing clubs were not clubs for eating I and drinking, but for reading and discussion, and it was much to be desired that they should be still more deeply rooted than they were. He proposed that the question be remitted to.the execvtive,—Mr. T. Clegg seconded the motion, which was carried—The Chairman said he felt sure good would result from the discussion, and they would all be obligedto Mr. Pickering for bringing it for- ward. (Hear, hear.) .
THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.

It was decided to ask the executive to watch the Local Government Bill about to be introduced into Par- liament, and to convene a meeting of the Council to con- sider any amendments which might seem desirable.

NEXT yEETING,.. ; It was unanimously agreed to hold the next meeting of the Council at ilortliWicli.:=Thanks to the Chair- man, voted on the 'airiottory, of. Mr. U. Arrommnith, secondeFl by Mr. Barrett, 'brought-the proceedings to a close. ;

• ' RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The (fortnightly meeting :was held at Dutton Workbpuse on Tuesday. Colonel Ashton presided. and thbre were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. 'Lockwood, Messrs. Speakman. Grice, Light- burn, Aaron, Lewis, Stokes, Campkin, Parr, Smith, Turner, Hamilton, Brandreth, Wallington. Hadfle)cl, and H. Linaker (clerk).
MR. BRUNNER OFFERS HIS SERVICES-BOORISH BUHBLEDON. •_- _ _

The Clerk read the following correspondence which he had received :—" Runcorn, February 24th, 1888. I send you herewith a communication I have received, which I pass on to you, knowing it will receive your kind atten- tion. Mr. Brunner is desirous of being of use to his con- stituents, and would esteem any service he can render as representative of the division as a pleasure and duty. With kind regards, lam, faithfully yours, W. HANDLEY. —Here follows the communication referred to :—" Trin- ity Parionage, Northwich, 17th February, 1888. Dear Mr. Brunner,—l see that a Bill dealing with Industrial' Schools is about to be introduced by Mr. Matthews. Please examine clausb I now send you, and if possible get it inserted. Yours sincerely, RICHARD MARSH."— Clause :7--" When a child is sent to an Industrial School the Poor Law Guardians of the Union in which his parents reside shall determine what contribution should be made by such parents towards the cost of the child's maintenance, and shall in- struct their Relieving Officer • to collect such contribution."—The subjoined letter was attached. —" Dear Mr. Handley, The above letter is an instance of the help which constituents can give to their member. You remember the chat on that point with Mr. Brunner at Winnington. What do you think of his suggestion? Truly yours, T. E. Ellis? The Clerk then read a letter from Mr.. Brunner similg in terms with the one printed in extenso in the proceedings of the Rural Sanitary Authority. During the reading of those communications several members' remarked "Mr. Brunner again," and there was much laughter.—Mr. Hadfield: How he is shoving himself ahead.—Mr. Brandreth : What does he want to do.—The Clerk: To send copy of the Local Govern- ment Bill when printed. Mr. Hadfield moved that the letters lie on the table, and added Mr. Marsh seems to be a very modest man. (Laughter.)—Mr. Parr asked if it was Mr. Marsh, the nuctioneer.—The Clerk replied that Mr. Marsh was a parson.—Mr. Hadfield: He is a very modest Parson then.—Mr. Aaron: Let it lie on the table.—Mr. Parr: Better throw it in the fire. (Laughter).--Mr. Hadfield: Give it to you, Mr. Parr, to frame. (Renewed laughter.)—Mr. Parr I would not bestow a frame on it. • (Much laughter).—The letters , were laid on the table.
Daring these proceedings several members were absent engaged in cominittee work. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

The Rev. T. W. N. Tanner brought forward the estimates for the School Attendance Comtnittee, which showed that £BO would be required. A rate of a fifth of a pennyin the £ would produce £B9, and he proposed that such a rate be levied. The proposition was carried.

div.head: FINANCIAL MATTERS.
div.p: FINANCIAL MATTERS.

The Rev. J. Lockwood submitted the estimates for the ensuing half-year ending Michaelmas. The report showed that the total capital for the current half year was £7,628, and the probable expenditure was .estia mated at £6,040, which showed a probable bal- ance in favour of the Union at Lady Day of £1,578. The probable expenditure during the next half year was as under : School fees for non- pauper children, £23; Union charges, £4,653; county rate, £2,462; balance and contingency fund, £2,318 ; total, £9,456. After taking credit for the probable bal- ance at Lady Day the amount required by contribution orders from the overseen was £7,88. The rateable value of the Union as per valuation lists in force was £223,109, being an increase of £8,965 as comptnd with the corresponding period last year. The increase was , principally owing to the revaluation of the Manchester ; Ship Canal Company Bridgewater Undertaking, and other works. The increase to the Company was £7,849. The company had appealed to quarter sessions against their assessment. A rate of 80 in the £ would produce £7,901 15s 6d, and it was recommended that a call to that extent should be made upon the overseers. This rate was a halfpenny in the pound more than the call for the corresponding period last year.—lii the course of a brief discussion that ensued, Mr. Speakman explained that the Assessment Committee commenced the revalua- tion against the Bridgewater Navigation Company, and of course when the Ship Canal .Company purchased that undertaking the proceedings took their natural course. He seconded the adoption of the estimates.---. Carried.

div.head: WORKHOUSE CROWDED.-SHIP CANAL 'WORKERS.
div.p: THE WORKHOUSE CROWDED.-SHIP CANAL 'WORKERS.

The Master (Mr. Cunnah) reported that the Workhouse was crowded, and he asked the Board to consider the ad- visability of providing more accommodation.—lt was stated that this increase in the number of inmates was owing to the influx of people into the district in search 0 work on the Manchester Ship Canal.—Mr. Lockwood said when the Ship Canal 'works were in full opera- tion there would be thousands of men in the neighbourhood. There would not be work for all of them, and it , was only likely that a lot of them would have to go to the workhouse.—Mr. Hadfield said it would be yery hard upon the ratepayers if they had to pa 7. for the mereasecl accommodation.—Mr. Lightburn pointed out that the Union would not lose in the long run, because of the increase in the assessment.—Mr. Lewis suggested that the relieving officers should be in- structed to send as few people to the workhouse as possi- ble, and give relief outside.—Mr. Speakman moved that the subject be referred to the Supervision Committee.— The Clerk: To see if they can make provision for more men by a rearrangementof the house.—Mr. Speakman: yes.—The.motion was seconded and carried.—Mr. Parr asked in ease a man was injured on the Ship Canal works, were the employers liable.—The Clerk replied yes, if it was through the employer's neglect. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: BANKRUPTCY OF A RUNCORN • PITBLIQAN.
div.p: BANKRUPTCY OF A RUNCORN • PITBLIQAN.

Samuel Spann, a beerhouse keeper, of Runcorn, came before Mr. Registrar Nicholson, at the War- rington Bankruptcy Court, yesterday morning, to undergo his first public examination. In his state- ment of affairs supplied to the Official Receiver, it was stated that the debtor was adjudged a bank- rupt on his own petition on the Bth of February. The bankrupt set forth that up to 1865 he was a policeman, but in Nov. of that year he took the Mersey Vaults, in Mersey-street, Runcorn, a beer- house, -where he also carried on a wholesale bottling business. In 1883 he left there and took the Royal Oak beerhouse, which he left in Nov., 1885, to take the Boathouse Inn at Runcorn. Last Nov. he returnee to the occupancy of the Royal Oak. From 1880 to 1882 he had a branch store in Wilton-street, Northwich. He had no capital of his own when he com- menced business. Although he only suspended payment of his debts on the 7th of February, he first became aware that he was insolvent early in 1885, and he admitted that he had been cdntracting debts with a knowledge of his insolvency, without any other expectation of being able to pay than. that he hoped trade would be better in consequence of the Ship Canal. The deficiency amounted to £340 6s sd. The bankrupt estimated bad debts at £7 3s 4d, and law costs incurred since 1884 at £77 14s. The balance. of the deficiency he could only explain as being the excess of his household and personal expenses over his profits dur- ing the last three years. As he had not got proper books, he could not show what the profits had been, but the expenses of the business were so heavy., that his profits must have been extremely small. He had never taken stock, and he had no account showing what his income and household and personal expenditure had respec- tively amounted to during the past three years.. In 1881 he filed a petition at the Warrington Court for the liquidation of his affairs. His creditors then accepted a tomposition of 3s 6d in the £. His liabilities were over £1,200. Bad debts were the main cause of that failure. In September, 1884, owing to credit being suddenly stopped, he had to make a private arrangement with his creditors, who accepted a composition of 6s 8d in the £. His lidbilities at the time were about £3002 He had paid off all those creditors but two. He pawned his watch about three mcliaths ago for 13s. It cost £5, but at was 20 y9ars ago. He used the money to pay a bill. The gross liabilities were put 'down at £385 12. s 11d, and the deficiency at £340 es sd. Failure was attributed to bad debts and want of capital. Mr. A. B. Potter, the assistant official receiver, put a number of questions to the bankrupt, and, then asked for the adjournment of the examination. He remarked that it appeared that the debtor had actually been spending more than his takings.—Mr. Nicholson asked the debtor if he had any further reason to give why he had continued his business Noliert insolvent, except the one that he thought the Ship Canal would improve mat- ters.—The Debtor replied that he, like everyone else in Runcorn, had been looking forward to an improved state of things.

SANKEY SCHOOL SOARD.-it meeting of the members of the Sankey School Board was held in the Board Schools, Great Sankey, on Thursday. There were present Mr. J. C. Ridgway (chairman), the Rev. E. S. Jackson, and Messrs. Hatton, Grange, Skelton, and S. Sutton (clerk.) —Thoßev. E. S. Jackson, in'accordance with his notice at the last meeting, introduced the subject of the desir- ability of giving religious instruction in the school. Mr. Clarke, the headmaster, he said, had prepared a scheme Which, he thought, would hurt the susceptibilities of no one.—Mr. Clarke having explained his proposed method of giVing religious instruction, the meeting fully agreed that there was nothing objectionable in it, and it was decided that religious instruction should be given ac- cordingly.-.. This, was the only business of public in- terest.

(Giacomo Peed) on Friday attained the an'6e of 78 years, his Holiness having been born on March 2,1810, at Carpineto: - The hearing of the Charge against Mr. pilhooly, M.P., commenced at Schull, countpCork, on Friday, and was adjourged until to-day week. Another case of small-Pox has been reported to the authorities of Blackburn, and the patient has been re- indVed to the small-pox hospital, making seven persons in all attacked.

A BRIDEGROOM SHOT DEAD.—On Friday morning a, man named Thompson was shot dead in Knocka.muckley Church, while being married to a woman named-Moffat. The fatal shot was fired by a brother of his first wife. DEATH AT A FIINERAL.—MT. Alexander Johns, a Lon- don merchant, dropped dead at East Croydon Station, on Friday morning, on his way to Caterham, to attend the funeral of Mr. Clarke, the editor of the ' Christian Wqrld." Mr. Gladstone has been the recipient ' of a memorial signed by two hundred Church of England clergymen declaiing the right hon. gentlefnan's policy tow,ards Ireland to be the only one consistent with justice and L charity.

A Lorair FARMER.—A small tenant farmer. named Martin Hind, residing at Fiddington A*hurch, near Tewkesbury, has just received intimation to the effect tlot he is the probable heir to the estate of a lately deceased uncle who emigrated to South America many years ago, and lately died worth over £200,000. RESIGNATION OF AN M.P.—The Earl of March, who sits in the House of Commons as a Conservative member for the Chichester Division of Sussex, on Friday morning announced his resignation for private reasons. The seat was not contested in 1886. Lord Walter Gordon Lennox is announced as his successor.

THE Local, GOVERNMENT BILL.—On Friday afternoon ; Lord Salisbury received at the Foreign- Office a deputa- tion from the Proportional Representation Sotiety. After 1 speeches from Mr. Courtney and other gentlemen, Lord 1 Salisbury, in reply, said his Local Government. Bill was on the point of being introduced into Parliament, and his mouth was closed. He thanked them for the lucid explanations they had given him of Their system, and would carefully consider them. LIVERPOOL BREWERS AND MR. JUSTICE GRANTHAM.— On Friday morning, Mr. Addison, Q.C., M.P., speaking on behalf of the Liverpool Brewers" Association, made a representaan to Mr. Justice Grantham with referenoe to the rentals made by his lordship in the case of a man named Gordon, convicted of attemped wife murder. Mr. Justice Grantham, in reply, said that he had not uttered the remarks without full consideration. It was impossible to see diet after night the drunkenness and offences committed without being, convinced that people were getting drunk somewhere. It was to the interest of the trade to sell as much liquor as they could, and al. though many brewers did not care to allow their managers to encourage drunkenness, still there were managers who did it.

div.p: THE ATTACK ON BRIi'ISH ISHERME.N.
Bausseui, FRIDAY AFTERNOON. -- The tribunal, at Bruges, has condemned to imprisonment and fine ,39 Belgian fishermen convicted of attacking British fisher- men at Ostend, last 4ugust.

div.head: CROWN PRINCE.
div.p: THE CROWN PRINCE.

According to a Berlin telegram, Queen Victoria in- tends to pay a very short visit to the Crown Prince and Princess in the second half of this month on her journey South. His Royal Highness shows no distinct signs of improvement.
LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at four o'clock.

MISCELLANEOrs.—The Marquis of LOTHIAN, replying to Lord Norton, said the Scotch Technical Instruction Act had not yet come into operation. A bill for England would shortly be introduced.—The Lunacy Acts Amend- ment Bill, which is the same as last session, was read a second time.--Lord STANLEY stated that the Railway Rates Bill would be taken in Committee on the. 13th inst. Thellouse then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met aethree o'clock: QUESTIONS.—The HOME SECRETARY, replying to MT. Firth, said 380 men had been added to the. Metropolitan Police Force, which now amounted to nearly 1,500 men. —Mr. Repos, replying to Mr. Mowbray, said the scheme of the Halfkienny Post Company will not directly inter- fere with the revenue. The envelopes of the company would only be allowed to pass through the Post Office under certain regulations. SIR J. GORST, replying to Mr. Atkinson, said regulations affecting the sale of opium. and spirits were now under the consideration of the Government of India.—The Hoax SECRETARY, replying. to Mr. Herbert Gladstone, said he had ditected inquiry into the ease of alleged burial alive at Leeds cemetery. THE RIGHT OF PUBLIC MEETING .—The adjourned de- bate on Sir C. Russell's motion relating to meetings •in Trafalgar-square was resumed.—Mr. Bnaor.stain moved the following addition to the motion: " In the opinion of the House it would ensure much greater confidence in the administration of the law if a full public inquiry was made into the alleged unlawful assembling in Trafalgar-. square on Sunday, the 13th November, and the conduct of the police connected therewith." He then made a charge against the police of having assaulted the people after they had been taken into custody.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL complained that the last speaker had kept back the names of parties in cases of alleged assault until he Could an- nounce them in that House. He supported every prin- ciple of law laid down.by the Home Secretary.—Sir W. -HARCOURT insisted that the Government had invaded that right of the people as to public meeting. He blamed the Government for want of common sense in all they had done in the matter.—Mr. WHI'TMOII.E opposed the motion and approved the action• of. the Government.— Mr. LAWSON supported the motion for inquiry; and, advo- cated local control over the police.

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

[FROM OUR OWN CORREBPONMINT.I 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. • The activity of :the previous week has been succeeded during the past by activity in two or three leading stocks, but such activity has not been healthy, being due en- tirely to heavy selling, with the natural result of con- siderable fall in prices. The most notable has been that of the Grand Trunk Railway. The selling in this stock commenced towards the close of last week, and continued without intermission into the middle of thii, when a slight reaction took place, checking further fall, and causing a slight rebound. It .is noteworthy that the present price of (hand Trunk Second Preference is actually 25 under the price at which they stood last September. From this fact investors, weighing the pros and cons, will be able to form their own opinion, which, for all practical purposes, would be as good as anyone else's, as to a, probable rise in the near future. It must net be forgotten that traffic returns have recently been unusually bad; but, on the other hand, it must also be remembered that this year the ctimpany has been able to declare a small dividend which they were unable to do a year ago. The other most active marwet has been in copper. In this, it need hardly be said, that Rio Tintos have ab- sorbed most attention. At the end of last week they closed at thelowest point they have touched sipce the syndicate took them in hand. Since then there has been considerable rise, and although, at the time of writing, they are not at the best point touched this week, there is a probability of their still going better for a time, but we should certainly not even sugg'est speculators giving a thought to them for a rise. In our opinion they must inevitably go back to the price at which they stood last September. At the same time we believe the French Syndicate is powerful enough to keep control of them for some time longer. . The mining market has been especially dull during the past week, and as a consequence there has been a re- lapse in prices. liad this state of affairs been even normal, there can be little doubt that by this time a rise

would have occurred in many of these shares, especiallY the:lndian mines. We are of opinion that the risC is only postponei, and is certain to occur, at any rate, a 5 far as Indian mines are concerned, before long. In these Mysore Gold, Orregurn, and Nundydroogs are likely to be the first to improve; Mysore Gold especially should show considerable advance on the present price. . , In miscellaneous mines, Don Pedros, Pines Altos and Esmeraldas also promise an early rise. Diamond 'Laren continue to occupy attention. • The reported amalgama- tion of De Beers with Central Kimberly caused these ' shares to go £2 higher in a day, and it is stated that one of the leading financial houses in London has been buy- ing 'wry largely, and in some quarters it is expected . that De Beers will before long touch 40. Whether this be so or no, the price is too prohibitive, in our opinion, for anionethen the professional speculator to have any- thing to do with. The miscellaneous market continues very quiet, and in many instances show cordiderable downward ten- dency. The brewerie9 are weaker, as also are Elotelriitt and kindred companies. On the other hand, R. Bell and Sons have recovered the loss of the previous week.

' Mr: Evelyn, who tesig,ned ,the Conservative seat for Deptford , because he does not agree •With the Coereion Policy of the Government, is just now the special' object' of 'the malice of his party. ELOPEMENT OF A MINISTER WITH A LADY CHORISTER. Much excitement has been caused in Warrington and Eccles by the elopement of a minister of the Reformed Church of England with a member of big choir. The minister, formerly settled in Warring- ton, who is about thirty-six years of age and good looking, went to the place from the South of Eng- land about four years ago, and soon gained the re- spect of his new congregation. A few months ago it was noticed that he paid very marked attention to the lady mentioned, and then the trouble began. The youdglady is about twenty years of age, of prepossessing appearance, and has several time sung at concerts in Manchester. On Monday week she had an engagement at Southport, and the rev. gentleman accompanied her. They did not return, and it was subsequently discovered that they had Set sail from Liverpool to America. The minister was married: and leaves two children.
